I

Part Two · Chapter I

Why we get out of tune: communication at home

Why two kind, reasonable people can end up in a tangle neither of them started, and how to get back in step.

In this chapter

  1. The tangle often isn’t about the words
  2. Nearly in step is the noisy part
  3. Three things knock you out of tune
  4. Stress changes your station
  5. Nobody has to be wrong
  6. Get back in tune before you carry on
  7. Go back in with a clear sentence
  8. Small daily check-ins keep you in tune
  9. Faith, culture and family voices
  10. On your own: your side of the tuning
  11. One example, followed through
  12. Common mix-ups

At a glance

  • A clash is often about how things were said. Pace, tone and urgency can be out of step even when both of you mean well.
  • Nobody has to be wrong. Say that you are out of tune, pause with a time to come back, and slow down.
  • Go back in with one clear sentence that says what happened, how you feel and what you would like.
  • A 90-second daily check-in keeps small drifts small.

Tuesday, 6:40pm

“I said I’d do it.”

“I know. I’m just asking when.”

“Why does it matter when?”

“It doesn’t, I just…”

Four sentences later nobody is talking about the trash. Somebody has brought up last Christmas. Neither of you could point to the moment it turned.

The radio picture in this chapter is my own. When two people who care about each other keep missing, what’s usually lacking is timing and a shared way of putting things, and this chapter is an attempt at the shared way.

Quickly: the trash is the surface. Underneath, two different paces, one fast and one slow. Underneath that, two bodies in two different states at the end of a long day. The roots are signal and noise, and state and setting. Then slowly, one knob at a time.

  1. The tangle often isn’t about the words.

    Two people can each say something perfectly reasonable and still clash, because the tone underneath doesn’t match. Think of two radios slightly out of tune with each other. Together they make a crackle neither of them was making on its own.

    “Is anyone using the oven tonight?” Lisa asked. Simple question. She had a lasagna in mind. Her roommate went pink and said, “Why, did I leave a mess?” and there was a pause in which the baking pan from Sunday, still soaking, became the only thing in the room. “I meant the lasagna,” Lisa said eventually. “I know,” said the roommate, who hadn’t known, and went and washed the tray.

    Dig deeper: the radio static

  2. Nearly in step is the noisy part.

    Radios on completely different stations don’t whistle at each other. The whistle comes when they’re close but not quite matched, which is why people who know each other well still clash. Research suggests we check our meaning less with people we’re close to, because we assume they already understand.

    Two sisters who are on the phone every single day argue about vacation plans far more than either of them ever does with the cousins they see once a year, at christenings and funerals. The cousins get things spelled out. The sisters get shorthand, half a sentence, “you know what I mean.” Quite often they don’t.

    With someone close to you, check one meaning today. “Just so I’ve got this right, you mean…?” It feels a bit formal, which is rather the point.

    Dig deeper: why close can be noisy

    Tidbit

    Compare your daily rhythms: whose engine runs fast in the morning, and whose at night? Different speeds aren’t wrong, they’re just different.

    Tool: Rhythms side by side spreadloveandacceptance.com/tools/frequency-calibration

  3. Three things knock you out of tune.

    Pace is one, and tone is another, as when a plain update lands as a complaint. The third is urgency, since “when you get a chance” can mean tonight to one person and some time before Easter to another. Texts lose most of their tone, so urgency is especially easy to misread there.

    We think our tone travels Across five experiments, people writing emails overestimated how well readers would pick up their tone, sarcasm or seriousness, largely because they couldn’t hear their own message without their own voice in it.

    Kruger, Epley, Parker and Ng (2005) · Strong: several experiments, widely cited

    Between meetings, Vikram texted his business partner two words. Need to talk. She read it as a crisis and lay awake until two in the morning running through every disaster available, including the bank, the landlord and a client she’d always slightly distrusted. At nine he called. It was about the printer. She has since asked him, politely and also not entirely politely, to add a time and the word “printer.”

    Ways to say it “By when would be good?” “Is this an update, or a worry?”

    Dig deeper: pace, tone and urgency

  4. Stress changes your station.

    When you’re tense you may talk faster and hear a pause as a snub. When you’re tired and low, your replies get slower and shorter. The Nervous System Ladder (spreadloveandacceptance.com/quick-checks), a thirty-second self-check, gives you a best guess at which state you’re in. People’s ordinary rhythms differ too, before stress even arrives, and Rhythms side by side (spreadloveandacceptance.com/tools/frequency-calibration) lets you compare whose engine runs fast in the morning and whose at night.

    Barry comes in off a night shift at the depot and his son asks him about Saturday. He gets “Fine” and “Yep” and “Later.” His son decides, on the spot, that his dad doesn’t care about Saturday or, by extension, him. Barry is simply running on empty after ten hours of forklifts and a forty-minute drive home with the window down to stay awake. He’d have told you so if he’d had any words left. He went to bed.

    Dig deeper: how stress shifts your tune

  5. Nobody has to be wrong.

    Two radios that both work perfectly will still crackle if they’re slightly off, and arguing about whose fault the static is won’t clear it. Retuning will, which just means getting back in step.

    On the doorstep, coat still on, Sylvia tells her grown-up son he looks tired. She means it as care. He hears “you’re not coping,” which is what he has been privately worrying about all week, and says “Thanks, Mom” in a voice that could strip paint. Both of them are right about what they meant and what they heard. That’s exactly why arguing about it goes nowhere. They manage to get through the visit, just, and both feel bad about it on the way home.

    You could say “I don’t think either of us meant it that way. Can we try that again?”

    Dig deeper: taking the blame out

  6. Get back in tune before you carry on.

    Say out loud that you think you’re out of sync, and check how tense you are. Either of you can call a pause, and whoever pauses names a time to come back. Slow down, take shorter turns, and only then go back to the actual topic.

    Two students sharing a room in the dorms agreed a pause word one calm Sunday. They picked “static,” mainly because it made them laugh. Three weeks later, at one in the morning, in the middle of a fight about someone’s music, one of them said it, through gritted teeth. They stopped. Both lay there fuming in the dark. They came back to it at nine the next evening, as agreed, and worked it out in ten minutes with headphones, a second set of headphones and a slightly sheepish package of cookies.

    Dig deeper: the four steps to retune

  7. Go back in with a clear sentence.

    The first three minutes In 124 newlywed couples, how the first three minutes of a disagreement went predicted which couples had divorced six years later. It’s one lab’s sample and not a crystal ball, but it’s a good argument for opening gently.

    Carrère and Gottman (1999) · Moderate: one research group’s sample; striking, not widely replicated as a predictor

    When you go back to the topic, say what happened, how you feel and what you’d like, in that order and in one go. “The trash goes out early on Wednesday. I get anxious when they’re late. Could you put them out tonight?” Or, from one co-parent to the other, on a Sunday evening, “The swimsuit wasn’t in the bag and I felt stressed at drop-off. Could you pack it on Sunday nights?” Write one about something small before you need it, so the shape is in your hand when you do.

    Dig deeper: going back in

    Professor Puddles

    When you go back in, one clear sentence beats a speech. Write it down first. Speeches have a way of growing.

    Workpaper WP-09: Say it so it lands spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-09

  8. Small daily check-ins keep you in tune.

    A short chat each day, like the 90-second daily check-in (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-13-daily-check-in), makes tiny corrections before small things drift into a big fight. Habit research suggests small routines at a regular time are easier to keep than big ones done rarely. The quiet, easy stretches are the ones that drift most, so keep it going even when nothing seems wrong (see Complacency, spreadloveandacceptance.com/complacency).

    Orla is in Chicago and Marc is in Toronto. Every morning each of them sends one 90-second voice note, usually something like “Trash went out, my boss is still weird, I miss you.” On the weeks they forget, they notice it by Thursday, usually as an odd phone call about nothing in particular that leaves them both slightly put out.

    Ways to say it “Today I was carrying quite a lot. One thing I liked today was…”

    Dig deeper: staying in tune

Your part, and only your part. You control what you send, whether you check how it landed, and whether you step out to retune. You don’t control how it’s heard or how fast the other person settles. Matching energy here means matching care and effort, never volume: if someone gets louder, you don’t have to follow. Stay at your level, and give the conversation the energy it gives back. More in Your wiring, weather and words (page 33)

Saturday, 10am

“The spare room needs sorting at some point.”

She meant this month. He heard today, has already canceled soccer in his head and is quietly furious about it. By lunchtime you’re both upset about a room nobody has touched. When you finally stop and ask each other what “at some point” meant, it turns out you still don’t agree.

zqaxchapterx1xxfaithxcultureqzFaith, culture and family voices

For many couples, faith is where they turn first, and a shared faith can be one of the strongest tools for staying in tune. Praying together, or a quiet moment after worship, can serve as a daily check-in. Some couples each pray on their own before they come back to a hard talk, with the pause still ending at a named time. Someone in your community you both trust can be a good first person to talk to.

Emeka and Ngozi, married twenty-six years, do their monthly look-back on a Sunday after church, over lunch, with the radio off. When a talk gets heated, either of them can say, “Let’s pray on it and come back at eight,” and at eight they do. Emeka says this works about nine times in ten. Ngozi says eight.

Culture shapes how you talk, too. In many families, respect for elders decides who can speak plainly to whom, and one habit helps a great deal. Each of you speaks to your own parents and relatives, once you’ve agreed the message together.

Words to try “Can we pray about this and talk again tonight?” “Mom, we love you, and we’ve thought about it carefully. This year we’ll visit in August instead of at Easter.”

From two faiths or cultures? See Two faiths or cultures, one family (spreadloveandacceptance.com/two-faiths). Dig deeper: faith, elders and family far away

On your own: your side of the tuning

Getting out of tune takes two, but retuning can start with one. You can learn your own pace and your own sense of urgency, so you notice when you’re the one running fast or slow. Learn your early signs of drifting. A clipped reply is a common one. So is a sudden urge to win. Learn how you take words in best and say it, once (“I hear things better in writing”). When you drift, step out, settle, come back. You don’t need anyone’s permission for that. Hamid lives alone and has noticed that his texts come out curt when he’s tired, so he now waits until morning to answer anything that matters (more in On my own, spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own).

One example, followed through

Cerys, Marisol and Dougie share a house and a car. Cerys and Marisol talk fast, while Dougie talks slowly and thinks before he does it. At house meetings he kept getting talked over, and for a while the other two took his silence as agreement. It came out in March, when he said, quite mildly, that he had never actually agreed to the new car schedule. Marisol said “Since when?” and Dougie said “Since always,” and there was a long, uncomfortable pause. They tried a simple change, a round where each person speaks once before anyone answers. It felt stilted, and Cerys kept wanting to jump in and sat on her hands, literally. By the third meeting Dougie was saying more, and the schedule he suggested is the one they use. Some evenings it still turns into two fast talkers and one quiet one, until somebody says “round” and they reset. Help by relationship (spreadloveandacceptance.com/by-relationship) has pages for many other kinds of shared life.

Two ways to read this

Out of tune, both ways

Some people think by talking and need the answer right away. Others think first and talk second, and a quick reply asked for too soon comes out wrong. If you talk to think, the slower person’s pause isn’t agreement, and it isn’t a protest. It’s thinking. If you think first, the fast talker isn’t trying to win. Out loud is where their thinking happens.

Where the fields meet. Music has a name for a good conversation: call and response, one phrase answering another at a tempo both can keep. Neurobiology explains why the tempo slips, since your state sets the volume, and a stressed body changes station without asking you.

Common mix-ups

Retuning isn’t giving in, because you still come back to the topic, at a time when you can hear each other. Being out of sync doesn’t mean one of you is wrong, either. Two fair points in two different tones will still clash. And a pause never means the topic is dropped, since a pause comes with a time to come back, or it isn’t a pause.

To try it, agree a shared phrase while things are calm (“I think we’re out of tune” does fine) so that it works as a signal when you need it. For a week, each of you note one moment you felt out of step, and on the weekend compare whether it was mostly pace, tone or urgency. Rewind the talk (spreadloveandacceptance.com/carrier-wave-decoder), Say it so it lands (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-09-say-it-so-it-lands) and the 90-second daily check-in are free on the site.

A pause is for both of you. If one person is never allowed to pause, or a “pause” is used to punish with days of silence, that isn’t retuning.

II

Part Two · Chapter II

Is the split working? A fair look at chores at home

One gentle question: can the way you share the work keep going, or is one of you quietly running on empty?

In this chapter

  1. Look at the month, not last night
  2. Three things go in
  3. Balance: how the hours split
  4. Ownership: does each job have a name?
  5. Stress: how full each stress tank is
  6. One number comes out, from 0 to 1
  7. Start with the biggest shortfall
  8. It judges the setup, never a person
  9. Words this chapter uses
  10. On your own: is your own load working?
  11. One setup, looked at twice
  12. Common mix-ups
  13. Small children and a new baby
  14. If only one of you wants to try this
  15. More for your situation

At a glance

  • Look at the month, not last night, using what you both wrote down.
  • Three things go in, which are how the hours split, whether each job has a name, and how full each person’s stress tank is.
  • One number comes out, from 0 to 1. Start with whichever part pulled it down most.
  • It judges the setup, never a person, and it is where a talk starts.

Any given week

One of you is quietly doing eleven small things a day that the other has never had to think about, like the trash schedule and the fish food, the reply to the school, the dentist reminder, and the bit at the bottom of the shopping list that just says “bulbs?”

When the other one says it feels pretty even, they mean it. From inside their own week, it does.

Eleven small jobs a day, seen quickly. On the surface, a split that feels even to one person. Underneath, jobs with no owner. Underneath that, stress tanks at very different levels. The roots are ownership and structure, and quiet incentives. Then the chapter takes the three parts of the score in turn.

  1. Look at the month, not last night.

    Ask whether the split is working and the answer usually comes from whatever happened most recently, which is usually last night’s pans. This chapter asks a calmer question, using what you both wrote down. Ask it again every few months, even when things seem fine, because a split that worked once can quietly go stale.

    Two roommates had one truly terrible week of dishes in May, the kind where you wash a fork in order to eat with it. They were all set for a big fight. Then they looked at the whole month, written down, and it was three ordinary weeks and one exam week. The fight didn’t happen, which was almost a disappointment after all that build-up. They bought paper plates for exam week and left it at that.

    Dig deeper: what the check is for

    Sugarfoot

    One bad evening isn’t the whole story. Give it a month, then run the check together, slowly, with something to eat.

    Tool: Fair split check: this week spreadloveandacceptance.com/is-the-setup-working

  2. Three things go in.

    The first is how evenly the hours are shared. The second is whether every regular job has a clear owner, from the job list in One owner per job (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-03-one-owner-per-job). The third is how stressed each of you already is from everything else going on. A workpaper is one of the site’s free fill-in worksheets. You don’t need any of them to start, since rough notes on the back of an envelope do fine.

    You could say “Let’s each bring our own numbers, so neither of us has to guess.”

    Dig deeper: where each number comes from

  3. Balance: how the hours split.

    From your week-long logs, work out each person’s share of the hours. An even split scores 1 and one person doing everything scores 0, whichever person it is. If you’ve agreed an uneven split that suits you, perhaps because one of you works longer hours outside the home, compare against that split instead. With three or more of you, compare each person’s share with an even share (100 divided by the number of people) or with the split you agreed. Three partners who log 30 hours of home jobs between them, at 15, 9 and 6, would each have 10 as an even share. The “Who does what?” page (spreadloveandacceptance.com/lemonade-stand), where each person lists their hours, does the arithmetic for you.

    Everyone’s share comes to more than 100% In a classic set of experiments, spouses asked for their own share of joint jobs gave answers that, added together, usually came to more than 100%. Nobody was lying. We simply remember our own contributions better, which is the best argument I know for writing the week down instead of guessing.

    Ross and Sicoly (1979) · Strong: a classic, widely replicated finding

    Log one week each, and put in the small jobs that take under ten minutes. Those are the ones that go missing. They are often the ones that start the fights, too.

    Dig deeper: the balance score

  4. Ownership: does each job have a name?

    Each job gets two names. The owner does the job from start to finish. The backstop notices if it slipped and checks in gently, which is very different from supervising. It can be the same person, though a second name gives the job a gentle check. Count the jobs that have an owner and divide by all the jobs on the list, and leave the unowned jobs on the list, because they matter most. A decision you make together, such as which school, can be marked “Both (decide together)” and counts as owned. A job that needs doing gets one name.

    Most of what goes wrong in shared work isn’t incompetence. It’s unclear ownership: work that belongs to everyone belongs to no one, and it quietly lands on whoever notices first.

    Two sisters care for their dad. Nobody owned his prescription refills. For two weeks each of them thought the other had ordered it, and each, it turned out, had thought about calling to check and hadn’t, so as not to seem pushy. He ran out on a Sunday. The late-night pharmacy was forty minutes away.

    Dig deeper: the ownership score

    Professor Puddles

    A job without a name tends to land on whoever notices first. Write one owner next to each job, and the guessing stops.

    Workpaper WP-03: One owner per job spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-03

  5. Stress: how full each stress tank is.

    Each of you rates how full your own stress tank is with How much are you carrying? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-02-how-much-are-you-carrying), where a higher score means more stress. Under 0.30 is light, 0.30 up to 0.60 is medium, and 0.60 or more is high. The score uses the average of your two scores, but if either of you is at 0.60 or more, talk about that first, even when the overall result looks fine. A setup that only works when you’re both well rested can’t last, so more stress lowers the result.

    How loaded it feels The Perceived Stress Scale, one of the most used stress questionnaires, asks how unpredictable, uncontrollable and overloaded life has felt lately, and its scores track symptoms of depression and illness. That’s close to what the stress tank asks: not how much happened, but how loaded it feels.

    Cohen, Kamarck and Mermelstein (1983) · Strong: one of the most widely used stress questionnaires

    Doreen is raising her two grandchildren and scores 0.70. Her son, who helps on weekends, scores 0.35. The average looks fine, but Doreen’s 0.70 is the headline, whatever the average says, and her son, looking at the two numbers side by side, went quiet for a long time. Each of you scores your own tank on the same day, before you look at the other’s.

    Dig deeper: the stress score

  6. One number comes out, from 0 to 1.

    A result of 0.70 or above reads as working well, meaning the setup is holding. From 0.40 up to 0.70 it reads as needs a look, because something is drifting, often who owns what, and below 0.40 it reads as needs a rethink, together. The result is called the setup score. It is a simple weighted sum, in which the hours count most, then the owners, then stress, and although it looks like a probability it isn’t one.

    Two friends who run a café together scored 0.55. So nothing was broken, just something drifting, and it took them about four minutes to find it, which was the Monday ordering. Each of them had assumed for months that the other did it, and it had been getting done, more or less, by whoever panicked first on Tuesday morning. Write the date next to your number, so you can compare next month.

    Dig deeper: the formula and what each range means

  7. Start with the biggest shortfall.

    The single number matters less than which of the three parts pulled it down most. The shortfall is how far one part fell below the most it could add, and in the middle band it’s often ownership, which is why the calculator suggests One owner per job first. A separated couple scored 0.62 and found their biggest gap was that nobody owned the school forms. That was the only thing they changed that month, and both of them were quietly relieved it wasn’t something bigger.

    Ways to say it “Which part pulled the number down most? Let’s start there.”

    Dig deeper: reading your result

  8. It judges the setup, never a person.

    When a measure becomes a target Goodhart’s law, from an economist writing about monetary policy, says a number tends to stop telling you anything once people are pushed to hit it. That’s the reason this score is for looking at together and never for winning.

    Goodhart (1975) · Moderate: an economist’s observation, later generalized and widely seen in practice

    The number isn’t a verdict on who’s better or whether the relationship works. It’s where a conversation starts, never how one ends.

    “So I’m the problem,” said Lee, looking at 0.35.

    “No,” said his partner. “The bathroom hasn’t got an owner and you work nights.”

    They started there. Before you begin, agree that either of you can say “pause” and come back later.

    Dig deeper: what the number is not

Your part, and only your part. The score describes the setup you share, but your levers are your own: your jobs, your hours and what you agree to take on. You can propose a fix; you can’t make the other person accept it. If the balance stays one-sided, step your load back toward your share on purpose, and say so kindly. Matching effort with effort protects your stress tank, and your tank is part of the score too. More in Your wiring, weather and words (page 33)

Sunday evening

Two week-long logs. Two cups of tea. One list has 31 rows and the other has 18, and for a moment neither of you says anything and the fridge hums.

“I honestly didn’t know about half of these,” one of you says.

“Which half?”

Words this chapter uses

A log is a simple list of the jobs you did this week and roughly how long each took. The owner does a job from start to finish, including remembering it, and the backstop notices if a job slipped and checks in gently. Your stress tank is how much stress you’re already carrying from the rest of life. The setup is the way you share the work right now, which can always be changed, and the setup score is the one number from 0 to 1 that sums up the three readings. Invisible jobs count too. Planning meals, remembering birthdays, booking the vet and noticing that the soap is running low all belong in your log.

On your own: is your own load working?

You can ask the same question of your own week. Are you spending more energy than comes back? Add up what you carry, jobs and worries both, and set it beside what refills you. If it runs in the red, change your side, by dropping, delaying, asking or saying no kindly. A limit describes your supply. It says nothing about your worth. After her breakup, Leanne had the children every other week and filled the quiet weeks with favors for friends, including one memorable assemble-it-yourself dresser that took nine hours and a hospital visit (her thumb). Writing it down showed her she never rested (more in On my own, spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own).

Words to try “I’d love to help, and I can’t this week. Can I let you know next week?”

One setup, looked at twice

Three people share an apartment above a bakery, and everyone agrees that cleaning matters while nobody owns the bathroom. Their first check scores 0.67, and the biggest shortfall is ownership: eight of the twelve jobs have a name, and the bathroom, the trash, the recycling and the hallway don’t. They give each of those four jobs an owner and a backstop. A month later, with the hours and their stress tanks about the same as before, the score is 0.79. Ownership went from 0.67 to 1.00, and that part counts for 0.35 of the score, so it adds 0.12. The bathroom is better. The recycling is still a sore point, because the one who owns it works late on collection night, and that’s the job they’re arguing about next. Shift work, illness and caring can all make hours look even while sleep or energy is not, and an uneven split agreed on purpose can be the fair one (see Different hours, spreadloveandacceptance.com/different-hours, and When one of you is sick or disabled, spreadloveandacceptance.com/when-one-is-ill).

Two ways to read this

Redoing a job, two ways

Some people care most that a job got done. Others care how it was done, because things have a system and a cup in the “wrong” place means hunting for it later. If you care that it’s done, a quiet reload of the dishwasher can feel like your work was graded. If you care about the system, saying the reason (“The bowls go at the back so the door shuts”) turns a silent redo into a plan you can share.

Where the fields meet. Politics would say a home is a small government, and a rule lasts when the people who live by it helped make it. That is why the score is filled in together, from both people’s own notes. The roots are ownership and structure, and quiet incentives.

Common mix-ups

A low number doesn’t mean the relationship is failing. It means the current setup needs changing, and setups change all the time. Please don’t guess the numbers. A guessed number is a feeling with a decimal point, so use your written logs. One of you can’t fill it out for both, either. Each person writes their own log and scores their own stress tank. And fair doesn’t have to mean exactly 50/50. Fair is what you both agree to with your eyes open, and an uneven split you chose together can be the fair one. Two kinds of fair (page 126) looks at this.

zqaxchapterx2xxsmallxchildrenqzSmall children and a new baby

Small children bring a flood of new jobs, and most of them are thinking jobs, from the daycare bag and the shots to the party invitations, the next size of clothes and the nights. That’s why the mental load (see the work nobody sees, page 71) often grows after a baby arrives, usually without anyone deciding it. Log the children’s jobs too, with the thinking time, and count the nights. Hand over whole jobs, like clothes and sizes or the doctor and the shots, so the new owner does the noticing too, in their own way. If a baby is on the way, write your first job list together before the birth, plan the nights, and agree to look again at six weeks, at three months and before either of you goes back to work. In the first weeks, share by energy more than by hours, so whoever was up in the night gets the rest.

Hollie and Gareth have Alfie, who is three, and Poppy, who is eight months, and Gareth is a nurse on shifts. Their logged minutes came out nearly even, yet Hollie did almost three-quarters of the jobs nobody asked for. They left the minutes alone and moved one whole job, the children’s clothes, to Gareth. In the first two weeks Alfie went to daycare in a vest in October. Hollie said nothing, heroically.

You could say “Could you own the daycare bag from now on, including noticing when we’re low on diapers? I won’t check it.”

Dig deeper: small children, new babies and shift work

zqaxchapterx2xxonexpersonqzIf only one of you wants to try this

That’s common, and you can still start. Log your own week, score your own tank, and then share one small thing you noticed, without asking the other person to agree with your numbers. A dad noticed he was spending five hours a week driving his sixteen-year-old to training and back. He said so, without any accusation in it, and they agreed on a bus pass for two days a week. His son grumbled for two weeks and then started to enjoy the bus, where nobody asked him how training went. Share one finding at a time, then let it rest for a few days.

If the other person refuses to talk about the split at all, ever, that isn’t a setup problem, and no score will fix it.

More for your situation

Money together (spreadloveandacceptance.com/money-together) · Gaming and time together (spreadloveandacceptance.com/gaming-and-time-together) · Friends (spreadloveandacceptance.com/friends) · Family rifts (spreadloveandacceptance.com/family-rifts) · Grown-up children (spreadloveandacceptance.com/grown-up-children) · Grandparents (spreadloveandacceptance.com/grandparents) · Co-parenting (spreadloveandacceptance.com/co-parenting) · Coming home (spreadloveandacceptance.com/coming-home) · Empty nest (spreadloveandacceptance.com/empty-nest) · At work (spreadloveandacceptance.com/work) · For counselors (spreadloveandacceptance.com/for-counselors)

To run the check, each of you first logs one week in Who did what (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-01), because the number only means something if you each wrote your own. Next, fill out the job list in One owner per job together, including any jobs nobody owns yet, and each score your own stress tank on the same day. Put the three numbers into the calculator (spreadloveandacceptance.com/is-the-setup-working), look first at the biggest shortfall, pick one small change together and check again in a month.

III

Part Two · Chapter III

Full tanks and different angles: stress and perspective

Why some reactions are bigger than what caused them, and why two people can see the same moment so differently.

In this chapter

  1. A full tank overflows
  2. Some stress is left over from earlier
  3. Check your stress tank in a minute
  4. Three everyday states
  5. There are seven angles on the same moment
  6. Both views can be true
  7. Say it instead of making each other guess
  8. A full tank means “later,” not “never.”
  9. Words this chapter uses

  11. Common mix-ups
  12. Two homes: co-parenting after a split
  13. If only one of you wants to try this
  14. More for your situation

At a glance

  • A full tank overflows, so stress left over from earlier makes small things feel big.
  • Check your tank in a minute, and say the band out loud so nobody has to guess.
  • Two people can see one moment from different angles, and both views can be true.
  • A full tank means later, so pause, name a time and come back.

Thursday, 5:15pm

“Did you remember to call the dentist?”

A perfectly pleasant question. What comes out of you in reply is about four sizes too big for it, with a bit about the car thrown in for good measure, and you can hear it happening while it happens, like watching yourself trip on a stair.

Eight in the morning after a night shift, quickly. On the surface, a question about the meter. Underneath, twelve hours on your feet. Underneath that, two people seeing one moment from different angles. The roots are state and setting, and signal and noise. The chapter slows down on the tank, then the angles.

  1. A full tank overflows.

    If you’re already tired or stretched from somewhere else, a small question can get a big reaction, which is simply human. Anything decided in that moment is worth coming back to once you’ve both calmed down.

    Stress from outside leaks in Daily diaries from newlywed couples showed that spouses under more stress outside the relationship reacted more strongly to everyday irritations inside it. Marnie’s morning is a fair example.

    Neff and Karney (2009) · Moderate: daily-diary studies of newlyweds; correlational

    It’s eight in the morning and Marnie has just done a twelve-hour night shift and is standing in the kitchen in her coat. Her roommate, eating cornflakes, asks if she saw his message about the electricity meter. She bites his head off, though really it was twelve hours on her feet that did the biting. The meter just happened to be standing at the end of them. She apologized at four in the afternoon, when she woke up, via a note under his door. The note said, “Sorry. That was bigger than the question. I’m running on empty.”

    Dig deeper: how full your tank is

  2. Some stress is left over from earlier.

    Ask yourself how much of this feeling is about the thing in front of you and how much you carried in with you. Being upset about the dishes and being exhausted, with the dishes as the thing you happened to notice, are different problems. Some of what we bring in is much older, like an understanding from growing up that whoever notices the mess has to clean it. If a feeling seems a lot older than the moment, Where your lens came from (spreadloveandacceptance.com/growing-up) helps you find where it started.

    Corey is fourteen and has had a horrible day at school, the sort he won’t talk about. He comes home and finds his brother has taken the phone charger, again. The explosion that follows can be heard two doors down. The charger was the last drop in a tank that had been full since lunchtime.

    Words you could use “I think I brought this in with me. Give me ten minutes.”

    Dig deeper: leftover stress

    Professor Puddles

    Before a hard talk, check how full your own tank is. Five quick questions, about two minutes, and you’ll know whether now is the time.

    Workpaper WP-02: How much are you carrying? spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-02

  3. Check your stress tank in a minute.

    How much are you carrying? measures how full your stress tank is, and a higher score means more stress in the tank. Score five things from 0 to 4, which are sleep, work elsewhere, any unsettled argument, how your body feels and time pressure today, then add them up and divide by 20. Under 0.30 is light, 0.30 up to 0.60 is medium and 0.60 or more is high. If it’s been high for a long time it can start to feel normal, so a quick reading each week is worth it.

    Vince has been looking after his wife since her hip operation. He scored 0.65 three days in a row. That told him something he hadn’t let himself think, which was that he needed help more than he needed to try harder. He sat with it for an evening, in the chair by the window with the radio on low. Then he called his son, who said, “Dad, I’ve been waiting for you to ask since March.”

    Dig deeper: the stress-tank score

  4. Three everyday states.

    Knowing whether you’re calm and connected, revved up or running on empty tells you whether now is a good time to talk. The Nervous System Ladder (spreadloveandacceptance.com/quick-checks), a thirty-second self-check, helps you make a best guess. The labels come from polyvagal theory, whose main claims are still debated by scientists, and here they’re used only as everyday words. In one long-distance couple, he takes the video call at midnight his time and is usually running on empty by then, so they’ve moved the hard talks to Saturday mornings. It helps to know one body clue for each state. A tight jaw is a common one for revved up.

    Dig deeper: the three states

  5. There are seven angles on the same moment.

    The seven angles are tiredness, time pressure, history, what home was like growing up, your sense of fairness, how you communicate and stress from outside. Many arguments are two people looking from different angles, each sure the other sees what they see. The “See their side” step of Rewind the talk (spreadloveandacceptance.com/carrier-wave-decoder) is built on these seven angles and helps you picture how the same moment might look from the other side, with questions to ask in place of guesses.

    Naive realism Lee Ross and Andrew Ward described the quiet assumption that we see things as they really are, so anyone who disagrees must be uninformed or unreasonable. Saying your angle out loud is a small way of admitting you have one.

    Ross and Ward (1996) · Strong: a foundational account whose predictions are well replicated

    Christmas, again, and Sasha sees it from family habit, because they always go to her mom’s. There’s a stocking with each child’s name on it, stitched in 2016, and her mom would be heartbroken. Kemi sees it from fairness: they went to her mom’s last year, and the year before, and, now that he counts, the year before that.

    Dig deeper: the seven angles

  6. Both views can be true.

    You can each be right about what you see and still be looking at different parts of the same thing, so the useful question is which angle each of you is seeing it from. Two brothers argued for a year about their late mom’s house. One saw thirty years of memories. Height marks on the kitchen door frame, the apple tree, the step where she sat to take her shoes off. The other saw a roof that needed $12,000 of work. Both of them were looking at the real house. In the end they sold it, and the one who saw the memories took the door frame with the height marks on it, which is now leaning against a wall in his garage.

    Words to try “You’re right about what you see. Can I tell you what I see?”

    Dig deeper: two true views

  7. Say it instead of making each other guess.

    Before a hard conversation, each of you says how full your tank is and which angle you’re seeing from, ideally right at the start.

    Two colleagues had a meeting about a missed deadline that both were dreading. One of them, feeling foolish, began with, “Before we start, I’m about half full today and I’m mostly seeing this from the time angle.” After a pause the other said, “Right. I’m pretty full. Fairness angle, if I’m honest.” It felt very odd, like reading out your own weather forecast. The meeting was shorter and calmer than the last one, and nobody cried in the restroom afterward, which last time somebody had.

    Dig deeper: using both together

    Tidbit

    Say your number out loud. “I’m running high today.” Two seconds, and nobody has to guess.

    Tool: My weather today spreadloveandacceptance.com/quick-checks

  8. A full tank means “later,” not “never.”

    A high score is a reason to pause and never a way out of the talk. Say when you’ll come back, and let the Calm-Down Kit (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-11) help in the meantime. After your calming steps, check your tank again. Under 0.50, go back at the time you said. From 0.50 to 0.59, take another round if you still feel hot, and if you are still at 0.60 or more after two rounds, pick a new time and say when.

    Flooding John Gottman’s long-term studies of couples gave a name to the point where someone is so physically overwhelmed in a conflict that listening and thinking become very hard. A full tank means later partly because a flooded person can’t really do now.

    Gottman (1994) · Moderate: large observational studies; some specific predictions are debated

    It’s about phone time, and a dad and his fourteen-year-old are both shouting. “I’m too wound up,” he says, “I’ll talk to you at seven.” She slams her door, and at seven he knocks. It matters more than anything he says once he’s inside. That isn’t much, or very good, and it is a lot better than not knocking.

    Dig deeper: pausing without avoiding

Your part, and only your part. Your stress tank is the only one you can empty. You can’t calm someone else’s tank for them, and pouring yours into theirs leaves two empty tanks. Protect yours: rest, say “later,” and give energy where it’s met. When both tanks are full, the kindest thing you control is the timing. More in Your wiring, weather and words (page 33)

Monday morning

The mail, eleven envelopes and a pizza menu, on the kitchen table, where they have been since Thursday. One of you sees a to-do list. The other sees proof that nobody in this house ever opens the mail except them. You try saying your angles out loud, like the book says, and it helps for about a minute. Then the gas bill comes up.

The pile is still there at lunchtime.

Words this chapter uses

Your stress tank is how much stress you’re already carrying before this moment even starts. Leftover stress is the part of a feeling you brought in from somewhere else, like poor sleep or a hard day, while this-moment stress is caused by what is in front of you right now. An angle is the point of view you’re seeing a moment from, such as tiredness or fairness.

On your own: reading your own tank

On your own, the most useful habit is a one-minute reading of your tank before you react. Check it for a few mornings in a row and look for a pattern. Ask yourself before a hard moment how much of it is left over from earlier. Decide on a calm day what settles you, so it’s ready when you need it. Living alone after a breakup, Beth noticed she snapped at her sister on the phone every single Monday. Her morning readings showed why. Sunday night was her worst sleep of the week, every week, without fail. Now she asks for Tuesday instead, and her sister has stopped asking what’s wrong (see On my own, spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own).

Two ways to read this

A full tank, two ways

Some people can say “I’m running high today” easily. Others only realize how full they were once they’ve snapped. If you can name it, the other person may genuinely not know their own number yet. Give them time. If you can’t, the one who names it isn’t making excuses in advance. They’re giving you a weather report so you can plan around it.

Where the fields meet. Neurobiology says your state sets the volume. Psychology adds that mood filters what we hear, and aromatherapy, read modestly, that the setting matters, a quieter room or a later hour. The evidence for particular oils is weak. The room and the timing are what help.

Common mix-ups

A big reaction sometimes means it was a big deal. Quite often it means the tank was already full. A high score is never an excuse, either. It’s a note to come back later, never a pass to skip the talk. You can’t tell how full someone else’s tank is, however well you know them, which is why each person scores only themselves. And a pause isn’t the silent treatment. The silent treatment is ignoring someone for days, again and again, to punish them, with no time to come back. A pause has a time to come back, which is why you always say when: “I need twenty minutes. Can we pick this up at eight?” If a pause of yours is being read as the other kind, describe it out loud rather than defending yourself.

Sometimes a reaction is far bigger than the moment, and part of it may belong to something older, from childhood or a past relationship or a frightening time. You can’t know someone’s history from outside, and guessing out loud (“This is about your ex”) rarely helps. Having lived through hard things is never the person’s fault, and nothing here is for diagnosing anyone. What you can change is your own half. Slow your pace, lower your voice, sit down, keep the doorway clear and use fewer words. If it’s still climbing, say when you’ll come back, step away, and then come back when you said you would. The same list works when the big reaction is yours.

zqaxchapterx3xxtwoxhomesqzTwo homes: co-parenting after a split

Children carry two homes, and changeover day fills their tank. Being quiet, extra close or cranky for a few hours after a handover is common and usually says nothing bad about the other home. Give them landing time, with a snack and something familiar and no questions about the other home for the first hour. The child is never the messenger. Adult news goes adult to adult. For money, follow any formal arrangement. Split the extras by a ratio you agree, and settle up once a month from one list. With an ex, share the band and keep the story, as in “I’m in a heavy week. Could we swap Wednesday?” and your private life stays yours. If an ex won’t cooperate, parallel parenting can work, with written messages only, short and business-like, handovers at school and your own list for your own home. When there are new partners, the parent stays the owner of anything involving the other home, and a stepparent starts as a friendly adult rather than the one who scolds the children.

Harriet gives Freya, who is eight, and Arlo, who is five, an hour of toast and blankets when they come back from their dad’s, and she has stopped asking “How was it?” at the front door. Sunday evenings are calmer. Arlo still cries at bedtime on changeover days, and she’s waiting to see whether that eases. Some weeks she thinks it is. Some weeks she isn’t sure.

Words you could use (a business-like message) “Hi Dylan. Freya’s school trip is on November 6 and costs $30. I’ve paid it and put it on the extras list. Thanks, Harriet.”

Dig deeper: two homes, money and stepparents

If only one of you wants to try this

You can do all of this from your own side. Check your own tank, name your own angle, pause and come back on time. The other person doesn’t have to use the words for it to help, and when one person starts saying it out loud, the other quite often follows. Lauren visits her dad every Sunday, and every week they clash about his health. She started opening each visit with, “I’m a bit tired today, so if I go quiet it isn’t you.” He never scored anything himself. He thinks the whole idea is silly. Still, the visits got calmer, and one Sunday in November he said, unprompted, while filling the kettle, “I’m a bit tired today too, sweetheart.”

A full tank explains a reaction, and the reaction still needs a repair. “I was running on empty” is a real reason the first time. It stops working as a reason when it closes the conversation every time and nothing about the week changes. Ask yourself whether you’re using the tank to start a conversation or to end one.

More for your situation

Before your next hard conversation, score the five things in How much are you carrying? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-02-how-much-are-you-carrying), add them up and divide by 20, then say one sentence out loud about your tank and your angle. If either of you scores 0.60 or more, put off anything that doesn’t need deciding in the next hour, and agree on a time to come back.

IV

Part Two · Chapter IV

Two kinds of fair: equal vs fair at home

Agree on what “fair” means before you argue about it, and give a comment a moment to land before you answer it.

In this chapter

  1. There are two kinds of fair
  2. Fair by results
  3. Fair by promises
  4. Once a job has an owner, look to the owner
  5. Covering is kind. Say it out loud
  6. Let a comment land before you react
  7. Notice, name, decide
  8. Keep the two questions apart
  9. On your own: your own kind of fair
  10. Common mix-ups
  11. Money between you
  12. A couple and a roommate
  13. More for your situation
  14. A shared agreement, or controlling rules?

At a glance

  • There are two kinds of fair, by results (did it all get done?) and by promises (did each of us do what we agreed?), so agree which one you are using.
  • Once a job has an owner, look to the owner, and when you cover for someone, say so out loud.
  • Let a comment land before you react by noticing it, naming it and then deciding what to say.
  • Keep the two questions apart, because whether the job was done is a fact and whether the comment hurt is a feeling.

The same argument, twice a month

One of you counts hours. The other counts who noticed the job needed doing in the first place. You are both counting honestly, in two different currencies, then arguing about the exchange rate. This usually happens on a Sunday evening and usually, for reasons nobody can explain, about the oven.

A Sunday-evening argument about the oven, seen quickly. The surface is the oven. Underneath, two currencies, hours and noticing. Underneath that, two kinds of fair nobody has named. The roots are balance and signal and noise. Slowly now, one kind of fair at a time.

  1. zqaxchapterx4xxextwoxkindsqz

    There are two kinds of fair.

    One kind asks whether everything got done. The other asks whether each person did what they said they would. Both are reasonable, and friction starts when each of you is using a different one without realizing.

    More than one kind of fair Morton Deutsch argued that equity (you get out what you put in) is only one fairness rule, alongside equality (the same for everyone) and need, and that people lean on different ones in different settings. Research broadly agrees that the setting decides.

    Deutsch (1975) · Moderate: an influential theory, broadly supported

    Nisha and Kezia share a room in the dorms. Nisha thinks a week was fair if the room is tidy by Friday, whoever tidied it. Kezia thinks it was fair if each of them kept her own half clean. For most of the first semester each thought the other was being unreasonable and said so to other people. Neither of them was. It came out at two in the morning over a shared package of noodles, and they both laughed until the girl next door banged on the wall.

    You could say “When you say fair, do you mean it all gets done, or that we each do our bit?”

    Dig deeper: the two kinds of fair

  2. Fair by results.

    This kind of fair judges by outcomes, by whether the right things got done by whoever had the time or energy. It’s flexible and easy-going, which is lovely when it works. Done carefully it counts the cost to whoever covered. Done carelessly it hides who is always stepping in.

    Marjorie is raising her grandchildren. Her grown-up son helps with whatever’s needed when he’s home, cheerfully and well. The house runs, and she is always, always the one who notices what’s needed. She didn’t see it herself until she marked, for one week, every job she picked up that wasn’t planned. It came to forty-one, and she showed her son. He said, “Forty-one?” and then, after a bit, “Right.”

    Dig deeper: judging by results

  3. Fair by promises.

    This kind asks whether each person did the jobs they agreed to own. It’s clear and steady, and it can feel rigid in a week when life gets in the way. Two business partners run a café. One owns the ordering, the other owns the staff schedule. When the schedule is late (it’s the Thursday before a long weekend, it is always late then) they ask the schedule owner about it, not “the team.” And nobody takes it personally, or not for long.

    Words you could use “It’s my job, and I can’t do it this week. Could you take it, and I’ll take out the trash?”

    Dig deeper: judging by promises

  4. Once a job has an owner, look to the owner.

    The owner is the person who does the job from start to finish. A second name on the list is a backstop, who notices if it slipped and checks in gently without supervising, and it can be the same person. If the job is yours, the question is whether you did it, and somebody quietly covering for you doesn’t answer that. It also protects the person who keeps filling the gaps.

    Opening the gate In 97 couples with babies, fathers did more of the day-to-day care when mothers actively encouraged them, and when mothers were very critical, fathers’ own beliefs about being involved made less difference. It’s one US sample, but Claire’s single “Dog’s dinner?” is gate-opening in miniature.

    Schoppe-Sullivan and colleagues (2008) · Moderate: an observational study of one US sample; correlational

    In one stepfamily, Ethan, who is thirteen, owns feeding the dog. His stepmom Claire is the second name. When the bowl is empty at seven and the dog is staring at it with enormous meaning, Claire says “Dog’s dinner?” once, just that. She doesn’t do it for him and she doesn’t lecture. For the first month this nearly killed her. Ethan now feeds the dog most nights before anyone mentions it, and the dog has stopped staring at Claire.

    Dig deeper: agreeing which kind you’ll use

  5. Covering is kind. Say it out loud.

    Helping out when the owner can’t is lovely, and it helps to mention it, so the help is seen. “I took the trash out this week, since you were away.” Help that stays silent turns into unseen work, and unseen help slowly becomes expected (see Complacency, spreadloveandacceptance.com/complacency).

    Two sisters take turns driving their dad to his appointments. When one covers for the other, she texts the same day. Took Dad Thurs, you were on late shifts. All fine, blood work normal, he flirted with the receptionist. It takes ten seconds to send and stops the help going invisible. The second half of the message is, they both agree, the important bit.

    Dig deeper: covering without resentment

    Sugarfoot

    Covering for someone is kind. Say that you did, gently, or it turns into the quiet sort of resentment that nobody mentions until Christmas.

    Tool: Small wins: Flip it spreadloveandacceptance.com/small-wins

  6. zqaxchapterx4xxexlandqz

    Let a comment land before you react.

    When a remark hits harder than it should, say “Give me a second.” The idea is borrowed loosely from brain science, where the brain turns down sounds and sensations automatically in a fraction of a second, while this pause is a few seconds you choose to take on purpose. Let the spike pass, then decide whether the remark needs an answer now or later, or at all.

    Two in the afternoon. Fran has come downstairs after a night shift, hair everywhere. Her husband looks up from the table. “Oh, you’re up.” She has been asleep for six hours, dreaming about hospital rounds, and what she hears is at last. She’s halfway into a reply before she stops and says, “Give me a second, I’m really tired.” He looks puzzled, because he’d meant he was glad to see her. He’d saved her the last of the soup (see Different hours, spreadloveandacceptance.com/different-hours). Agree your own “give me a second” phrase today, while things are calm.

    Dig deeper: giving a comment time to land

    Professor Puddles

    When a comment stings, give it a minute to land before you answer. This workpaper is a short check for your reply.

    Workpaper WP-09: Say it so it lands spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-09

  7. Notice, name, decide.

    First notice that a comment landed hard. Then name it, kindly (“That hit harder than you probably meant”). Once you’ve settled, decide how to reply. Say it so it lands (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-09-say-it-so-it-lands) helps with the words.

    “You never listen,” his fifteen-year-old said, on the stairs. Andy felt his chest go tight, and a speech started assembling itself somewhere behind his teeth. He wanted very much to list the times he had listened. What he said was, “Ouch. That stings. And I do want to hear you properly.” Then he decided it needed a real talk, the next evening, after her swimming, in the car, which is where they talk best, both looking at the road.

    Dig deeper: the three steps

  8. Keep the two questions apart.

    Whether the job was done is a question about a fact. Whether the comment hurt is a question about a feeling. Both matter, and each goes better in its own conversation.

    Separated parents share their children across two homes. The bag came back on Sunday without the school shoes, and with it a text about the shoes that felt, to the one who received it, very cold. They settled the shoes first, on the phone, in about two minutes. They talked about the text the following Sunday. It took longer and was more awkward, and it was better for waiting a week (see Co-parenting, spreadloveandacceptance.com/co-parenting). When a talk tangles, “Fact or feeling?” is a good question to ask out loud. Finish one before you start the other.

    Dig deeper: facts and feelings, separately

Your part, and only your part. You control whether, when and how you bring something up, and whether you cover a job out loud. How the other person responds is theirs. If you cover again and again with no thanks and no change, match the energy: cover less, and say so kindly. Fair by promises only works when both people keep theirs. More in Your wiring, weather and words (page 33)

The weekly catch-up

Sam and Alex share a home. Alex owns the trash but works late on Tuesdays, and Sam has quietly taken them out three weeks in a row. At the catch-up Sam mentions it, not very smoothly. Alex goes a bit red and admits that Tuesday nights aren’t realistic with the late shifts. They agree to try a swap for the rest of the month, with Sam taking out the trash and Alex taking the recycling and the weekly grocery order, and to settle it at the monthly look-back in Chapter V (page 143).

Wednesday, 7pm

“Thanks for doing the dishes,” one of you says, a little deflated. It was meant as a thank-you, and it came out sounding like a criticism. Before you know it you’ve answered the criticism, the person who said thank you is defending a thank-you, and the dishes are still in the rack.

On your own: your own kind of fair

Fair starts with knowing what it means to you, and which jobs are truly yours. Write down what fair means to you in one sentence, and list the jobs you own alongside the ones you picked up without ever agreeing to. Errol lives alone and has his children every other weekend. His sentence, after a lot of crossing out, is that fair means not doing their jobs for them just because he misses them (see On my own, spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own). He finds this very hard on Sunday afternoons, when he’d happily do everything if it meant another hour. Pick one job you took on without agreeing, and either keep it on purpose or raise it on a calm day.

Two ways to read this

“On time,” two ways

Some people learned at home that seven means seven sharp, and arriving at five after feels like a small slight. Others learned that seven means from seven, and arriving on the dot is a little too eager. If you’re a seven-sharp person, the other person isn’t careless. They’re being polite by their own rule. If you’re a from-seven person, saying “Is that seven sharp?” costs nothing and saves the wait.

Where the fields meet. Philosophy asks you to agree which kind of fair you’re using before you argue about it. The art of debating adds: say their strongest point first. And music explains why “Thanks for doing the dishes” can still go wrong, because tone carries more than the words.

Common mix-ups

If it got done, there may still be a problem, because someone may be paying for it in time and energy. Holding the owner to the job isn’t being strict. It’s keeping the agreement you both made, which is kinder than quiet resentment. Letting a comment land doesn’t mean ignoring it. It’s about timing, and you still get to answer. And please don’t save up months of covering to bring out all at once. A long list lands like a bill, so mention covering as it happens.

zqaxchapterx4xxmoneyqzMoney between you

Money is where the two kinds of fair meet most often. Some couples put everything into one pot. Some keep their money separate and pay agreed bills, often half each, which is fair by promises, the same rule for both. Others each pay into a shared pot in line with what they earn and keep the rest, which is fair by results, since each is left with a similar share. Many couples mix them, with a joint account for bills and food and some money each that nobody has to explain. The right way is the one you both chose with your eyes open. To talk about it, start with your money stories, how money worked at home when you were growing up, then move on to the numbers and to a “talk first” amount for big purchases that applies to both of you.

Having a say Procedural justice research, which began with Thibaut and Walker, finds that whether people feel a decision was reached fairly, and above all whether they had a voice in it, shapes how they feel about the result. A good reason to work a split out together rather than hand one over.

Thibaut and Walker (1975) · Strong: one of the more robust findings in social psychology, though early lab methods were criticized

Niamh takes home $3,300 a month and Tariq $2,400, and their rent and bills will be $1,900. They split it 58/42, in line with their pay, so she pays $1,100 and he pays $800.

Words to try “Can we each say how money worked in our families growing up?” “Would half each, or in line with our pay, feel fairer to you?”

Dig deeper: money, step by step

zqaxchapterx4xxhousemateqzA couple and a roommate

A couple sharing a home with a roommate who isn’t a partner is a different shape from three equals. It helps to keep two lists, house jobs for all three of you, such as the trash, the bathroom, the bills and the landlord, and couple jobs for the two of you. Decide house questions with all three of you there, not in bed the night before. Hear the roommate first on anything that affects them, keep couple arguments out of shared rooms, and never ask them to referee. Ollie and Hamza share an apartment with their friend Bex. They split the rent by room, since the couple has the bigger one, and the bills by person, and all three hold a short house meeting on the first Sunday of the month, with cookies, which Bex insists is the only reason she shows up. Anything that comes up in between gets the stock answer, “That’s a house question, let’s decide it when Bex is here.”

Dig deeper: two lists, and money with three

More for your situation

Each of these pages takes the ideas in this chapter into one kind of relationship. Start from your relationship (spreadloveandacceptance.com/by-relationship) lists them all.

  • Friends (spreadloveandacceptance.com/friends) · More than two partners (spreadloveandacceptance.com/more-than-two) · Sharing a room (spreadloveandacceptance.com/sharing-a-room) · Money together (spreadloveandacceptance.com/money-together)
  • Foster and kinship families (spreadloveandacceptance.com/foster-and-kinship) · When a child has ADHD (spreadloveandacceptance.com/adhd-kids) · Grown-up children (spreadloveandacceptance.com/grown-up-children) · Family rifts (spreadloveandacceptance.com/family-rifts)
  • Different hours · Coming home (spreadloveandacceptance.com/coming-home) · When one of you is sick or disabled (spreadloveandacceptance.com/when-one-is-ill) · Two faiths (spreadloveandacceptance.com/two-faiths) · On my own

On a calm, easy day, each of you can say which kind of fair comes more naturally, results or promises. Then pick three regular jobs and write an owner for each in the job list in One owner per job (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-03-one-owner-per-job), with a second name for someone who notices if it slips. Finally, agree a short phrase for when something lands hard (“Give me a second” does fine), along with the promise that whoever asked for a second will come back to it.

A shared agreement, or controlling rules?

A promise is something both people chose and either can ask to change. It can still feel strict (“no new subscriptions without a chat first”), and that’s fine, because it binds you both. “Controlling” is a serious word, and it gets used for ordinary disagreements far too often.

For something to be controlling, these are usually all present:

  • one person sets rules for the other’s ordinary life, such as money, friends, time, clothes or phone,
  • the rules bind one side and not the other,
  • they’re enforced by checking or by a penalty nobody agreed to, such as money held back, days of coldness or threats to leave,
  • the other person’s no isn’t accepted, and it has become a pattern rather than one bad week.

Not enough on its own:

  • a shared agreement you both chose, even a strict one,
  • a partner who likes budgets, plans or detail more than you do,
  • asking where you are, or worrying when you’re late,
  • a limit someone sets on their own behavior (“I won’t lend money again”),
  • a need for routine or knowing what’s coming.

If a rule feels one-sided, name the rule rather than the person. “The talk-first amount seems to apply to my spending and not yours. Can we set one that covers us both?”
