V

Part Two · Chapter V

The monthly look-back: a calm relationship check-in

Once a month, look back for the problems that keep coming back, and fix the setup instead of having the same argument again.

In this chapter

  1. Weekly check-ins miss patterns
  2. You need four weeks of notes and one list
  3. Mark an ✗ for each week a job slipped
  4. A problem that keeps coming back usually has no real owner
  5. Sort each repeat into one of three kinds
  6. Count the gaps each month
  7. Look back even when nothing is slipping
  8. It’s not a review of either person
  9. Keep it short and kind
  10. A look-back, three months in
  11. Common mix-ups
  12. Starting out: before you move in
  13. Raising a grandchild (kinship care)
  14. More for your situation
  15. On your own: a monthly look at yourself

The third Tuesday in a row

The trash again. You could have the same ten-minute back-and-forth you had last Tuesday, word for word. You know your lines and so do they.

Or you could notice that this is the third Tuesday running, and wonder what it is about Tuesdays.

The trash on a third Tuesday, quickly. On the surface, the same short argument. Underneath, a job that keeps slipping. Underneath that, a job nobody owns. The roots are feedback loops and ownership and structure. Then the chapter slows down and walks through the look-back.

  1. Weekly check-ins miss patterns.

    Latent conditions James Reason, writing about accidents in organizations, showed how they grow out of latent conditions, gaps that sit quietly in a system until they meet an ordinary slip on an ordinary day. A job with no owner is a latent condition.

    Reason (1997) · Strong: foundational in safety science

    Four roommates had an overflowing bathroom trash can every week, and every week it seemed like bad luck, until they looked at the month together and saw it had happened every single week since September. One missed job looks like bad luck. The same job missed week after week is a pattern, and patterns are easiest to see when you look at a whole month at once.

    In my old job the step that got skipped more than any other was going back afterward to check that the fix had actually held, and skipping it is exactly how the same problem turns up again three years later. This chapter is that step, made small. A careful, friendly glance over the month, closer to a self-check than an inspection. Choose a monthly date now, the last Sunday, say, and put it in everyone’s calendar.

    Dig deeper: why once a month

  2. You need four weeks of notes and one list.

    Bring the month’s four weekly notes from Who did what (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-01), where a few lines a week is enough, and your job list from One owner per job (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-03-one-owner-per-job). Twenty minutes is usually plenty. If either of your stress tanks is high that day, at 0.60 or more on How much are you carrying? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-02-how-much-are-you-carrying), move it a day or two.

    Kat and Nathan work different shifts and keep their weekly notes in one shared note on their phones, mostly typed at red lights. They do the look-back on the one evening a month they’re both off, with takeout from the Nepalese place. It has become, slightly to their embarrassment, the evening of the month they look forward to most.

    Dig deeper: getting ready

  3. Mark an ✗ for each week a job slipped.

    A job slipped if it was noticed and not done, only done after being raised more than once, or quietly covered by someone who isn’t its owner. Look closely at every job with two or more ✗, because three or four in a month is a real pattern.

    Two foster caregivers found the reading log had been missed three weeks out of four. Both of them had an explanation ready. They marked the ✗ in pencil first, together, before either of them said anything at all, which is much harder than it sounds and much the best order. Then the explanations, which turned out to be the same one.

    Dig deeper: gathering the month’s notes

  4. A problem that keeps coming back usually has no real owner.

    That kind of problem gets patched every week and never fixed. The owner is the person who does the job from start to finish, so the fix is to give the job one owner whose name sticks, or to talk honestly about whether anyone has the time and energy for it.

    Diffusion of responsibility In a famous experiment, people who thought others could also hear someone having a seizure were slower to help, and less likely to, because each felt less responsible. A grocery order is a long way from an emergency, but “whoever’s free” runs on the same arithmetic.

    Darley and Latané (1968) · Strong: classic and widely replicated, though weaker in clearly dangerous emergencies

    In a house with three partners, “whoever’s free” did the online grocery order. It was late three times this month, once by a whole day. With nobody owning it, everybody assumed someone else had it in hand. One Friday there was no milk at all in the house, and four jars of mustard.

    Dig deeper: spotting the gaps that keep reopening

  5. Sort each repeat into one of three kinds.

    If a job has no clear owner, update the job list. If its owner can’t keep up, have a kind, honest talk. If there was a short-term cause, like a bout of flu, note it and move on.

    The homework folder kept coming back unsigned. Two separated parents looked at it at the look-back and went through the three kinds, out loud, quite carefully, because last time they’d argued. Was nobody sure which home signs it, was one of them swamped, or was it just the week one of them had the flu? It was the first one. It had been the first one since September (see Co-parenting, spreadloveandacceptance.com/co-parenting).

    Dig deeper: sorting each gap

  6. Count the gaps each month.

    Write down how many gaps of each kind you found. If the number of jobs with no clear owner falls over several months, the setup is working, and a single month can be a normal wobble. If it keeps going up, something bigger has changed and it’s worth a talk. Two business partners write their monthly count on a whiteboard in the back office, next to the fire-drill notice. In March four jobs had no clear owner. By June, one did, and they argue quite cheerfully about whose fault that one is.

    Dig deeper: keeping count

    Professor Puddles

    The look-back has its own workpaper: a month of notes, one list, and an ✗ for each week a job slipped. It makes a pattern easy to see.

    Workpaper WP-04: What keeps coming back? spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-04

  7. Look back even when nothing is slipping.

    A month with no gaps is good news. It’s also the month most likely to go unchecked. When something has worked for a while, people stop looking, and nothing breaks on the day that happens. Keep the look-back going in quiet months and add one question, “What’s something we’ve stopped noticing or mentioning?,” which is how a look-back guards against complacency (spreadloveandacceptance.com/complacency).

    The children have left home and nothing whatsoever is slipping. The look-back takes eleven minutes. At the end Dave says, quietly, looking at his plate, that they don’t really talk at dinner anymore. Jan had noticed it too, months ago, without knowing how to say it. No list would have shown it.

    Dig deeper: the quiet months

  8. It’s not a review of either person.

    A just culture Sidney Dekker argues for a just culture, one that separates honest mistakes from reckless ones, and points out that who draws that line matters as much as where it’s drawn. At home, I’d draw it together, on a calm day.

    Dekker (2007) · Moderate: an influential book; the evidence is mainly case studies

    You don’t add up old hours or punish old mistakes. You can thank someone for what they carried before, and you leave the past unbilled. The only question is where the setup isn’t working yet and what you’ll try next month. After a month in the hospital, Yusuf came home to a long list of what had slipped while he was away. His partner had been dreading showing it to him. He read it, and then he said thank you for the bits that hadn’t slipped, which was most of them, and they set up the month ahead. That was all.

    Dig deeper: what the look-back is for, and what it isn’t

    Tidbit

    Start the look-back with something that went well. It changes the temperature of the whole twenty minutes.

    Tool: Kitchen-table check-in spreadloveandacceptance.com/check-ins

  9. Keep it short and kind.

    Start with something that went well and talk about the job instead of the person. If a gap needs a real talk, set it for another day using Check-ins (spreadloveandacceptance.com/check-ins). If a talk starts going badly, either of you can call a pause, and whoever paused names a time to come back. A mom and two teenagers hold their look-back over pizza on the last Friday. Each says one good thing first (the younger one’s is always “the pizza”). One gap gets a new owner. It’s over in fifteen minutes and nobody has stormed off, which in that house is a result.

    Dig deeper: how to talk about a pattern

Your part, and only your part. In the look-back you can only fix the gaps you own, and offer help with the rest. You can’t make someone keep a rhythm. Keep the rhythms you can keep, notice which ones are kept in return, and let your effort follow: more where it’s shared, less where it isn’t, so the rhythm doesn’t run on one person’s energy. More in Your wiring, weather and words (page 33)

The last Sunday of the month

Two mugs of tea, four weeks of notes and about twenty minutes. You go down the list together, and most weeks were fine. Two jobs keep coming up, the recycling and the call to the landlord about the window that won’t shut. You give each of them a name, and the landlord one goes to whoever’s least scared of the landlord. You finish your coffee while it’s still warm, which hasn’t happened on a Sunday in months.

A look-back, three months in

Sam and Alex’s trash cans slipped three weeks in a row because Alex works late on Tuesdays. After the trial swap they make it official, so Sam owns the trash and Alex takes the recycling and the weekly grocery order, which keeps the hours even. The second month is clean. In the third, the grocery order slips twice, both times in a week when Alex’s mom was in the hospital, so they mark it as a one-off and leave the list alone. What actually changes in month three is that Alex mentions, almost in passing, while stacking the plates, that he has stopped enjoying their Saturday mornings. No list had shown that. They agree to talk about it properly on Thursday, and Sam spends most of the week worrying about it.

You could say “I don’t think anyone dropped this. I think nobody ever picked it up.”

Two ways to read this

In writing, two ways

Some people remember a spoken plan easily and find a written list a bit formal. Others lose spoken words as they’re said, because holding them in mind while doing the job splits their attention. If you remember easily, a request for writing isn’t mistrust. It’s someone trying to get it right. If you need it written, offering to write it yourself (“I’ll send us both a note”) keeps it light.

Where the fields meet. Behavioral science says habits beat good intentions, so a look-back works best as a routine too small to skip. Holistic therapies would start with the body, a cup of tea before the list, and some of these practices are well studied while others are debated. A shared laugh, which the research says only modest things about, is still a good way to start.

Common mix-ups

This isn’t where you settle who owes what. Past hours are never billed to anyone, though you can still say thank you for them. You only fix the setup going forward. A slipped job doesn’t mean its owner failed, either, because the gap might be in the list, or in the owner’s capacity, or in one strange week. And you can’t skip the weekly notes and just do this. The look-back only works if the weekly notes feed it.

A look-back is something you both choose. It looks at the month and the setup, using notes you each kept about your own side. Monitoring is different. It means one person asking for the other’s every hour, checking their phone without agreement, or using the ✗ marks as evidence against them. A partner who simply likes detail, or asks “How did the week go?” isn’t monitoring. If the look-back starts to feel like being checked up on, pause it and talk about how it’s being used before you go on.

zqaxchapterx5xxmovingxinqzStarting out: before you move in

If you are new together and about to share a home, the tools work best now, before habits set, at about one step a week. In the first week, each of you writes down the rulebook from the home you grew up in (spreadloveandacceptance.com/growing-up) and then you swap, with curiosity. In the second, talk about money, starting with your money stories and moving on to the split (Chapter IV, page 139). In the third, write your first job list, with one owner per job and the thinking jobs included (One owner per job, spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/fill/wp-03), and in the fourth, make a pause plan (spreadloveandacceptance.com/pursue-withdraw) on a calm day. In the fifth, each name three things that matter most to you about a home (Part Three, Chapter 10, page 294). After the move, log one ordinary week once two weeks have passed, and do your first short look-back after four. None of it is a test. The point is that neither of you has to guess.

Niamh and Tariq, eight months together, find that their families meant very different things by “tidy.” They agree on the kitchen every night and the rest on Sunday, and on Tariq’s mother never being told about the rest.

Dig deeper: the plan, week by week

zqaxchapterx5xxkinshipqzRaising a grandchild (kinship care)

Many grandparents and other relatives raise a child whose parents can’t, and much of it involves things that keep coming back, such as canceled calls and the hard evenings after contact. A monthly look-back helps. Some repeats you can own. Some, like a parent who misses calls, you can’t, and for those you can own the plan for the evening after. The child may love both the parent who can’t look after them and you, so tell them they don’t have to choose, and don’t run the parent down in front of them. Explain an absent parent in a few true words that fit their age, always with the message that it isn’t their fault. When the parent is your own grown-up child and things are hard between you, keep messages about the child short and civil for the child’s sake, and leave the door open. Look after yourself too. Ask family and friends for regular breaks, and swap notes with other kinship caregivers.

Maureen, who is sixty-three, is raising her grandson Tyler, who is nine. Her look-back shows that his mom’s Sunday call fell through three times this month. She can’t fix that. So she plans those evenings instead, with hot chocolate and his soccer book, and asks her brother to take Tyler swimming on Sunday afternoons, so there’s something to look forward to that doesn’t depend on a phone ringing.

Words you could use, with the child “Mom loves you. She isn’t well enough to look after you right now, and that’s not your fault.”

Dig deeper: loyalty, explaining by age, and rifts with your adult child

More for your situation

A look-back works in every kind of relationship, with small changes. Start from your relationship (spreadloveandacceptance.com/by-relationship) lists pages for each one.

  • Foster and kinship families (spreadloveandacceptance.com/foster-and-kinship) · When a child has ADHD (spreadloveandacceptance.com/adhd-kids) · Grown-up children (spreadloveandacceptance.com/grown-up-children) · Family rifts (spreadloveandacceptance.com/family-rifts) · Empty nest (spreadloveandacceptance.com/empty-nest)
  • Different hours (spreadloveandacceptance.com/different-hours) · Coming home (spreadloveandacceptance.com/coming-home) · When one of you is sick or disabled (spreadloveandacceptance.com/when-one-is-ill) · Two faiths (spreadloveandacceptance.com/two-faiths) · On my own (spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own) · For counselors (spreadloveandacceptance.com/for-counselors)

On your own: a monthly look at yourself

Once a month, look back at your own month kindly, more like a weather report than a scorecard. What filled your battery and what drained it? Which of your limits held and which slipped? Choose one small thing to keep and one to change. Rhiannon lives on her own after a divorce, and her look-back showed the same ✗ three weeks in a row. She’d skipped her Thursday swim to answer work emails, every week, telling herself it was just this once. So she moved the emails to Friday morning, and kept the swim (see On my own).

To begin, put a relaxed twenty-minute date in the calendar once a month and keep your weekly notes somewhere you can both find them. At the look-back, start by naming one thing that went well, and end by writing down how many gaps of each kind you found, so that over the next few months you can see whether the number is falling. What keeps coming back? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-04-what-keeps-coming-back) is the workpaper for that conversation.

That’s the end of Part Two. The book goes on in Part Three: Understanding people (page 160), chapters on how people work, for anyone. To put Parts One and Two into practice first, try the six-week program (spreadloveandacceptance.com/prog-01): six gentle weeks, with one chapter and one small tool each week.

What to remember

  • Weekly check-ins miss patterns.
  • Mark an ✗ for each week a job slipped.
  • Sort each repeat into one of three kinds.
  • Look back even when nothing is slipping.
  • Keep it short and kind.

Part Three · Chapter 1

How feelings work: signals, the body, and naming what you feel

What feelings are for, where they start, and why putting a name to one can make it easier to carry, whether you’re on your own, at home, with friends or at work.

In this chapter

  1. A feeling is a signal, not a verdict
  2. Feelings start in the body
  3. Naming a feeling helps you hold it
  4. More words, better tools
  5. Feelings come in layers
  6. Feelings rise and pass like waves
  7. Feelings spread between people
  8. If you weren’t brought up to talk about feelings
  9. Feeling it isn’t the same as doing it
  10. In everyday life
  11. Common mix-ups
  12. If you want to help someone else with this
  13. Workpapers, tools and reading on this site
  14. More for your situation

At a glance

  • A feeling is a signal that something matters to you. It doesn’t tell you what to do about it.
  • Feelings start in the body. A tight chest or a hot face often arrives before the word for it.
  • Naming helps. “I feel let down” is easier to hold than a big, nameless rush.
  • You can let a feeling be there and still choose what you do next.

Thursday, 4:50pm

A message from your manager. Have you got a minute tomorrow? No period, no smiley, nothing else at all.

By the time you get in you’ve snapped at the cat, decided you’re not hungry, and gone back over every mistake of the past month, plus one from March that nobody else remembers. Nobody has said anything bad. You check the message again anyway, in case it’s grown a period.

Feelings sit underneath nearly everything else in this book, so they get looked at first. Two tools elsewhere lean on this chapter. My weather today and the daily check-in (Part One, Now, page 33; Part Two, Chapter I, page 76) ask for one word about how you are, because naming a feeling turns its volume down a little and a daily word catches feelings while they’re still small. And Say it so it lands (Part Two, Chapter IV, page 126) asks you to describe a feeling, because “I felt let down” is a good deal easier to hear than “you never care.”

Here is the knot in the stomach in quick strokes. On top, a short message from a manager. Under it, the body’s alarm, which has already decided something is wrong. Under that, the meaning your mind gives the alarm. The roots are state and setting, and signal and noise. Then, slowly, each layer gets its own page or two.

  1. A feeling is a signal, not a verdict.

    Feelings are fast messages about what matters to you. Fear says watch out. Anger says this seems unfair, or this is in my way. Sadness says something that mattered has gone. A signal is worth listening to. It can also be badly wrong about the details, the way a smoke alarm goes off for burned toast with exactly the same urgency it would give a house fire.

    Sunny days and big questions In a classic study, people phoned on sunny days rated their whole lives as more satisfying, and the bad-weather dip vanished once the interviewer mentioned the weather. Much bigger studies later found the weather effect itself is tiny. The useful part survives: spotting where a feeling comes from stops it coloring everything else.

    Schwarz and Clore (1983) · Moderate: a classic study of feelings as information; the weather effect proved very small

    Hayley’s best friend has a new best friend, or that’s how it feels, and Hayley is jealous and a bit ashamed of being jealous at thirty-four. The jealousy proves nothing about her, and nothing about whether the friend is drifting off either; it just shows how much the friendship matters, which is worth knowing, and possibly worth saying. “I’m being silly,” she texts eventually, “but I miss you.” The friend rings within the minute.

    Things to tell yourself “This feeling is telling me something matters. What is it?” “Is this the fire, or the toast?”

    Dig deeper: what feelings are for

  2. Feelings start in the body.

    Often the body goes first. Racing heart, hot face, a weight on the chest, a knot in the stomach. Then the brain tries to work out what the signal means. It guesses, and it isn’t always a good guesser. Which is why being hungry, or cold, or in pain, can feel so much like being upset.

    Reece is fifteen and has come home in a fury about a towel. Specifically, about his mom asking where his gym towel was. There is a good deal of door involved. After a grilled cheese sandwich and twenty minutes on the couch with the dog’s head on his knee, most of it has drained away, and he admits, through a mouthful, that he didn’t have any lunch. “I wasn’t hungry,” he says. Then, “I was a bit hungry.”

    A few times today, stop and ask what your body feels like right now, and whether any of it is simply hunger, or cold, or a sore back.

    Dig deeper: the body and the brain’s best guess

  3. Naming a feeling helps you hold it.

    Putting a feeling into words can turn its volume down. In brain-scan research by Lieberman and colleagues (2007), simply putting a name to a feeling (“I feel scared”) turned down the brain’s alarm response. A name gives a big, cloudy rush some edges, so you can see it and talk about it and decide what to do.

    It works even when it doesn’t feel like it A review by Torre and Lieberman found that naming a feeling can turn down its intensity even though, in the moment, it doesn’t feel as if you’re doing anything at all. So carry on with “something like sad” even when it seems pointless.

    Torre and Lieberman (2018) · Moderate: consistent lab evidence; how it works is still being worked out

    Two roommates spent a whole evening passing each other in the hall without a word. Nobody had done anything, as far as either of them knew. At about ten, one of them stopped on the stairs. “I think I’m embarrassed about the noise complaint,” she said, “and I’ve been taking it out on you by being weird.” The other one, who had spent two hours going back over everything she’d said that week, laughed so hard she had to sit down. Then she made some tea.

    Once a day, name one feeling, out loud or on paper. A guess like “something like sad” counts.

    Dig deeper: why naming works

    Professor Puddles

    If the words won’t come, weather words often will. “Foggy” or “stormy” is a perfectly good place to start.

    Tool: My weather today spreadloveandacceptance.com/quick-checks

  4. More words, better tools.

    “Bad” is a blunt instrument. Disappointed is different from left out, and both are different from overwhelmed or ashamed. Each one needs something different. A review by Kashdan, Barrett and McKnight (2015) found that people who can tell their feelings apart more finely tend to cope with them in healthier ways. You don’t need a big vocabulary. A number does the job. So does a color.

    Stephen told his partner he felt bad about his mom and they went around in circles for half an hour. Bad how? Bad about what? Then, out of nowhere, staring at the fridge: “I feel guilty I haven’t been up since Easter. And I’m scared she’s getting worse.” Within ten minutes they were looking at trains to Carlisle, and the cheapest one turned out to leave at 6.12 in the morning, which led to a whole different conversation about who was going to drive them to the station.

    Words you could use “On a scale of one to ten, I’m about a six.” “It’s less angry and more… let down.” “It feels heavy, like a gray day.”

    Dig deeper: finer words, finer tools

  5. Feelings come in layers.

    The feeling you show first isn’t always the one you felt first. Anger very often sits on top of hurt or fear, because anger is a stronger place to stand. And we have feelings about our feelings (ashamed of being sad, mad about being scared) and that second layer can sting more than the first.

    School break has been canceled again, for the second time. Brenda’s daughter rings to say so, with a lot of reasons, all of them good ones, and Brenda says, “Fine. Well. Another time,” in a voice like a closing door. Under that is hurt, and under the hurt, if she let herself look, there is a quieter worry that she isn’t needed much anymore by anyone, which is the one she has spent the last two years carefully not looking at. She doesn’t look. She puts the phone down and sits next to it for a while with her coat still on.

    Next time you’re angry, you might ask whether there’s hurt or worry underneath. You don’t have to tell anyone what you find.

    Dig deeper: first feelings and feelings about feelings

  6. Feelings rise and pass like waves.

    Most feelings, even big ones, rise and peak and settle, as long as you don’t keep feeding them. Moods are something else. A mood is more like weather, a background feeling that hangs about for hours or days and colors everything without announcing itself.

    Not every wave is the same length Of 27 emotions in one study, sadness lasted longest, and shame, fear and disgust were among the shortest. The long ones tended to follow events that mattered, and to be chewed over.

    Verduyn and Lavrijsen (2015) · Moderate: a single self-report study, in line with other research on how long feelings last

    By eleven o’clock on a Saturday morning Rachel had decided her whole life was going nowhere. In fairness it had been a morning. The water heater, a letter from the city, and a dream about her ex in which he was, for some reason, a dentist. By seven that evening, after a walk along the canal and an hour with her sister, the same life looked fairly ordinary and mostly all right, with an actual dentist on Tuesday and a library book she wanted to finish. Nothing in her life changed between eleven and seven.

    So if you can, leave big decisions until the wave has gone past. Write it down. Look at it tomorrow.

    Dig deeper: waves and weather

  7. Feelings spread between people.

    We catch each other’s feelings from a tight voice, a sigh, a door shut slightly too hard, usually without noticing we’ve caught anything. It’s part of how people bond. It also means stress can go around a house or a team like a cold in February.

    Bryony came into the Monday meeting late and rattled, and within ten minutes six people who had been perfectly fine at nine o’clock felt behind on everything. The following Monday she stood outside the door for two slow breaths before going in. The meeting finished on time. In that office this was regarded as a minor miracle and nobody could work out why.

    You can care about someone’s feeling without catching the whole of it. Good moods are catching too, and Stay close (spreadloveandacceptance.com/bonding) has small ideas for passing one on. Notice who you tend to catch things from, and give yourself a minute before you next talk to them.

    Dig deeper: how feelings spread

    Tidbit

    Good moods are catching too. If you’d like a small way to share one, there’s a tool for it.

    Tool: Stay close: one small idea spreadloveandacceptance.com/bonding

  8. If you weren’t brought up to talk about feelings.

    Lots of people grew up in homes, generations or cultures where feelings were kept private. “Don’t make a fuss.” “Big boys don’t cry.” “We don’t talk about that.” It’s especially common among men and older people, and in some cultures keeping your feelings to yourself is a sign of respect and strength.

    It isn’t a flaw, and it doesn’t mean you don’t feel. Many people who rarely put a feeling into words show it every day by doing things, fixing the faucet or driving someone to the ER at two in the morning and waiting in the parking lot till it’s over. They turn up. Caring by doing is real caring. Words can be added slowly, a few at a time, if you want them.

    Len was a builder for forty years and his wife died in the spring. He has never in his life said how he feels about anything, apart from the Steelers. On the touchline at his grandson’s match, during a long dull bit of the first half, he says to his son, “I wasn’t brought up to say this. But I miss her. Every morning.” His son puts a hand on his shoulder and leaves it there. Neither of them says anything else for the rest of the match. They watch the second half, which is also dull, and it’s one of the better afternoons either of them has had all year.

    Ways to say it “I wasn’t brought up to say this, but I miss her.” “I’m not good with words for this. It’s been a hard week.” “I don’t know what to call it. I just feel heavy.” “I’m not one for talking, but I wanted you to know I’m proud of you.”

    If one of those fits, you could say it once this week, to one person, or just out loud in the car. A text counts.

    Dig deeper: when feelings weren’t talked about

  9. Feeling it isn’t the same as doing it.

    A feeling usually arrives with an urge attached, to shout or leave or hide or send the text you’ll regret by dinnertime. You don’t choose the feeling, but you get rather more say over the urge. Pushing a feeling down tends to bring it back bigger, and acting on every urge hurts people, so the middle way is to let the feeling be there and choose the action.

    A crash from the yard. Through the kitchen window, Imran’s son is standing very still beside the greenhouse with a soccer ball, and there is a lot less greenhouse than there was. Imran feels the heat go up his neck. He opens the back door, says, “I’m too angry to talk about this. Ten minutes,” shuts it again, and goes to find the dustpan. By the time he comes out his son has picked up most of the big bits, very carefully, in gardening gloves two sizes too large.

    Dig deeper: feelings, urges and choices

Friday, 9:05am

The knot’s back. This time you give it a name, which is scared, and then you do the thing you’d been avoiding and just ask. Your manager looks honestly baffled. “Oh God, no. It’s the summer schedule.” You go back to your desk and eat the breakfast you skipped, a banana that’s been in your bag since Wednesday.

Two ways to read this

A feeling, sent and received

Some people feel first and find the words later, sometimes much later. Asked “What’s wrong?” they honestly may not know yet. Others name a feeling almost as it arrives and expect everyone else to as well. If you name things fast, the quiet person may not be hiding anything. Their words are still on the way. If you need time, the quick namer may not be pushing. To them, saying it is how a feeling gets smaller.

Where the fields meet. Music has known for a long time that tone and tempo carry more than the words, and a feeling is often heard in the tune before the lyrics. Psychology adds that mood filters what we hear, so the same sentence lands differently on a bad day.

In everyday life

If you live on your own, nobody is going to notice how you are, so a one-word check-in with yourself each day matters more (see On my own, spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own). With a partner, “What are you feeling?” can sound like an exam. “Do you want to tell me, or shall I just sit with you?” is much easier to answer. Children learn feeling words from the grown-ups near them, and hearing you say “I’m frustrated, so I’m going to take a breath” teaches more than any lesson. At work, “I’m a bit low today and I’m not upset with anyone” can stop a whole team guessing. And if someone close to you shows care by doing, like clearing the drive on your bad day, you can thank them for it in words. They may not know what to do with it the first time.

Common mix-ups

Some feelings hurt and some actions do harm, but a feeling on its own isn’t bad. It’s information. Feeling stupid doesn’t make you stupid, either, so treat a feeling as something to check before you obey it. People also expect to know right away what they feel, and plenty can’t, some of them most days, which is why body words and numbers count as answers here. The most stubborn mix-up is the idea that a face tells you what someone feels. Faces are a poor guide. People show the same feeling in very different ways, and asking is kinder than guessing and a lot more accurate.

If you want to help someone else with this

Ask before you name it for them. “You’re angry” can land like a label. “You seem upset, am I reading that right?” leaves them room to put you straight. Then help the feeling make sense (“Of course you’re upset, that was a lot”), which does more than advice and doesn’t mean you agree with everything they did. Ask whether they want ideas or just company. A lot of people only want the second and are relieved to be asked. Take other ways of saying it, a number or a text or “I’m at a seven.” And settle yourself first. If their sadness makes you anxious, calm down before you go in, or they’ll end up looking after you.

You could say “That sounds really hard.” “Do you want to talk, or would company help more?” “You don’t have to find the right word. A number is fine.”

Part Three · Chapter 2

Stress and the nervous system: the ladder, flooding, rest and recovery

What stress does to your body and your mind, why kind people say things they don’t mean when they’re flooded, and which kinds of rest actually put something back.

In this chapter

  1. Stress is your body getting ready
  2. Stress depends on what you have to meet it
  3. The ladder: three everyday states
  4. When you’re flooded, thinking goes offline
  5. Stress adds up, like a tank filling
  6. Settle the body first
  7. Rest isn’t one thing
  8. Sleep and stress feed each other
  9. Stress is easier to carry when it’s shared
  10. In everyday life
  11. Common mix-ups
  12. If you want to help someone else with this
  13. Workpapers, tools and reading on this site
  14. More for your situation

Monday, 7:52am

The bus is late. One school shoe is missing, last seen under the sofa on Saturday. Your phone buzzes with a message from work that begins “Quick one,” which it never is. From the hall your partner calls, “Have you seen my keys?” and you hear yourself shout, “I’m not your secretary!”

A second later you’re standing there wondering where that came from. It wasn’t the keys. You were behind before anyone had said a word, before the shoe went missing, probably before you were even out of bed.

Feelings got their own chapter (Chapter 1, page 160). This one goes a layer down, to the nervous system underneath them, and what it does when the pressure’s on. Knowing how stress works won’t make Monday any quieter. It does make your own reactions, and other people’s, a lot less mysterious.

It also explains why some of the tools elsewhere work at all. The stress tank in Part Two, Chapter III (page 109) asks how full you are before you judge the moment, because stress piles up from small loads. The Calm-Down Kit in Part One, Now (page 33) settles the body before any words, and it asks you to name a time to come back, so a pause doesn’t look like walking out. And the setup score in Part Two, Chapter II (page 90) counts stress as well as hours, since a split can look fair on paper and still leave one person running on empty.

In quick strokes: the surface is a missing shoe. Underneath it, a body already in alarm before anyone spoke. Underneath that, a week with no recovery in it. The roots are limited capacity and state and setting. Now one at a time, starting with the body.

  1. Stress is your body getting ready.

    Something needs dealing with, and your body gears up before you’ve decided anything. Heart faster, breath quicker, muscles tight, stress hormones up. Which is exactly what you want when a glass is sliding off the table. The trouble starts when the body stays geared up for hours and never gets the message to stand down.

    Morag is a nurse. She handles a cardiac arrest on the ward calmly and well. She gets home at nine, eats half a sandwich standing up at the counter, and at 10:30 finds herself sobbing at an ad for car insurance. Car insurance has never moved her to anything before. Her body is still running the emergency it thinks she’s in.

    So after something stressful, give your body a clear sign that it’s over, whether that’s a walk around the block or a hot shower or one song played much too loud in the car on the way home. The body takes its cue from what you do far more than from what you tell it.

    Dig deeper: the stress response

  2. Stress depends on what you have to meet it.

    The same deadline lands on two colleagues on a Thursday afternoon, and one of them has a quiet evening ahead and a takeout menu. The other has a seven-year-old at home with a temperature and a partner away in Chicago till Saturday. On paper it’s one task. Guess which of them is awake at 3am.

    Stress grows when a demand looks bigger than what you’ve got to meet it with, whether that’s time or energy or money or help or sleep. That’s why a small thing tips you over on a bad day. It’s also why giving someone more support can shrink their stress without changing the job at all. When something feels huge, I’d write two lists side by side, one for what it asks of you and one for what you’ve got. Then ignore the first list for a minute and ask what would make the second one a line longer.

    You could say “It’s less the task than how little I’ve got left today.” “What would make this feel more doable?”

    Dig deeper: demands and resources

  3. The ladder: three everyday states.

    The ladder is a picture of the states your body moves between in a day. Near the bottom you’re calm and connected, breathing easily, able to hear something difficult without bristling. Higher up you’re revved up, tense, and small things start to feel urgent or personal. Then there’s running on empty, which is low and slow, with the words just out of reach.

    Most people go up and down it many times a day. Derek minds his granddaughter on Wednesdays, and at two o’clock he’s calm and connected and they’re doing a jigsaw. By four she has found the felt-tips and the wall, and he’s revved up. By six, when her mom comes, he is sitting on the kitchen floor eating a fish stick off her plate and can’t remember the word for colander. Neither of them had changed, only the hour, and how much afternoon was left in him.

    The Nervous System Ladder (spreadloveandacceptance.com/quick-checks) is a thirty-second check that gives you a best guess at where you are. If you’d rather not use a screen, set three reminders on your phone for today, and each time one goes off, notice which called you’re on. Don’t do anything about it, just notice.

    Dig deeper: the ladder

  4. When you’re flooded, thinking goes offline.

    At the top of the stress curve your body is in full alarm, and the things a hard conversation needs most (careful thinking, listening, seeing the other side) get much harder to reach. Lots of people call this being flooded. You might say something you don’t mean, or freeze, or want nothing in the world except to be out of the room.

    Two brothers start clearing their dad’s house one wet Saturday in March. Within twenty minutes they are shouting at each other about a standard lamp. Neither of them likes the lamp. Neither of them wants it. One of them says “Fine, take it then!” and the other says “I don’t want it!” and they stand there either side of it, breathing hard, while the actual subject sits in the boxes all around them and nobody says it.

    A flooded person is still a decent person whose body has to come down before the talk can go anywhere. Know your own flood signs in advance. Heat in the face is a common one. So is a racing heart, or the room going narrow, or a voice in your head that has gone very loud and very certain. Two at once is your cue to stop. Then say so in plain words, something like “I’m too flooded to listen well. Can we stop for twenty minutes and come back at four?”

    Dig deeper: flooding

  5. Stress adds up, like a tank filling.

    Picture a tank holding everything you’re already carrying today. The traffic goes in. So does the meeting that overran, and the noisy store, and the text from your mom that just says “Call me when you can.” It’s all one tank, and by the evening something tiny makes it overflow and gets the blame for the whole lot.

    Hassles beat headlines In a classic study, everyday hassles predicted how people were doing better than major life events did, even once the big events were taken into account. Which is why a missing shoe can be the thing that tips you over.

    Kanner and colleagues (1981) · Moderate: a classic study; many later studies agree

    Asked to empty the dishwasher, Kyle, who is fifteen, explodes. Really explodes, a whole speech about how he does everything in this house. It’s days later, from a friend’s mom at school pickup, that his own mom finds out his closest friendship fell apart at lunchtime that Monday, over something said in a group chat. The dishwasher was just the next thing anyone asked of him.

    Small daily hassles count as much as big events here, which surprises people. Before you react to a small thing in the evening, ask how full you were before it happened. How much are you carrying? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-02-how-much-are-you-carrying) is five quick questions, and Part Two, Chapter III (page 109) uses it to tell old stress from new.

    Dig deeper: why stress adds up

    Professor Puddles

    Stress fills up a little at a time, like a puddle in a long spell of rain. Five quick questions tell you how full yours is today.

    Workpaper WP-02: How much are you carrying? spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-02

  6. Settle the body first.

    You can’t think your way out of a body in alarm. You can help the body come down, though, and the thinking usually follows. Slow breathing with long out-breaths works for a lot of people. So does moving, or humming something you know by heart, or steady pressure like a heavy blanket, or simply leaving the noisy room. What works is personal, which is why it’s worth finding your own short list on a calm day and not in the middle of a fight.

    Before she has to give some difficult feedback, Bridie feels her heart going. She walks once around the staff parking lot, breathing out slowly past the dumpsters and the smokers’ shelter, and goes in a little steadier, if not exactly calm. Put your list on your phone. The Calm-Down Kit (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-11) helps you build it. If you only keep one line from this section, keep “body first, words second.”

    Dig deeper: settling the body

  7. Rest isn’t one thing.

    An hour on the couch scrolling can leave you more tired than when you sat down. That’s because recovery comes in different kinds, and sleep is only one of them, alongside switching off from work in your head, real relaxation, doing something absorbing that you enjoy, and the plain feeling of being in charge of your own time for once. None of them stands in for the others.

    Four kinds of recovery Researchers who study unwinding after work separate four things: switching off in your head, relaxing, doing something absorbing that stretches you a little, and being in charge of your own time. An evening that gives you none of the four isn’t much of a rest, however long you sit down.

    Sonnentag and Fritz (2007) · Strong: a widely used measure; recovery research is large and consistent

    Two roommates have friends over on a Saturday for a takeout and a game show on TV. One wakes up on Sunday buzzing. The other spends the whole of Sunday in her room with a library book and the door shut, and comes out at dinnertime feeling human again. Company fills some people up and drains others, and neither of them is doing rest wrong.

    Ask yourself which kind of tired you are, whether it’s your body or your brain, or people, or feelings, then pick a rest that matches rather than the one you always go for. Calm sounds and music (spreadloveandacceptance.com/soundscapes) is one kind, if you like that sort of thing.

    Dig deeper: kinds of rest

    Sugarfoot

    Rest can be a nap, a walk or ten minutes of quiet music. Find the kind that suits you, and keep it somewhere you can reach it.

    Tool: Cool-down corner: calm sounds and music spreadloveandacceptance.com/soundscapes

  8. Sleep and stress feed each other.

    Stress makes sleep harder, and poor sleep makes stress land harder. After a short or broken night small things feel bigger, tempers are shorter, and people pull away from each other. This one is well studied. In a brain-scan study by Yoo and colleagues (2007), one night without sleep made the brain’s alarm center react more strongly to upsetting pictures.

    In a daily study by Gordon and Chen (2014), couples reported more conflict after nights of poor sleep. In experiments by Ben Simon and Walker (2018), people who had missed a night’s sleep kept others at a greater distance and felt lonelier.

    Saoirse comes off her third night shift at the nursing home and bursts into tears in the parking lot over a parking ticket. Her sister, on speakerphone, says, “You’ve had no sleep, leave it, we’ll deal with it Thursday.” By Thursday it is a parking ticket again, annoying and payable, and she pays it online on her lunch break between a granola bar and a yogurt.

    You can’t always fix sleep, but you can notice when it’s part of the story. Before a hard conversation, ask whether you’ve both slept, and if not, pick another time. At night, do the same few calm things before bed in the same order, so your body learns the signal.

    You could say “I slept badly, so if I’m short with you today, that’s why.” “Can we talk about this after we’ve both slept?”

    Dig deeper: sleep and stress

  9. Stress is easier to carry when it’s shared.

    People calm each other down. A steady voice, a hand on the shoulder, or just a quiet person in the same room can help a nervous system settle. Saying your state out loud helps too, because “I’m stressed about work” stops your partner wondering if it’s about them.

    Fish sticks again, Tuesday. Kwasi says to his ten-year-old, without quite looking at him, “I’m a bit stressed about money this month. Sorting it is my grown-up job, and you’re not in trouble.” His son nods and carries on eating. Nothing else is said. Over the next few days the boy stops tiptoeing around him, and on Friday he brings his math homework to the table again and asks for help with it, which he hasn’t done since school break.

    Dig deeper: stress between people

Monday, 7:58am

Six minutes later your partner is by the front door, still patting their pockets. “Sorry,” you say. “I was full up before you opened your mouth.” And then, after a moment, “Bathroom shelf, next to the toothpaste.” They laugh, and ask if it’s been a bad start. The bus is still late and the shoe is still missing.

Two ways to read this

A full tank, two ways

For some people, stress shows up loudly: a sharp voice, a slammed cupboard. For others it goes inward and quiet, and the first sign anyone sees is a person who has stopped answering. If you get loud, the quiet one may be just as full, only less visible. If you go quiet, the loud one is probably not angry with you. They are usually full, and it’s coming out sideways.

Where the fields meet. Neurobiology’s idea is that your state sets the volume, and stress left over from earlier still counts. Economics says the same thing in money terms: a household or a person running at full stretch has no margin left for an ordinary bad day.

In everyday life

Living on your own means nobody’s there to notice when you’re running on empty, so build rest into the week before you need it. With a partner, agree a pause word on a calm day, plus the rule that whoever pauses names a time to come back (One of you wants to talk now, the other needs space, spreadloveandacceptance.com/pursue-withdraw, has more on this). A child can’t settle until the nearest grown-up does. Your calm is something they borrow for years before they can make their own. At work, a flooded colleague can’t take in feedback, and waiting an hour usually beats pushing on.

Some people run on empty for reasons built into their lives, like shift work, a long-term illness or caring for someone. What that needs is a different setup. More effort won’t do it (see Different hours, spreadloveandacceptance.com/different-hours, and Caregivers, spreadloveandacceptance.com/caregivers). If you have ADHD, just keeping track of everything can fill the tank before breakfast. Get the remembering out of your head and into the world, with labeled alarms and one hook for the keys, and plan hard talks for your better time of day. More in the expanded version (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-2-stress-in-depth).

Common mix-ups

People often think all stress is bad, and it isn’t. Short bursts help you rise to something, and the harm comes from stress that never gets a recovery. Being calm doesn’t mean not being upset, either. You can be calm and sad, or calm and extremely firm. Pausing gets mistaken for avoiding, but a pause with a time to come back is how you finish a talk well. Avoiding is the pause that never comes back. Rest gets called lazy, though bodies and minds that never recover tend to break. And short replies with a flat face get read as not caring, when far more often they mean someone is worn out.

If you want to help someone else with this

Nobody in the history of the world has calmed down because they were told to. A lower voice, slower words and a steady presence do far more. Taking one job off someone’s list beats any pep talk. Ask what kind of help they’d like (practical help, company, distraction, some space) instead of guessing. Don’t argue with someone who’s flooded. Offer a break and a time to come back, because the facts will still be there in twenty minutes. And if someone has been running on empty for weeks, say so kindly and take one job off their list.

You could say “You seem really stretched. Is there one thing I could take off your plate?” “We don’t have to sort this now. Shall we pick it up after dinner?”

Part Three · Chapter 3

How we see each other: perception, bias, and the stories we tell

Why two people can watch the same moment and come away with two different stories, and how to see others, and yourself, a little more fairly.

In this chapter

  1. Seeing is a best guess
  2. You see what you’re looking for
  3. We fill the gaps with stories
  4. We judge ourselves by our reasons, and others by their actions
  5. Quick shortcuts can lead us astray
  6. Everyone feels like the one who sees clearly
  7. “Us” and “them” changes what we see
  8. Ask, don’t guess
  9. In everyday life
  10. Two memories of one evening, or gaslighting?
  11. Common mix-ups
  12. If you want to help someone else with this
  13. Tools and reading on this site
  14. More for your situation

At a glance

  • Seeing is a best guess. Your brain fills in a lot of what you think you see and hear.
  • We fill gaps with stories, and the story often feels like a fact.
  • We judge ourselves by our reasons and others by their actions, and that gap causes a lot of hurt.
  • Asking is kinder and more accurate than trying to read someone’s mind.

Wednesday, 12:15pm

You wave at a colleague across the canteen, tray in one hand, soup slopping. She looks straight through you and walks out.

All afternoon. All afternoon you go back through Monday’s meeting, that thing you said about the budget, the email you didn’t reply to. At four o’clock she messages. Sorry I didn’t stop earlier, I’d just had a call about my dad. She hadn’t seen you at all.

How feelings work (page 160) and Stress and the nervous system (page 174) look inward. This chapter looks outward, at how we see other people, and why misunderstandings are so common even between kind and clever people. Before I built any of this I spent my career as a government auditor, walking into situations where nobody could tell me straight what had happened. Almost everyone, it turned out, was doing their best with the piece of the picture they could actually see. This chapter is more or less about that.

Some of the tools elsewhere depend on it. Who did what (the Preface to Part Two, page 62) exists because everyone sees their own effort more clearly than other people’s, so two honest guesses of “I do about 60%” can add up to well over 100%, and one shared page settles it. Rewind the talk (Part Two, Chapter III, page 109) slows down the habit of judging ourselves by our reasons and others by their actions. And the Chat analyzer follows this chapter’s last idea, that asking beats guessing.

A wave that wasn’t returned, quickly. The surface is a colleague who walked past. Underneath, a story your mind wrote in a second. Underneath that, a brain saving effort with a shortcut. The roots are signal and noise, and limited capacity. Then slowly, shortcut by shortcut.

  1. Seeing is a best guess.

    Your eyes and ears take in far less than you think, and your brain fills in the rest from what it expects. Most of the time this works well, and fast. It also means what you see is partly what you expected, so two people can watch the same moment and honestly see different things.

    They saw a game Students from two rival universities, Princeton and Dartmouth, watched the same rough American football game and saw it very differently, right down to how many fouls each side committed. Same match, two games.

    Hastorf and Cantril (1954) · Moderate: a classic single case study, widely cited

    Under-12 soccer, a freezing Sunday morning, a field that is mostly mud. Archie’s mom sees him giving up, and says so, quietly, into her scarf. His dad, beside her with the flask, sees him being careful with the ankle he went over on last week. They argue about it all the way home and Archie, in the back, says nothing, because he was actually thinking about dinner.

    Dig deeper: perception as a best guess

  2. You see what you’re looking for.

    Attention is like a flashlight in a dark room. You see what it lights up and can miss what it doesn’t, even when it’s right in front of you. If you’re looking for proof that someone doesn’t care, you will notice every missed call and none of the little kindnesses.

    In her first week Rosie decided her new manager didn’t like her. For a month she noticed every short email he sent, and there were a lot. He sends short emails to everyone, including, as it turned out, his wife. What Rosie somehow didn’t clock was that he’d given her the best project on the team. A colleague pointed it out at the bar after somebody’s going-away party, and Rosie said, “Oh.” Then, “Oh no.”

    If there’s someone you’re struggling with, try writing down one kind thing they do each day for a week. It’s an odd exercise, and it tends to move the flashlight.

    Dig deeper: the flashlight of attention

  3. We fill the gaps with stories.

    When we don’t know why someone did something, the mind makes up a reason, fast. A late reply becomes anger, and a closed door becomes rejection. And the story arrives feeling like a fact. Memory works the same way, because every time we remember something we rebuild it a little, so two people can honestly remember the same evening differently.

    Two days without a reply. By Sunday evening you have decided she’s fed up with you, and you’ve drafted, then deleted, a message saying you’re sorry for whatever it was. On Monday morning she sends seventeen photographs from a campsite in Snowdonia with no signal, most of them of the same sheep. One message, “The story I’m telling myself is that you’re upset with me. Is that right?” would have saved two days of it.

    Dig deeper: stories and memory

  4. We judge ourselves by our reasons, and others by their actions.

    When you’re late, you know why, because it was the traffic or a phone call or a child who lost a shoe. When someone else is late you only see the lateness, and it’s very easy to decide they’re careless. We all tend to blame other people’s character for things that are really about their situation.

    The fundamental attribution error Lee Ross gave this habit its name: when we explain what someone else did, we tend to underrate the situation and overrate their character. It’s well replicated, though weaker in some cultures than in others.

    Ross (1977) · Strong: foundational and widely replicated

    A driver cuts in front of you on the beltway and you call him an idiot, not quite under your breath. The next week your mom has a fall and you’re racing to the hospital, and you cut someone off yourself, badly, at the intersection. You know exactly why you did it. You’d quite like them to know too. They don’t, and in their car, right now, you are an idiot.

    Thoughts you could try “What might be going on for them that I can’t see?” “If I did this, what would my reason be?”

    Dig deeper: actions and reasons

    Professor Puddles

    We know our own reasons and only see other people’s actions. Try writing out their side, in their words. It’s irritatingly effective.

    Tool: Rewind the talk spreadloveandacceptance.com/carrier-wave-decoder

  5. Quick shortcuts can lead us astray.

    The brain uses shortcuts to save time, and plenty are useful. Some lead to unfair judgments, like a first impression that colors everything after it, or one bad moment that outweighs ten good ones, or a quick guess about someone from their age or accent or looks or group. Everyone has these, and the trouble only starts when nobody notices them.

    Bad is stronger than good That’s the real title of a wide review, which found that bad events, feedback and behavior usually hit harder and last longer than equally good ones. There are exceptions, but it explains how one box in the hall can outweigh months of tidiness.

    Baumeister and colleagues (2001) · Strong: a widely cited review; the pattern is accepted, with known exceptions

    On day one, the new tenant left a box in the hall, just the one, for an afternoon. Tash decided there and then that he was messy, and every bit of mess after that was proof. Her own mug collection on the landing, eleven mugs at the last count, went entirely unseen, by her, though he saw it. He didn’t say anything for months, which, when it finally came out, was its own small argument.

    Dig deeper: shortcuts and bias

  6. Everyone feels like the one who sees clearly.

    Most of us feel we see things as they really are, and anyone who disagrees must be missing something. The other person feels exactly the same about you. Each of you can see the other’s lens much more easily than your own.

    Two brothers in their fifties argued, at their mom’s eightieth, about how they’d been brought up. “I’m just being realistic,” said one. “So am I,” said the other. They were both right. Each was being entirely realistic about the childhood he had lived through, which turned out, when they finally compared notes in the parking lot, to have been quite a different childhood, in the same house, four years apart.

    Words you could use “I think we’re both seeing this from where we stand. Can you tell me how it looks from yours?”

    Dig deeper: why we each feel like the realist

  7. “Us” and “them” changes what we see.

    People split into groups quickly, even over tiny things. We tend to see our own group as varied and full of individuals and other groups as all the same, and we give our own side the benefit of the doubt. Spending real time with people from the other group, as equals, is one of the best ways to soften this.

    At one depot the night shift calls the day shift lazy and the day shift calls the night shift sloppy, and has done since before anyone can remember. Then there was a joint training day, with a bad buffet and a fire drill in the rain. By the afternoon people were using each other’s names. It didn’t fix everything, though the notes on the kettle stopped.

    Have one real conversation this month with someone from a group you tend to see as “other,” and ask about their day before you ask about their views.

    Dig deeper: us and them

  8. Ask, don’t guess.

    Imagining yourself in someone’s shoes is a kind start, though research suggests it doesn’t make us much more accurate about what they think, while asking does. A plain, curious question like “What was that like for you?” beats the cleverest guess.

    Every Sunday Moira’s grandson sat at her kitchen table glued to his phone, and every Sunday she decided a bit more firmly that he hated coming. One week she just asked. “Don’t you like coming here, sweetie?” He looked up, horrified, with his thumb still on the screen. He’d been messaging a friend who was having a terrible time. He liked her house because it was calm, he said, and for the crumble. He wouldn’t have mentioned the crumble if she hadn’t asked. She makes two now, and sends one home with him in a container she never gets back.

    Dig deeper: seeing more fairly

Thursday, 12:20pm

She’s in the canteen again. This time you go over and ask how her dad is. She tells you about the hospital and the waiting and the parking lot charges, which seem to be the thing she’s angriest about. You end up sharing a table until the end of the break. Your soup goes cold. You don’t mind.

Two ways to read this

Blunt feedback, two ways

Some people hear softening as part of the message and take a bare comment as a sign that something’s wrong between you. Others hear the softening as noise and want the point first, because a clear point is quicker to fix. If you like softening, “The second half doesn’t work” may be the most helpful thing that person can say, with no judgment of you in it. If you like it plain, adding one warm sentence for the other person costs very little and lets the point land.

Where the fields meet. Philosophy’s habit of separating the fact from the guess is most of this chapter. Economics explains why the guess comes so fast: attention is a budget, and the brain saves it with shortcuts that are usually right and sometimes badly wrong.

In everyday life

We tell stories about ourselves too, and “I always mess things up” is usually built from a few bright memories that leave a lot out. After years together, partners stop checking and start assuming. And “I know what you meant” can do a lot of quiet damage in a long relationship. Children get labeled early, the difficult one, the easy one, and the label becomes a lens that only sees what fits. With ADHD, attention gets pulled by whatever is new or urgent and can lock on hard, so someone may genuinely not have seen or heard. Get their attention first and put requests in writing. More in the expanded version (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-3-seeing-in-depth).

Two memories of one evening, or gaslighting?

Two people often remember the same evening differently. Memory isn’t a recording. Each person noticed and kept different parts, and stress, tiredness and strong feelings blur it further, so most “That’s not what happened!” arguments are two honest memories. Gaslighting describes something much rarer, and the word does real harm when it’s used for an ordinary disagreement.

For something to be gaslighting, these are usually all present:

  • the same person denies, again and again, things the other person saw, heard or knows happened,
  • they know it happened, so the denial is deliberate,
  • the aim is to make the other person doubt their own memory or judgment in general,
  • it usually gains them something, such as winning, avoiding blame or getting their way.

Not enough on its own:

  • two people remembering it differently,
  • someone misremembering, especially when tired, stressed or upset,
  • disagreeing about what something meant,
  • one heated “That never happened!” in the middle of a fight,
  • “I don’t think I meant it like that.”

Ask whether it happens in both directions, and whether the conversation settles when you look at a message or a calendar. Then talk about what each of you remembers rather than the word itself. “I remember you saying Saturday. You remember Sunday. Can we check the message and plan from there?” keeps both memories in the room.

Common mix-ups

Nobody sees things exactly as they are. Everyone sees through a lens, and knowing that is where fairness starts. Memory isn’t a recording, either, since it gets rebuilt each time, so two honest people can remember the same evening differently and both be telling the truth. Giving someone the benefit of the doubt doesn’t mean ignoring what happened. It means checking the story before you decide, and if something hurtful keeps happening, that matters. And a face or a tone is a clue to what someone meant. Faces and tones vary a lot between people and between cultures, so a face is a weaker clue than it feels.

If you want to help someone else with this

Start with how they feel, and make sense of the feeling first, and only then wonder aloud whether there might be another way to see it. Offer information instead of verdicts. “I know she had a hard week” helps more than “You’re being unfair to her.” Check your own guesses out loud (“I assumed he was annoyed, I’ll ask”), which shows how it’s done. Be careful with labels for children and colleagues, because they stick and then shape what everyone sees. And believe people about their own experience. Seeing other angles never means telling someone that what happened to them didn’t happen.

Words to try “That sounds really hurtful. Do you know what was going on for them?” “It might be worth asking. Want to plan what to say?”
