Part Three · Chapter 4

How communication works: meaning, listening, repair and messages

Talking feels simple because we do it all day, yet every message has to travel from one mind to another, and a lot can change on the way. This chapter follows that journey and looks at what helps a message arrive the way you meant it.

In this chapter

  1. Meaning is made between two people
  2. Every message says two things
  3. Listening is something you do
  4. Check, don’t guess
  5. Hard things land better when they start soft
  6. Mix-ups are normal. Repair is the skill
  7. Messages lose their tone on the way
  8. Different styles aren’t wrong styles
  9. Small talk has a job, and it can be short
  10. In everyday life
  11. Going quiet can mean very different things
  12. When the past joins the conversation
  13. Common mix-ups
  14. If you want to help someone else with this
  15. Workpapers, tools and reading on this site
  16. More for your situation

At a glance

  • Meaning is made between two people. What you say and what they hear can differ without either of you being wrong.
  • Every message says two things, the words themselves and what they seem to say about the two of you.
  • A short question saves a long misunderstanding, so check before you guess.
  • Mix-ups are normal, and repairing them is the skill. Small talk is allowed to be short.

Thursday, 8:15am

Ana texts her brother. Can you call me when you’re free?

She means no rush, small question about the weekend. He reads it at the back of the 8:10 bus, and for eleven stops, past the hospital, which doesn’t help, he works out who is ill.

Small habits help a message arrive. Listening, checking, starting softly, mending quickly. A few ready-made lines make small talk easier for anyone who dreads it. And three tools elsewhere lean on this chapter. Say it so it lands (Part Two, Chapter IV, page 126) asks for what happened, how you feel and one clear request, because every message carries a second message about the relationship. The 90-second daily check-in (Part Two, Chapter I, page 76) keeps repairs small and frequent. And the Chat analyzer’s whole-conversation view shows where a written conversation lost its tone.

A text with no kisses, in quick strokes. On the surface, three words. Underneath, the tone the reader added. Underneath that, what it seemed to say about the two of you. The roots are signal and noise, and feedback loops, since every reply changes the next one. The chapter slows down from here.

  1. Meaning is made between two people.

    Words don’t carry meaning on their own. The speaker has a meaning in mind, and the listener builds their own from the words, the tone, the timing and everything they already expect. Most of the time the two match well enough. Sometimes they don’t, and neither person can see the gap from where they’re standing.

    “Let’s chat tomorrow,” the manager wrote to the new hire at 4:50, meaning a friendly catch-up and possibly a cookie. The new hire went home and reread his last three emails looking for the mistake. He found two, neither of which existed. In the morning there was a cookie, which he couldn’t face. The sentence that would have saved him an evening is a dull one, “I think what you meant and what I heard might be two different things. Can we check?”

    Dig deeper: how meaning travels

  2. Every message says two things.

    There is what you say, and there is what it says about the two of you. “You’re late” is a fact about time, though it can also mean “I was worried” or “I don’t matter to you.” People argue about the fact when the hurt is in the second layer.

    I take one eight-word sentence apart on the website’s About page: “don’t worry about it, I’ll take care of it.” Said kindly, in passing, it’s reassurance. Said for the third time that month about the same job, it also says a job has no owner and a decision has been put off again, and both of those are in the same eight words.

    Content and relationship Watzlawick and colleagues made this one of their axioms of communication: every message has a content level and a relationship level, and the relationship level often decides how the content is heard. It’s a framework rather than an experiment, and a remarkably durable one.

    Watzlawick, Beavin and Jackson (1967) · Theory: influential in communication and family therapy

    Or take Tomasz, who wants to know whether his roommate used his good pan. On the surface it’s a question about a pan. Underneath, it’s a question about whether his things are respected in this house, and no amount of talk about the pan is going to settle that. “Honestly,” he said in the end, “I don’t care about the pan.” His roommate, who had in fact used the pan, washed it and put it back in the wrong cupboard, looked baffled. “Then why have we been talking about it for ten minutes?”

    Dig deeper: the two layers of a message

  3. Listening is something you do.

    Hearing happens by itself. Listening is a choice, and most of us do a lot of it partly in order to reply. To fix, or defend, or advise, or tell our own story. Real listening means following what the other person is trying to say, and letting them know you got it, before you add anything of yours.

    “School is pointless,” Mollie announced, thirteen, coat still on. Her dad started explaining, at some length and with examples, why it wasn’t. She stopped talking and went upstairs, and the door shut harder than it strictly needed to. The next time she said it, a week later, he bit his tongue, hard. “Pointless how?” he said. “Tell me about today.” She talked for twenty minutes, mostly about a supply teacher and a seating plan, and he said almost nothing, which nearly killed him.

    Dig deeper: what good listening is

  4. Check, don’t guess.

    Once we know something it’s very hard to imagine not knowing it, so we leave out steps, assume the other person can tell what we mean, and guess what they meant instead of asking. We do it most with the people we know best, which is unfortunate, because they’re the ones we most want to get it right with. A short check costs you a sentence, whereas a wrong guess can cost a whole evening.

    Closeness makes us lazy listeners In three small experiments, people overestimated how well they got through to friends and spouses even more than to strangers. Closeness seemed to switch off the checking we do without thinking with people we don’t know.

    Savitsky and colleagues (2011) · Moderate: three small experiments, extended in later work

    “Something low-key,” they agreed, for Fliss’s fortieth. Fliss pictured a Chinese takeout on the couch, in pajamas, with the good crackers. Her best friend booked a quiet table at the Italian, ironed a shirt, and turned up at seven with flowers. Fliss opened the door in her pajamas, and for a second they just looked at each other, both disappointed, both having thought it was obvious. They ate the takeout in the end, the friend in her ironed shirt, and it was a good night, eventually.

    Dig deeper: why we guess, and how to check

    Professor Puddles

    Checking what someone meant takes ten seconds and can save a whole evening. When you’re ready to reply, this workpaper helps.

    Workpaper WP-09: Say it so it lands spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-09

  5. Hard things land better when they start soft.

    How a hard conversation starts often decides how it ends. A complaint about one thing (“The trash wasn’t taken out”) is easier to hear than a criticism of the person (“You never help”). A simple shape works for most hard things, which is to say what happened, how you feel and what you would like.

    A woman wants her eighty-one-year-old father to stop driving at night. She has “You’re not safe anymore” on the tip of her tongue. She leaves it there and says, “You had two near-misses last month and I lie awake worrying. Could I drive us in the evenings?” He says he’ll think about it, which in his language is nearly a yes.

    Dig deeper: saying hard things kindly

  6. Mix-ups are normal. Repair is the skill.

    Even close, kind people misunderstand each other constantly, several times a day if you’re counting, and what keeps a relationship steady is noticing it and fixing it rather than never doing it. “That came out wrong.” “Can we start again?” Small repairs made often build trust much faster than big apologies made rarely.

    “Excuse me!” a woman snaps in the supermarket, because your cart is blocking the cans. “I’m moving,” you snap back. A second later you hear yourself add, “Sorry. Long day.” And she sags a bit and says hers has been too, and somehow you end up talking about the price of coffee for five minutes by the chopped tomatoes.

    Dig deeper: how repair works

    Sugarfoot

    A mix-up isn’t the end of anything. Come back, sit close, and go through it a step at a time.

    Tool: Rewind the talk spreadloveandacceptance.com/carrier-wave-decoder

  7. Messages lose their tone on the way.

    A text or email carries the words without your face or your voice, so the reader fills in the tone with however they feel right now. A tired reader hears a tired, irritated message. Short replies, missing greetings and late-night timing all get read as meaning something.

    The period problem In one study with students, short text replies ending in a period were rated less sincere than the same replies without one, while handwritten notes showed no such effect. Later work suggests it fades with longer messages, so this one is early days.

    Gunraj and colleagues (2016) · Early: one study with students

    In the group chat for the school summer fair, somebody proposes the tombola goes by the gate. One parent replies, “Fine.” Period and everything. Within four minutes two other parents have privately decided she’s furious and started composing careful messages. She was stirring a pan of soup, typing with one thumb, and genuinely thought it was fine.

    Before you send your next tricky message, read it out loud in the grumpiest voice you can manage. If it sounds harsh, add a warm word. This is my favorite test in the whole book, and it takes four seconds.

    Dig deeper: texts, email and tone

  8. Different styles aren’t wrong styles.

    Some people say exactly what they mean. Others hint, and expect you to read between the lines. Some talk fast and overlap, and others need a pause to think. Families and cultures and different kinds of mind all shape this, and a clash between two styles is usually a translation problem, with nobody being difficult on purpose.

    “Is the report ready?” “No. I need two more days.” Her manager heard that as rude, for about a month, until he decided to ask what she meant, over a coffee he didn’t want. She said she’d rather tell him the truth plainly than make him guess, and that where she grew up a straight answer was the polite one. After that he started finding her clarity a relief, and then, slightly to his surprise, a model.

    Words to try “I’m quite direct, so if I sound blunt, it doesn’t mean I’m upset.” “It helps me if you say exactly what you need.”

    Dig deeper: styles, cultures and minds

  9. Small talk has a job, and it can be short.

    Small talk (“Cold today, isn’t it?” “Busy weekend?”) isn’t really about the weather. Its job is to say that you see the other person and that the two of you are okay. In 1923 the anthropologist Bronisław Malinowski called this “phatic communion,” talk whose main purpose is bonding more than information. Small moments like this matter more than people expect. Sandstrom and Dunn (2014) found that people who had a short, friendly exchange with a coffee-shop barista felt more belonging and a better mood than people who kept it purely efficient.

    Small talk is hard work for many people, though, including many autistic people, shy or anxious people and people speaking a second language. The rules are unwritten, and it uses energy that some people would rather keep. A few ready-made lines, sometimes called social scripts, take the guesswork out, and keeping it short is allowed. For what it’s worth, this is the part I had to learn on purpose.

    Phil dreads school pickup. He has three lines ready, a “Morning! How’s your week going?” an “Oh, nice” and a “Right, I’d better get going, see you Friday.” Some mornings he still sits in the car with the radio on until the bell rings. Most days he gets through it. One of the other dads now saves him a spot by the fence, and has never once asked him how his week is going, which Phil appreciates more than he can say.

    You could say “Morning! How’s your week been?” “How do you know Nico?” “Oh, how was that?” “Great to see you. I’d better get going.” And to opt out kindly, “I’m not great at chit-chat, but it’s really nice to see you.”

    Dig deeper: small talk and social scripts

Thursday, 9:02am

He calls the second he’s off the bus. “Who’s ill?”

“Nobody! I wanted to know if you’re free Saturday. Dresser.”

He laughs, a bit shakily, and says he’ll bring the van. The week after, her text says, No rush and nothing’s wrong!! Quick q about Sat, call when free.

Two ways to read this

A message, two ways

For some people, “Fine.” with a period is just fine. For others it reads as a door being shut. Some people say exactly what they mean and hear exactly what’s said. Others wrap a request in a hint and expect it to be found. If you’re literal, the hint is a real request in soft packaging. If you hint, the literal person isn’t ignoring you. They need the ask said out loud.

Where the fields meet. Psychology’s short answer is that intent isn’t impact. The art of debating adds a habit that works at a kitchen table as well as in a debate: say the strongest version of their point back before you answer, and the disagreement turns into a shared problem.

In everyday life

On your own: how you talk to yourself

You send yourself messages all day, from “Typical, I always mess this up” to “That was hard and I handled it.” The same things apply. Notice the tone, check whether it’s fair, and mend it when it’s harsh. Catch one harsh sentence you say to yourself today and rewrite it the way you’d say it to someone you like.

zqaxunderstandingx4xcommunicationxxwithxothersqzWith other people

Between partners, “We never go out anymore” sounds like a complaint about evenings, and underneath it may mean “I miss you,” so answering that layer goes further than defending the calendar. “Stop that!” tells a child what not to do without saying what to do instead. “Feet on the floor, please” is easier to follow. In meetings, silence gets taken as agreement until a quieter colleague says afterward that she never agreed, and a round of “Anyone see it differently?” catches that early. “Are you eating properly?” is care in one generation’s language and checking up in another’s.

  • Feedback at work. Talk about the work rather than the person, with one recent example of what good looks like. Then ask, “What’s been getting in the way?” When you’re the one receiving it, “Thanks. Can I think about it and come back tomorrow?” is a fine first answer. The expanded version (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-4-communication-in-depth) walks through a whole performance conversation.

Going quiet can mean very different things.

When someone stops talking in an argument, it might be a shutdown, a need for space or the silent treatment, and from outside they can look the same. A shutdown happens when a person is flooded or overloaded and words go offline for a while. Autistic young people in Phung and colleagues (2021) described shutdowns as something that happens to them, separate from choosing to withdraw. Needing space is a choice to pause so the talk can go better later.

For something to be the silent treatment, sometimes called stonewalling, these are usually all present:

  • the silence is used as a message or a penalty,
  • it lasts well beyond the argument, often for days,
  • it ends only when the other person gives in or apologizes,
  • there’s no offer of a time to come back, and it’s often aimed at one person while everyone else gets warmth.

Not enough on its own:

  • going quiet when flooded or overloaded,
  • asking for a break, even an abrupt one,
  • needing time to think before speaking,
  • a quieter person’s normal pace.

One pattern is very common and nobody’s villainy. One person pushes to talk and the other pulls back, and each move makes the other stronger. A large review by Schrodt and colleagues (2014) linked this push-and-pull pattern with less satisfaction for both people, whichever role they played. If you’re the quiet one, a short line keeps the door open: “I can’t talk yet. I’m not punishing you. Give me an hour.” If you’re waiting, “Take your time. Can you tell me when?” asks for a time without putting a label on the pause.

When the past joins the conversation

Sometimes the size of a reaction belongs to an older moment. A raised voice can sound like a parent’s, and a closed door can feel like being shut out again. From outside you can’t know someone’s history, and guessing out loud (“This is about your dad”) usually makes things worse. What you can notice is the shape. The reaction is much bigger than the moment, the voice or face changes suddenly, or the person wants to leave or freezes.

You can’t calm someone down by telling them to calm down. You can change what you bring to the moment, and all of these are within your control:

  • Your pace. Slow down and use fewer words.
  • Your tone. Lower your voice and soften the volume.
  • Your body. Sit down if you’re standing, unclench your hands, and breathe out slowly. Slow breathing tends to calm the body (Zaccaro and colleagues, 2018 · Moderate evidence).
  • Space. Give the other person room, and don’t block a doorway or follow them.
  • Your words. Name what you see without blame (“This feels big. Let’s slow down.”). Putting feelings into words can turn them down a notch (Lieberman and colleagues, 2007 · Moderate evidence).
  • Timing. Agree to come back at a set time rather than pushing on.
  • Stepping away and coming back. “I’m going to step out for twenty minutes, and I’ll come back to this at seven.” Then come back at seven.

The same list works when the big reaction is yours.

Common mix-ups

“If they loved me, they’d just know” is the big one. Closeness makes us check less without making us understand any more, so saying it clearly is a kindness, and no test of love. Listening isn’t agreeing, either, because you can understand someone completely and still see it differently, and the understanding comes first. A repair doesn’t mean you’re confessing to being the bad one. It just says that didn’t go the way you wanted, and either person can make one. And texts feel safer for hard things because they’re easier to send. They’re also much easier to misread, so for anything tender, add warmth, or call.

If you want to help someone else with this

Maybe a friend keeps having the same argument with their partner, or your teenager feels nobody listens. You can’t talk for them. You can be the one person who really hears them, without fixing, which is often the most useful thing anyone does all week. You can help them pull the two layers apart, by asking what it was about and then what it seemed to say about the two of them. You can offer the simple shape (what happened, how they feel, what they’d like) and let them find their own words. And stay out of judging the other person’s character, since you only hear one side and they may make up next week. Notice if it’s more than a mix-up.

Words you could use “Do you want me to just listen, or help you think about what to say?”

Workpapers, tools and reading on the website

Try one of these this week with one real conversation. Say it so it lands (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-09-say-it-so-it-lands) helps you shape a hard sentence, Rewind the talk (spreadloveandacceptance.com/carrier-wave-decoder) walks you back through a talk that went wrong, and the wiring card (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wiring-card) puts how you communicate on one page.

Part Three · Chapter 5

Attachment, trust and belonging

Why we need each other, how the bonds we had early on shape what we expect today, and how trust and belonging are built and lost and built again, one small moment at a time.

In this chapter

  1. Belonging is a basic need
  2. Early bonds teach us what to expect
  3. Patterns, not boxes
  4. Trust is built in small moments
  5. Feeling safe with someone calms the body
  6. Fitting in isn’t the same as belonging
  7. When trust breaks, rebuilding takes time
  8. You can start building connection from wherever you are
  9. If you’re a teenager
  10. In everyday life
  11. Common mix-ups
  12. If you want to help someone else with this
  13. Reading on this site
  14. More for your situation

At a glance

  • Belonging is a basic need. Feeling lonely or left out is a signal, like hunger.
  • Early bonds set expectations that can change. What we learned about being cared for can soften over time.
  • Trust grows in small moments. Doing what you said, again and again, matters more than big gestures.
  • You can start small, with one friendly exchange or one kept promise.

Sunday, 9:30pm

Kai sent his friend a long message at lunchtime. Four paragraphs about the new job, and a question at the end. It says Read 12:47, and there’s nothing after that.

By dinnertime he’s gone from “she’s busy” to “she’s annoyed.” By nine thirty he’s wondering whether anybody really likes him at all. The friend, meanwhile, is at her nephew’s sixth birthday at an indoor play place in Columbus, and her phone is in her coat pocket under nineteen other coats.

Two tools elsewhere rest on this chapter. One owner per job (Part Two, Chapter II, page 90) works because trust is built from small promises kept, and a named owner turns “someone will probably do it” into a promise people can rely on. The monthly look-back (Part Two, Chapter V, page 143) looks at the month and keeps both people out of the dock, because feeling safe is what lets anyone say what went wrong.

Quickly, then slowly. On the surface, a message that hasn’t been answered. Underneath, an old expectation about whether people come back. Underneath that, a body that has been on its own too much. The roots are state and setting, and feedback loops, since trust grows in small repeated moments. The chapter takes them in order.

  1. Belonging is a basic need.

    People need to feel connected, the way we need food and sleep. When we feel left out it can hurt in a way that feels almost physical (Naomi Eisenberger and colleagues, 2003). That hurt works like hunger, pushing you to reach for someone.

    Friendship takes hours Studies of adults who had recently moved found that more time together, especially relaxed time, went with moving from acquaintance to friend. The hour counts are rough. The message isn’t: friendship is mostly built out of time spent.

    Hall (2019) · Moderate: survey studies; the hour estimates are rough

    Rhea moved to Pittsburgh for work. She’s busy and doing well and likes the job. And by the third month she’s low and teary every Sunday afternoon, when the office is shut and nobody in the whole city knows her well enough to call. She found this embarrassing for a while, and told her mom on the phone that she was “just tired.” Then she joined a running club, which she hated, and a bar trivia team, which she loved.

    Dig deeper: why we need each other

  2. Early bonds teach us what to expect.

    As children we learn, from the people who looked after us, whether others will come when we need them. If help usually came, we tend to expect it. If it came sometimes, or rarely, we may learn to cling harder, or stop asking. These lessons are a starting point that later relationships can change. This is the idea of attachment, first described by John Bowlby (1969) and studied by Mary Ainsworth and colleagues (1978).

    Watch a toddler at the park. He runs off toward the ducks, then runs back to check his grandma is still on the bench, then off again, a bit further, and back, and further still, right to the edge of the pond, where he stands and shouts at a goose. He gets braver every time, because he knows exactly where she is. If you’re the one on the bench, “I’m right here, go and look, come back whenever you want” is more or less the whole job.

    Dig deeper: what attachment is

  3. Patterns, not boxes.

    As adults, some of us worry a lot about being left, and reach out more when we feel unsure. Some of us pull back when things get close and need more room. Many of us feel mostly secure. Most of us mix all three, depending on the day and the person.

    These are patterns that can soften and change, especially in steady, kind relationships. Cindy Hazan and Phillip Shaver (1987) first described them in adults, and later work, such as R. Chris Fraley and colleagues (2015), suggests they work as sliding scales.

    When things get tense, Ronan wants to talk it through, now, immediately. His wife Clara needs to go quiet first, usually in the yard, usually with the pruning shears. He reads her quiet as her leaving, and she reads his questions through the back door as pressure. It took them nine years to see it. Now she says “I need an hour, and I’m coming back,” and he waits, which for about the first month he found almost unbearable.

    Dig deeper: anxious, avoidant and secure

  4. Trust is built in small moments.

    Trust rarely comes from big gestures. It grows from small, ordinary things done again and again, like doing what you said, and being the same person on a hard day as on a good one. Honestly, it’s a bit boring, which is probably why it works.

    The new hire said she’d send the figures by Thursday, and she did. The following week she warned on Monday that something would be late on Friday. By the third month her manager trusted her completely, and if you’d asked him when that happened he couldn’t have told you. It hadn’t happened at any one moment, more like in forty small ones.

    Dig deeper: how trust grows

    Professor Puddles

    Trust grows in small moments that repeat. This workpaper helps you notice the little rituals you already have, and keep them going.

    Workpaper WP-15: Keep your little rituals alive spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-15

  5. Feeling safe with someone calms the body.

    Being with someone we trust can settle the nervous system. In one study, holding a trusted partner’s hand calmed the brain’s response to threat (James Coan and colleagues, 2006). A calm voice, a hand to hold, or just someone nearby can make a hard moment easier to bear. It works both ways, so we can be that for other people, often without saying much.

    After his panic attack, Kieran’s friend didn’t try to fix anything. He sat down next to him on the cold step outside the apartments. “Take your time. I’m here.” Then nothing else, for about twenty minutes, while a man walked past twice with a very small dog. Eventually Kieran’s breathing slowed, and he noticed how cold the step was. “Thanks,” he said. “Any time,” said his friend, and meant it.

    Notice who helps you feel calmer, and tell them. “I always feel better after seeing you” is a lovely thing to hear, and almost nobody says it.

    Dig deeper: a safe haven

  6. Fitting in isn’t the same as belonging.

    Fitting in means changing yourself to be accepted. Belonging means being accepted as you are. Teams, families, clubs and communities can offer either. Being left out of a group hurts even when the group doesn’t matter much to us, and real belonging grows where people feel safe to be themselves and to speak up.

    At her new job Ola laughs at jokes she doesn’t find funny. She orders a club soda with lime “for the drive,” every Friday, so nobody asks why she doesn’t drink. She goes home wiped out. At her book club, in the back room of the library on alternate Tuesdays, she says exactly what she thought of the book, which last month was “I hated every single character,” and someone said, “Oh, thank God,” and they talked till the custodian turned the lights off.

    You could say (in a group) “I see it a bit differently. Is it okay if I say why?” “Has everyone had a chance to say something?”

    Dig deeper: groups, work and community

  7. When trust breaks, rebuilding takes time.

    When someone lets us down badly, trust doesn’t come back with one apology. It comes back slowly, as words are matched by actions over time. The person who broke trust can own what happened and be patient. The person who was hurt can decide, at their own pace, whether and how much to trust again.

    At Sunday dinner, for a laugh, Jen told the whole table a story her sister had told her in confidence. Nobody else at the table thought it was a big deal, but her sister left before dessert. The apology, two days later, was a start. What actually rebuilt things was the months after, when the story never came up again, and Jen started checking before she told anyone anything. “Can I mention the thing about work?” “No.” “Okay.”

    Dig deeper: rebuilding trust

  8. You can start building connection from wherever you are.

    If you feel alone right now, big friendships can seem a long way off. Belonging can start far smaller than that. A chat with a neighbor. A regular class. An online group about something you love. Even small, light contact with people we barely know can lift our mood (Gillian Sandstrom and Elizabeth Dunn, 2014).

    We underestimate strangers Commuters asked to talk to a stranger on their train or bus had a better journey than those told to keep to themselves, even though most people predicted the opposite. Misjudging how pleasant it will be is part of what keeps people apart.

    Epley and Schroeder (2014) · Moderate: field and lab experiments, replicated since

    After his divorce, Martin started saying more than “thanks” to the man at the coffee stall outside the station. It was the weather, at first. A few weeks later they were talking football every morning, mostly about the Eagles’ defense, which they agree about entirely. It’s a small friendship, and it makes Mondays bearable. Small rituals like that are worth keeping going on purpose, and Keep your little rituals alive (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-15-keep-your-little-rituals-alive) helps you notice the ones you already have.

    Dig deeper: building connection

    Tidbit

    One small hello is a fine start. If you can’t think of one, there’s a tool that picks one for you.

    Tool: Stay close: one small idea spreadloveandacceptance.com/bonding

Monday, 8:10am

SO sorry, phone was in my coat all day, soft play hell. LOVED your message. Coffee Thursday?

Kai reads it twice. He thinks about how far last night’s story got, all on its own, with no help from anybody. Next time a reply is slow, he decides, he’ll send something light, no rush, just thinking of you, and leave it at that.

If you’re a teenager

Ezra is sixteen when he sees a photo of his three closest friends at the movies and finds out there’s a group chat he isn’t in. It hurts like being punched, because being left out really does register a bit like pain. He drafts something sharp, deletes it, and messages one friend instead, saying he’s a little hurt not to be asked and was it something he did. It turns out they thought he’d be at football. One of the friendships really is drifting, though, and that’s allowed to hurt too.

Words to try “Kind of bummed not to be asked. Did something happen?” “I’d like to come next time, even if I can’t always make it.” “I miss how we used to be. Are we okay?”

Dig deeper: more worked examples

Two ways to read this

Going quiet, two ways

In an argument, some people need to keep talking until it feels settled, and silence feels like being shut out. Others flood fast, and going quiet is how they stop words they’d regret. If you need to talk it through, their silence is usually a brake, not a punishment. If you go quiet, a short line (“I need ten minutes, then I’ll come back”) tells the other person the door is still open.

Where the fields meet. Holistic therapies start with the body, and belonging is felt there first: a calmer breath beside someone safe. Some of these practices are well studied and some are debated. Laughter belongs here too, since a shared laugh tells the body it’s among friends. The research on laughter is still growing, so it’s offered as a small thing.

In everyday life

When one partner texts a lot while apart and the other forgets, agreeing on one goodnight message can keep both feeling connected. A child who acts up at pick-up may simply be letting go of a long day with the safest person they know. A friend who keeps canceling may be overwhelmed, and “Is it easier if we do something short?” keeps the door open. At work, a team where mistakes can be owned without blame builds trust faster than one where everyone hides them. And in a shared house, one simple weekly meal can turn people who share a kitchen into people who look out for each other. Stay close (spreadloveandacceptance.com/bonding) has small ideas if you’re stuck for one.

zqaxunderstandingx5xbelongingxxonxyourxownqzOn your own: belonging with yourself

Belonging includes how you treat yourself. If you’re kind to yourself on a bad day, you carry a small safe base wherever you go, and people who can comfort themselves often find it easier to let others in, because they’re less afraid of being let down. You’re allowed to need people. A lonely day is hard. It isn’t a forecast. On my own (spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own) has more for people living alone.

Common mix-ups

“Needing people means I’m needy” is the one people say most quietly. Everyone needs connection, including the people who hide it well. Attachment style isn’t fixed for life, either, and patterns can change, especially through steady, kind relationships and a bit of reflection. And forgiving isn’t the same as trusting again right away. Trust can return slowly, or not at all, and that’s your call.

  • “Jealousy and checking up show how much they love me.” Jealousy is a common feeling, and asking for reassurance (“Are we okay?”) is ordinary, especially for people who feel rejection keenly, which Downey and Feldman (1996) called rejection sensitivity. A worried text is a feeling looking for comfort. Checking someone’s phone without asking, needing to know where they are all day, or deciding who they can see is a different thing, whatever feeling sits underneath it. The question to ask is whether the request leaves the other person free to say no.

If you want to help someone else with this

Be steady, and turn up when you said you would, which matters more than any big gesture. If someone says they feel alone, listen before you remind them how many friends they have. Invite, and keep inviting. People who feel left out may say no a few times, and a warm invitation with no pressure still counts every time. In groups, notice who’s on the edge and ask what they think. And leave the labels out. Telling someone they’re “so avoidant” or “so clingy” has never helped anyone, as far as I can tell. “What would help?” often does.

You could say “I’m here, and I’m not going anywhere.” “We’re having a few people over on Friday. No pressure, but I’d love you to come.”

Part Three · Chapter 6

Habits and change: why change is hard and how small steps work

Why it’s so hard to change, even when we really want to, and what actually helps: small steps, a kinder setup, patience with slips, and remembering that other people’s change belongs to them.

In this chapter

  1. Change is hard for good reasons
  2. Habits run on cues
  3. Start smaller than feels useful
  4. Change the setup, not just your willpower
  5. Being in two minds is normal
  6. Slips are part of change
  7. Change sticks when it fits who you want to be
  8. You can support change, but not force it
  9. In everyday life
  10. Common mix-ups
  11. If you want to help someone else with this
  12. Workpapers, tools and reading on this site
  13. More for your situation

At a glance

  • Change is hard for good reasons. Habits save effort, so the old way is always the easy way.
  • A small step and a kind setup outlast willpower. Make the first step tiny and change what is around you.
  • Slips are part of change. A missed day tells you something about the plan and nothing about your character.
  • Other people’s change is theirs. You can support it, though you can’t force it.

Monday, 7:05am

The plan was a walk before work. The sneakers are by the door. Somehow the phone is in your hand instead, and at 7:40 you are watching a man in Finland restore a rusty ax, next to a coffee that went cold twenty minutes ago. You don’t even like axes.

By the evening a quiet voice is telling you that you never stick to anything. What you actually ran into this morning was a habit with about six years of practice behind it. It won, as it usually does for the first few rounds.

This chapter is why several tools in these books are so small. One small step a week (Part One, Next, page 48) starts smaller than feels useful and decides ahead of time. The setup score and One owner per job (Part Two, Chapter II, page 90) change the setup instead of asking anyone for more willpower. And What keeps coming back? (Part Two, Chapter V, page 143) treats a repeat as information about the plan, because slips are an ordinary part of changing anything.

Quickly: a phone in your hand at 7:40 is the surface. Underneath, a habit with years of practice behind it. Underneath that, a setup that quietly makes the old way easier. The roots are feedback loops and quiet incentives. Then the chapter slows down and takes them one by one.

  1. Change is hard for good reasons.

    A lot of what we do each day runs on autopilot. That saves energy, and it’s the whole point of a habit. The catch is that the old way is always quicker and easier than the new one, so changing asks your brain to do something effortful again and again, for weeks, until the new way becomes the easy one.

    Every night Jodie decides she will not snap at the children in the morning, and she means it. Every morning, somewhere between the lost reading book and the toast going cold and Lily’s hair, she snaps. The morning has worn a groove deeper than her good intentions, which says something about mornings and not much about her as a mother.

    Pick one thing you’d like to change, and write down when it usually happens, where, and what’s going on just before.

    Dig deeper: why change is hard

  2. Habits run on cues.

    Most habits have a trigger, which might be a time or a place or a feeling or a person, or simply the thing you’ve just done. The cue starts the routine, and some kind of reward (relief, comfort, a small buzz) keeps it going. Once you know the cue, you can plan for it.

    Stale popcorn In one field experiment, people with a strong movie-popcorn habit ate stale popcorn about as much as fresh, but only in a movie theater. Somewhere else, they didn’t. The setting drove the habit more than taste or good intentions did, rather like Nigel’s laptop.

    Neal and colleagues (2011) · Moderate: two field experiments, in line with wider habit research

    Nigel noticed, eventually, that he reached for the cookie jar the moment he opened his laptop after dinner, hungry or not, every night, and the laptop was the cue. So now he makes tea before he opens it and makes a pot. By the time the tea’s brewed the urge has mostly wandered off. On Fridays it doesn’t wander anywhere and he has a custard cream, and that seems fair.

    Dig deeper: cues and routines

  3. Start smaller than feels useful.

    Big goals are inspiring and easy to drop. Tiny steps feel almost silly, and they work precisely because they’re easy enough to manage on a bad day. Tie the new step to something you already do (“After I make my coffee, I’ll…”), and only grow it once it’s stuck.

    Two roommates had been promising each other a big Sunday clean of the kitchen since March. It had happened once, so they agreed something smaller. After dinner, each of them wipes one surface, which takes two minutes. By the second week the stove had stopped being a source of tension. By the fourth, someone had descaled the kettle without being asked, which caused a small sensation.

    You could say “Let’s start with something tiny, and see if it sticks.” “After I …, I will …”

    Dig deeper: why small steps work

  4. Change the setup, not just your willpower.

    Willpower runs low when you’re tired or hungry. Your surroundings stay the same all day. So make the new habit easier, by putting it in sight or getting things ready the night before, and make the old one a little harder, by moving it out of reach. I’d back a small change to the setup over a big push of effort almost every time. At home that can be as simple as one owner for each job (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-03-one-owner-per-job).

    Willpower isn’t a fuel tank, probably A popular idea says self-control runs out like fuel. When 23 labs tried to repeat the classic experiment together, they found an effect close to zero. The argument isn’t over, but it’s one more reason to change the setup rather than lean harder on yourself.

    Hagger and colleagues (2016) · Strong: a large pre-registered replication; the debate continues

    Callan is seventeen and wants to sleep better, and for weeks he tried to stop scrolling in bed by sheer force of will. It didn’t work once. Then his mom suggested charging his phone in the kitchen overnight, next to the bread box. He said this was ridiculous, and did it anyway, mainly to prove her wrong, and within a week he was asleep before midnight most nights. Every few weeks he tells her it’s ridiculous, without much conviction.

    Dig deeper: shaping your setup

    Professor Puddles

    Changing the setup is often easier than changing a person. At home, that can be as simple as one owner for each job.

    Workpaper WP-03: One owner per job spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-03

  5. Being in two minds is normal.

    Part of you wants to change and part of you doesn’t, and the reluctant part usually has its reasons. The old habit may give comfort, or protect you from something. Pushing harder against it rarely works, and listening to it often does.

    Asif wanted to drink less, and he also loved Friday nights at the bar with his team. When he finally asked himself what Friday actually gave him, the answer wasn’t really the beer. It was the people, the laughing, the end of the week. So he kept the Friday and switched to alcohol-free after the first beer. If anyone at the table noticed, they didn’t say, which is its own sort of kindness.

    Try two lists, one of what you like about how things are, one of what you’d like about changing. You’re allowed both, and I suspect the first one will be the more honest of the two.

    Dig deeper: readiness and mixed feelings

  6. Slips are part of change.

    Nearly everyone who changes something slips back sometimes, and one slip doesn’t undo the progress. What does the damage is usually the thought that follows. “I’ve blown it, so why bother?” Being kind to yourself after a slip makes it a good deal more likely you’ll start again.

    There’s a name for “why bother?” Relapse-prevention research calls it the abstinence violation effect: after one slip, guilt and a sense of total failure make a full slide back more likely. It comes from addiction treatment, but the shape is the same for cookies and evening runs.

    Marlatt and Gordon (1985) · Moderate: a foundational clinical model, widely used in addiction treatment

    Three calm weeks, and then Lewis shouted at his son over spelling homework. Really shouted, the old way. That night he sat on the end of the bed in the dark. “I shouted, and I’m sorry. I’m working on it.” A small voice from under the comforter said “Okay.” The next evening they did the spelling homework at the kitchen table with the radio on. Nobody raised their voice. The word was “necessary,” which neither of them could spell.

    Things to tell yourself “A slip is one moment out of many.” “What made today harder, and what can I plan for next time?”

    Decide now, while things are going well, what you’ll do after a slip. Have one kind sentence to say to yourself and one small step to start again. A game can help some people practice, and the Re-check Drive (spreadloveandacceptance.com/recheck-drive) turns small kind steps into calm football.

    Dig deeper: slips and starting again

    Tidbit

    A slip is a stumble, not a fall. Try the tiny step again tomorrow. A game for small kind acts can make the practicing easier.

    Tool: Gentle games: the Re-check Drive (calm football) spreadloveandacceptance.com/recheck-drive

  7. Change sticks when it fits who you want to be.

    Change made only to please someone, or out of shame, is hard to keep up. Change that connects to what you care about has deeper roots, and each small action becomes a vote for the person you’re turning into.

    Rania kept meaning to be better at keeping in touch, and kept not being. What shifted it was a different sentence in her head. She stopped telling herself she must message people and started thinking of herself as someone who shows up for her friends. A voice note on Sunday evenings became part of that. Some weeks it’s thirty seconds of nonsense and some weeks it turns into an hour on the phone.

    Dig deeper: values and who you’re becoming

  8. You can support change, but not force it.

    It’s natural to want the people we love to change, to drink less, or look after themselves better. Their change belongs to them, though, and pressure tends to make people dig in. It helps more to say clearly what you need, ask what would help, and notice their small steps out loud.

    Grant kept missing deadlines, and his teammate had the lecture about being organized all ready, she’d been polishing it for two weeks, and at the last minute she didn’t give it. She asked what would make the handover easier, and he looked surprised. Between them they set up a shared checklist, and he fills it in every Friday before lunch, mostly. She has kept the lecture, though, in a note on her phone.

    Ways to say it “I can’t change this for you, but I’d love to help if you want me to.” “I noticed you did that this week. That really helped.”

    Dig deeper: change with other people

Two weeks later, 7:05am

The sneakers are still by the door. The phone sleeps in the kitchen now, and the plan has shrunk to shoes on, out to the end of the road. Some mornings that’s all. Most mornings it turns into a loop past the community gardens and back. On the Thursday you miss, the voice starts up again, and you tell it you’ll get to the end of the road tomorrow. It says you won’t. You do.

Two ways to read this

Change, two ways

Some people love a fresh start and throw themselves at a new plan. Others need to change one small thing and see it hold first. If you’re a fresh-starter, the slow one isn’t lacking willpower. They’re protecting what already works. If you’re slow and steady, the fresh-starter isn’t being reckless. Novelty is part of what keeps them going.

Where the fields meet. Behavioral science says habits beat good intentions, and business adds the simple check: one owner for a change and one small look each week at whether it held. The root is feedback loops, small things repeated with a check each time.

In everyday life

Take a couple who want to spend less of the evening on their phones. Earlier attempts failed because each of them watched the other. This time they put a basket by the door, both phones go in at nine, and there’s one exception for whoever’s on call for an elderly parent. The first week is awkward. On the Wednesday one of them sneaks a look at the football. By the third week the basket is part of the furniture and the evenings have a shape again, a movie or a crossword or an early night.

Big life changes, a move or a new baby, break old routines, which is disruptive and also a good moment to start new habits. If you have ADHD, make the cue impossible to miss, do the step the moment it appears, and make the reward come right away. Expect the novelty to wear off, and swap the method when it does instead of blaming yourself. More in the expanded version (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-6-change-in-depth).

On your own: a kind plan for change

If you’re working on something alone, the whole chapter fits into one small plan. Choose one change, the one that would make the most difference or the one that feels most doable. Give it a cue, written as “After I ___, I will ___.” Make one tweak to your surroundings so it’s easier to start. Decide on the smallest version you could still manage on a tired day. And write down one kind sentence to use after a slip. The self path (spreadloveandacceptance.com/self-path) and Know yourself, next (page 48) walk through it step by step.

Common mix-ups

“If I really wanted it, I’d just do it” is the cruelest of these, and it’s wrong. Wanting is only the start. Habits, setup, tiredness and stress all get a vote. Then there’s the famous 21 days. There’s no magic number. In one study, led by Phillippa Lally (2010), it took about two months on average, with a very wide range. Being hard on yourself doesn’t keep you on track, either. Harshness makes people give up, and kindness makes it easier to try again. And routines don’t have to mean being rigid. For a lot of people, autistic people especially, routines are what make life manageable, and change can respect that.

If you want to help someone else with this

Ask before you advise (“Would ideas help, or would you rather just talk it through?”), and help them find their own reasons by asking what would be different for them if this changed. Practical help with the setup, like a ride to the gym, often does more than encouragement. Notice small steps out loud and be kind about slips. Look after yourself too. You can care a great deal and still have limits on what you’ll put up with.

Words to try “I’m on your side with this. What would help?” “You’ve done this three days in a row. That’s not nothing.”

Workpapers, tools and reading on the website

Pick one tiny change and try it for a week. The 90-second daily check-in (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-13-daily-check-in), the quick checks (spreadloveandacceptance.com/quick-checks) and the self path can help you keep track.

Part Three · Chapter 7

Self-worth, shame and self-compassion

Why your worth isn’t a score you keep earning, how shame differs from guilt, and why being kind to yourself makes it easier to grow.

In this chapter

  1. Your worth isn’t a score
  2. Guilt says “I did a bad thing.” Shame says “I am bad.”
  3. Shame makes you want to hide
  4. The inner critic is trying to protect you
  5. Self-compassion isn’t letting yourself off
  6. Comparing yourself pulls your worth outside you
  7. You can own a mistake without drowning in it
  8. Worth is learned between people, and we can give it
  9. In everyday life
  10. Feedback, criticism and put-downs are three different things
  11. Common mix-ups
  12. If you want to help someone else with this
  13. Tools and reading on this site
  14. More for your situation

Thursday, 11:20pm

You sent the wrong spreadsheet to the whole team. Last quarter’s, not this one’s. Priyanka spotted it in four minutes, sent the right one and added “no worries!!” with two exclamation marks, which somehow made it worse.

It’s nearly midnight. The file stopped being the point some time around ten. The voice has moved on to bigger things now, like how you’ve always been a bit useless, really, and now they all know.

This chapter is about how self-worth and shame work, and then about what you can actually do with them. None of it is a diagnosis. Take what helps.

A wrong spreadsheet, read quickly, has layers. On the surface, a file sent to the whole team. Underneath, guilt about the file, which is useful. Underneath that, shame about yourself, which isn’t. The roots are signal and noise, what the mistake really says, and balance. The chapter slows down on the second and third layers.

  1. Your worth isn’t a score.

    A lot of us carry a quiet scoreboard, on which we’re worth something when we’re useful, or liked, or slim, or busy, or top of the class, or never any bother to anybody. Psychologists call these “conditions of worth,” and the trouble with a score is that it can drop. If your worth goes up and down with each day’s results, then every bad day is a verdict.

    Pam taught third grade for forty years. In the September after she retired she found herself in the supermarket at ten on a Tuesday morning, holding a basket with nothing in it, feeling lost in a way she couldn’t have explained to anyone. Nothing was wrong. But for four decades being needed was how she knew she mattered, and the bell had stopped ringing.

    Try finishing “I feel okay about myself when I…” three times, then look at what you wrote. Those are your scores. Just noticing them is enough for now.

    Dig deeper: worth that doesn’t have to be earned

  2. Guilt says “I did a bad thing.” Shame says “I am bad.”

    Guilt is about something you did, so it points somewhere useful. Say sorry. Put it right. Shame is about who you are, which feels impossible to fix, and so it makes people hide, or freeze, or blame someone else, or lash out. Research on the two feelings, such as June Tangney and Ronda Dearing’s (2002), suggests guilt is the one more likely to lead to repair.

    Rhys is twelve and he has just knocked his mom’s favorite mug off the counter, the one with the hare on it that she bought on the boardwalk in Cape May years ago and drinks her first tea of the day from, and there are two ways this can go. Guilt says go and tell her, and maybe offer some birthday money. Shame says you ruin everything, and this time shame wins. He wraps the pieces in yesterday’s paper and pushes them right down to the bottom of the trash can, under the potato peelings, where his mom finds them on Sunday.

    It was the hiding that upset her. She told him so. It took him a while to see what she meant.

    Dig deeper: guilt, shame and repair

  3. Shame makes you want to hide.

    You feel shame in the body before you think it. Hot face, eyes down, stomach dropping, a strong wish for the floor to open. It also comes out sideways, as sudden anger or a closed, cold face, which is how a small comment turns into a big fight.

    “Didn’t we already cover this?” It was a mild question, asked in a Tuesday meeting by a man who genuinely couldn’t remember. Becky snapped at him, properly, in front of nine people. That evening, scraping a plate into the trash, she worked out that it had nothing to do with him. She’d felt stupid in front of everyone, and stupid had come out as sharp.

    Learn your own signs, if you can. Next time you suddenly want to vanish, or bite, you can name it quietly to yourself, and now and then out loud. “Sorry, I think I felt embarrassed and it came out sharp. Can I try that again?”

    Dig deeper: how shame works in the body

  4. The inner critic is trying to protect you.

    That harsh inner voice usually started as protection. If you criticize yourself first, perhaps nobody else gets the chance. If you’re hard enough on yourself, perhaps you’ll never fail again. It meant well, in its way. But a voice that only threatens keeps your body on alert, and it’s exhausting to share a head with.

    Perfectionism has been creeping up Students’ perfectionism scores rose between 1989 and 2016, according to a meta-analysis by Curran and Hill, with the sharpest rise in the feeling that other people expect you to be perfect. It’s questionnaire data from Western countries and it can’t say why, but if that feeling is loud for you, you have company.

    Curran and Hill (2019) · Moderate: questionnaire data from Western countries; does not explain the cause

    Every time Craig forgets something for the baby he calls himself an idiot. Out loud, sometimes. The wipes. The rabbit she won’t sleep without. It’s the word his own dad used about him, all through his childhood. Patting his pockets in the daycare parking lot for a rabbit that’s on the kitchen table, he hears it in his dad’s voice, exactly, and it strikes him as odd that he’s still using it.

    Write down one thing your critic says a lot. Would you say it to a friend you loved? Some people find it helps to answer the critic directly. “Thanks. I know you’re trying to protect me. I can take it from here.”

    Dig deeper: the critic and the soothing system

  5. Self-compassion isn’t letting yourself off.

    Self-compassion means treating yourself the way you’d treat a good friend who’s having a rotten time. One well-known model has three parts. Kindness instead of attack. Remembering that everyone struggles. Noticing the pain without drowning in it. Studies, such as one by Juliana Breines and Serena Chen (2012), suggest that people who are kind to themselves after a failure are often more likely to try to improve.

    Lindy failed her driving test for the third time, on the reverse around a corner again, clipping the same curb she had clipped in March, and afterward she sat in the DMV parking lot for a while with the engine off. Then she told herself what she’d have told her sister, more or less. This is hard. Lots of people need more tries. You’re fine everywhere except that one corner. On Sunday morning she was on the empty industrial park by the beltway with her dad in the passenger seat, backing around the same lamp post eleven times.

    If it feels all right, try putting a hand on your arm once today and saying, slowly, “This is a hard moment. Other people feel this too. What do I need?” It will feel silly the first time, and probably the second.

    Dig deeper: what self-compassion is, and isn’t

    Sugarfoot

    Speak to yourself the way you’d speak to a friend having a hard day, slowly and kindly. Writing it down first helps.

    Tool: Write it through spreadloveandacceptance.com/write-it-through

  6. Comparing yourself pulls your worth outside you.

    Everyone measures themselves against other people. It’s how we work out where we stand. But a feed full of other people’s best moments makes the measuring wildly unfair, and self-esteem that depends on being better than others swings about all over the place.

    Why we compare at all Leon Festinger proposed in 1954 that people judge their opinions and abilities by comparing themselves with others, especially when there’s no objective standard to go by. Worth has no objective standard, which may be exactly why comparing goes so badly there.

    Festinger (1954) · Strong: a foundational theory with a large body of later research

    Two old friends met for a curry, one of them having just bought a house. The other rents a room in a shared apartment in Queens where the shower only works if you hold it. The renter spent the whole evening quietly ranking herself, and she missed what was right in front of her. Her friend was lonely in the new house, and had wanted to say so all evening, and kept waiting for a gap in the conversation that never came because the renter was so busy ranking herself. You’re comparing your inside with somebody’s outside. When you catch yourself at it, try a question instead. “How are you, really?”

    Dig deeper: comparison and steady self-worth

  7. You can own a mistake without drowning in it.

    Owning a mistake gets a lot easier once it doesn’t mean you’re worthless. Say what you did. Say what it did to the other person. Say what you’ll do now. Then stop. Beating yourself up afterward proves nothing about how sorry you are, it just pulls everyone’s attention back onto you.

    Jess forgot to pay her share of the broadband and it got cut off for the whole long weekend. On the Tuesday, after a weekend of the others tethering their laptops to their phones and one of them going to the library to finish an essay, she put her head around the living-room door. “I forgot to pay, and it left you all without internet for three days. I’ve paid it and set a reminder for the 28th.” Someone said “Thanks,” and that was more or less the end of it.

    If it went wrong in a conversation, Rewind the talk (spreadloveandacceptance.com/carrier-wave-decoder) helps you find the words. Then decide whether to send them or let it rest.

    Dig deeper: owning it, repairing it, letting it rest

    Professor Puddles

    Owning a mistake can be short and plain: what happened, that it was yours, what you’ll do. If it went wrong in a talk, Rewind the talk helps you find the words.

    Tool: Rewind the talk spreadloveandacceptance.com/carrier-wave-decoder

  8. Worth is learned between people, and we can give it.

    Children learn their worth from how they’re treated, and adults never entirely stop. The words matter, because “You did a careless thing” leaves room to change, while “You’re so careless” shuts the door. Notice effort, and who someone is, as well as results, and people feel they matter on bad days too.

    Gill took over a team that hid its problems until week ten, and from her first month she started every project review with the same question, “What did we learn?” and refused, politely and repeatedly, to discuss who had got what wrong. Within six months people were bringing problems to her in week two, which saved everyone a great many Friday evenings, and the sappy question stayed.

    Today you could say one thing to someone that has nothing to do with how well they’ve done. Even just “I’m glad I know you.”

    Dig deeper: how worth is given and learned

Your part, and only your part. You can’t control how other people judge you, or what you were taught about your worth growing up. You can control how you speak to yourself now, whether you repair what you can, and where you spend your time. Give your energy to people who treat you as someone who matters. More in Your wiring, weather and words (page 33)

Friday, 9:15am

You send one line. Sorry about the mix-up with yesterday’s file, right one attached. When the voice starts up again you try answering it the way you would a friend. You got it wrong and you fixed it, which is what a decent colleague does. The voice is not convinced. Priyanka sends a thumbs-up, and by lunch you’ve mostly stopped thinking about it.

Two ways to read this

A mistake, read two ways

For some people a correction is just information: “slide four has a typo” means slide four has a typo. For others, the same sentence lands as a verdict on them, often because a lot of earlier corrections were. If you’re the first kind, it can help to say the plain part plainly and add one warm sentence. If you’re the second, it can help to ask, “Is this about the slide, or about me?” Usually it really is the slide.

Where the fields meet. The art of debating has a rule that fits this chapter well: separate the claim from the person. “I did a bad thing” is a claim about an act. Laughter, used gently, can help too, laughing with yourself and never at yourself. The research on laughter is young and modest, so treat that as a small help.

In everyday life

Shame turns up in very ordinary places. Between partners, “You forgot to call” can land as “You’re a terrible partner,” so what comes back is a defense instead of a sorry. A child who hears “You’re so naughty” learns something about who they are, while “That was a naughty thing to do” leaves a way back. A friend who says yes to everything may be quietly burning out, because no feels like risking being dropped. At work, someone may sit on a small error for weeks because owning it feels like proof they never belonged there.

On your own: a kinder voice to keep

You don’t need anyone else for this. Notice how you talk to yourself and practice one gentler sentence. Catch the critic’s favorite words (“always,” “useless,” “pathetic,” “should”) and swap one for a plain fact. “I’m hopeless” becomes “I was late twice this week.” On bad days, keep a short list of what you did, and let getting up count. You’re allowed to be disappointed in what you did and still be on your own side.

Feedback, criticism and put-downs are three different things.

Feedback is about something you did and what would work better, and it usually comes with a reason. Criticism aims at you as a person (“You always…,” “You never…”). It’s common in tired, stressed moments. In couples studied by Gottman (1994), criticism went with more unhappiness later, while a plain complaint about one specific thing did not. A put-down is something else again, and it’s worth being exact about it, because the label hurts if it’s wrong.

For something to be a put-down, these are usually all present:

  • it’s about who you are, not one thing you did,
  • it keeps happening over weeks or months,
  • it carries on after the thing is fixed or explained,
  • it often lands in front of other people or on what you care about most.

Not enough on its own:

  • one sharp comment on a bad day,
  • plain words without padding, or a family where everyone talks bluntly,
  • a fair complaint that came out badly,
  • teasing that both of you enjoy and either of you can stop.

If you raise it, describe what was said and how it landed, and leave the label out. “When you called me useless in front of your sister, I felt small. What was really bothering you?” gives the other person something to answer.

Common mix-ups

People worry that self-compassion is just self-pity. They feel quite different from the inside. Self-pity says “only me, poor me.” Self-compassion says “this is hard, and other people go through it too,” which joins you to other people instead of shutting you away from them. Others fear that being kind to themselves will make them lazy. The research leans the other way, because it’s fear of your own attack that makes people stop trying and hide their mistakes. And self-worth doesn’t mean thinking you’re great, only that you go on mattering on the days when you plainly aren’t.

If you want to help someone else with this

Talk about what happened, never about what sort of person they are. Arguing with someone’s shame (“You’re not useless!”) can feel like being told they’re wrong to feel it, so you might try “It sounds like you feel really low about it. I don’t see you that way.” Helping them find one small thing they can do gives the feeling somewhere to go. And kindness on ordinary days, when nothing has gone wrong, teaches worth far better than anything said in a crisis.

You could say “That sounds like it’s weighing on you. Want to work out one thing that would help?” “You don’t have to earn being cared about.”

  • Your worth isn’t a score.
  • Shame makes you want to hide.
  • Self-compassion isn’t letting yourself off.
  • Comparing yourself pulls your worth outside you.
