Part Three · Chapter 8

Loss, grief and big life changes

What grief is, why it comes in waves, how it shows up in the body, and how to carry a loss, or a big change, without having to “get over it.”

In this chapter

  1. Grief is love with nowhere to go
  2. Grief comes in waves, not neat stages
  3. Grief lives in the body, too
  4. Some losses nobody sees
  5. People grieve in different ways
  6. You don’t have to let go
  7. Big changes are losses too, even the good ones
  8. Most people find a way through, and support helps
  9. Losing a partner in later life
  10. In everyday life
  11. If you want to help someone else with this
  12. Tools and reading on this site
  13. More for your situation

At a glance

  • Grief is love with nowhere to go. It hurts because the person, place or life mattered.
  • It comes in waves. A good week followed by a bad day is part of grieving, and it doesn’t send you back to the start.
  • You don’t have to let go. Many people keep a bond with the person they lost, and that is healthy.
  • Most people find a way through. Support helps, and some griefs stay heavy for a long time.

Saturday, 9:05am

Six months on, you’re doing fine, or that’s what you tell people, and on most days it’s even true.

Then, in aisle seven, there’s the cereal, his cereal, the faded blue box he always said tasted of cardboard and ate every single morning for thirty years. You leave the cart where it is, next to the oatmeal, and walk out to the car and sit in it with the engine off. A woman loading her trunk two spaces down glances over and then, kindly, doesn’t.

This chapter is for anyone who has lost someone or something. It might be a person, or a pet, or a marriage or a friendship, their health or a home or a job, a country they had to leave or a future they’d pictured. It looks at how grief works and then at what can help. There’s no right way to grieve. Nothing here is a schedule, and if any of it doesn’t fit you, leave it.

Aisle seven, in quick strokes. On the surface, a box of cereal. Underneath, six months of being fine. Underneath that, love with nowhere to go. The roots are balance and state and setting, what was given and is now missing, and where the wave happens to land. The chapter goes through them slowly.

  1. Grief is love with nowhere to go.

    Grief is what we feel when something we were attached to is gone, and it isn’t only for deaths. A divorce, a miscarriage, a diagnosis, a move, a friend who drifted off, children leaving home. Its size usually matches the size of the bond, whatever anyone else thinks the loss ought to mean.

    When Bramble died, his owner was shaken by how hard he took it, and his friends at the bar told him, kindly enough, that it was only a dog. That dog walked beside him along the same stretch of river every morning for twelve years, through two jobs and a divorce. The lead is still on its hook by the back door, and he can’t move it yet.

    It can help to say a loss out loud to yourself, especially one you’ve never called grief. “I’m grieving the friendship.” “I’m grieving the life we planned.” They’re small sentences, and they can bring a surprising amount of relief.

    Dig deeper: what grief is, and what counts

  2. Grief comes in waves, not neat stages.

    You may have heard of five stages of grief, running from denial through anger, bargaining and depression to acceptance. They came from listening to people who were dying, and they were never meant as steps that everyone goes through in order. Most people swing back and forth, some hours deep in the loss and some hours getting on with life, and researchers who study grief see that swing as healthy.

    Back and forth is normal The dual process model describes healthy grief as moving back and forth between facing the loss and getting on with life, with breaks from grief included. In this model Val’s laugh at lunch isn’t a lapse. It’s part of the grieving.

    Stroebe and Schut (1999) · Moderate: a widely used framework with partial support

    Three months after Gerald died, Val laughed properly at lunch. Her sister had told a story about a man at the bowls club and a wasp, and Val laughed till she had to put her fork down. On the bus home she felt terrible about it. That evening she cried for two hours. The lunch was grief too, and so was the bus.

    Dig deeper: waves, and the swing between loss and life

  3. Grief lives in the body, too.

    Grief can bring tiredness, bad sleep, no appetite or too much, aches, a tight chest, forgetfulness and a foggy head. Your brain is slowly learning that someone or something it expected to be there has gone, and the learning takes time and uses a lot of energy.

    An assistant principal whose mother has just died loses her car keys three times in one week. She drives to school on a Saturday, and walks into a school board meeting that is happening on Thursday when it is in fact Tuesday. She starts to wonder, quietly, if something is wrong with her memory. It’s grief fog. It lifts as the months go on, though nobody can tell her when, and she’d really like somebody to.

    While it lasts, look after a few basics, like one real meal a day and a regular bedtime and a short walk outside, and it’s fine to tell people, “I’m grieving, so I’m slower than usual. Could you send me a reminder?”

    Dig deeper: the grieving body and brain

  4. Some losses nobody sees.

    Some losses are hard to explain to anyone else. Someone may still be alive but changed by dementia or illness, or gone without having died, like an estranged parent or a missing relative. Other losses go unrecognized, such as the death of an ex-partner, a pregnancy loss or a friend you only ever knew online.

    A loss without an ending Pauline Boss named this ambiguous loss: someone gone but still present in the mind, or present but changed, as with dementia. Part of what makes it so hard is that there’s no clear ending to grieve.

    Boss (1999) · Moderate: a widely used framework, backed by clinical and interview research

    Every Sunday at two, Teresa visits her dad at the nursing home. He’s always pleased to see her. He thinks she’s his sister, Connie, and asks after their mother, who died in 1987. Teresa has stopped correcting him, and they talk about Connie’s life, which Teresa now knows a surprising amount about. She is grieving someone who hasn’t died. There’s no funeral for that, no cards, and at work nobody thinks to ask.

    If a loss of yours had no ceremony, you can make a small one, a candle or a letter or a bulb in the yard, or just going to stand for a while somewhere that mattered.

    Dig deeper: ambiguous and unrecognized grief

  5. People grieve in different ways.

    Some people grieve by talking and crying. Others grieve by doing, fixing things, organizing, working, building. Neither is more loving. Families often clash because one person thinks another isn’t grieving, when they’re grieving differently, and culture and faith and age and how your mind works all shape how it comes out.

    After their son died, Janet wanted to talk about him every evening. Steve went into the garage every weekend and worked on the old Raleigh that Ryan had never got around to fixing. She thought he was hiding. He thought she was making it worse. It took a friend of the family about forty minutes to point out, gently, that they were both doing exactly the same thing. In March Steve brought the bike out, finished. Janet cried and he let her. Then she asked him what was wrong with the gears, and he told her, for some time.

    Dig deeper: grieving styles and families

  6. You don’t have to let go.

    An older idea said healthy grief meant moving on and cutting ties. Many grief researchers now see it differently. People often keep a bond with the person they lost, in memories, rituals, conversations in their head and the values they carry on, so the relationship changes shape without having to end.

    Continuing bonds This is the book that challenged the cut-the-ties view of mourning, showing that inner bonds with someone who has died are common across many groups and often healthy. Later research adds a fair caveat: for some people the bond comforts, and for others it hurts.

    Klass, Silverman and Nickman (1996) · Moderate: influential; effects differ from person to person

    Ama wears her grandpa’s watch to every exam. It’s far too big. She has to push it up her arm to write. She doesn’t believe in luck, and if you asked her why she does it she would probably shrug and say “dunno,” but the honest answer is that it feels as if he’s in the room.

    You could pick one way of keeping a bond, cooking their recipe, or telling one of their stories at Christmas, or keeping one of their habits going. Some people find it helps, in a hard moment, to ask what the person would have said. Often it’s something rude.

    Dig deeper: continuing bonds

  7. Big changes are losses too, even the good ones.

    A new baby, a promotion, retiring, moving country, a child starting school, coming out, getting well after a long illness. All of them can bring grief for the old life. Change often has three parts, an ending, a confusing middle bit, and a new beginning. The middle is the hardest part and also the easiest to rush.

    Ifeoma and Olu moved to Denver for a job they both wanted. They toasted it with fizz in the empty apartment. Six months in, Olu felt low, and then guilty for feeling low, since this was the plan. What nobody had toasted was what they’d left behind, a circle of friends, a café where nobody had to ask what they wanted, and a whole Saturday that used to run itself. You can be glad about a change and still miss what came before.

    Dig deeper: endings, the in-between, beginnings

    Professor Puddles

    When a loss is hard to talk about, writing can come first. Put the words down at your own pace. You never have to send them.

    Tool: Write it through spreadloveandacceptance.com/write-it-through

  8. Most people find a way through, and support helps.

    Research suggests that over time many people find they can live with a loss and still feel joy, though they never forget. Being around people who let you talk, or let you stay quiet, helps. For some people, though, grief stays at full strength for a long time and makes daily life very hard.

    This is called prolonged grief. It means a strong longing for the person, or being taken over by the loss, most days, still going many months after the death (6 to 12 months or more, depending on the guideline) and getting in the way of life. It has nothing to do with weakness.

    A year after his wife died, Dennis still couldn’t go into their bedroom. He slept on the couch and had stopped answering his friends’ calls. His brother stopped asking how he was and started saying, “I’m making dinner Thursday. Come or don’t.” After a few weeks Dennis came. It became one evening a week at his brother’s, watching the game and not saying much. Things moved, slowly. He’s back in the bedroom now, on his own side of the bed.

    Dig deeper: resilience, support and stuck grief

Your part, and only your part. You can’t control the loss, how long grief lasts, or how other people react to it. You can control small things: eating something, resting, telling one person how you are, and saying no to what you can’t manage right now. That is enough for a hard season. More in Your wiring, weather and words (page 33)

Saturday, 9:40am

You let it come, for ten minutes maybe, and then you blow your nose on a napkin from the glove box and go back in. The cart is still there by the oatmeal, and you put the cereal in it, without knowing why.

At home you text your sister. Saw Dad’s cereal. Cried in the parking lot. She’s typing right away. Same thing happened to me with his aftershave in the drugstore. Call tonight?

zqaxunderstandingx8xlossxxlaterxlifeqzLosing a partner in later life

After a long marriage the loss is in everything, in the empty chair and the jobs that were always theirs and the paperwork, done alone, and in the first birthday and the first anniversary without them. Do one small thing at a time, and let one drawer count as a day’s work. It’s fine to ask someone to sit with you while you fill out the forms.

Your grown-up children have lost a parent while you’ve lost a partner, and you may grieve on different clocks. If they start calling every day, that comes from love and worry. It isn’t control, and you can still say what helps. “I love that you call. Could we make it two evenings a week, and I’ll call you if I need you?”

Dig deeper: the first year, and grown-up children

Two ways to read this

Grief, read two ways

Some people grieve by talking, crying and remembering out loud. Others grieve by doing, mending, fixing the bike. If you talk, the doer may look as if they’ve moved on. Usually they haven’t, and the doing is the grief. If you do, the talker isn’t wallowing. Telling the story again is how they carry it.

Where the fields meet. Philosophy has asked for a long time what makes a life go well, and part of its answer is that the people we lose stay part of it. Laughter, oddly, belongs here too: a shared laugh can tell a grieving body it’s safe for a minute. The research on laughter is still young, so read that as a small comfort.

In everyday life

After a miscarriage one partner may want to talk while the other goes quiet, and each can end up worrying the other doesn’t care. A child may laugh and play the day after a funeral and cry at bedtime, and both are grief. A friend who stops calling after your diagnosis is usually stuck for words more than cold. Colleagues who avoid the subject when someone comes back after a death can leave that person feeling as if the loss has been rubbed out. And a whole town can grieve together, when it loses its library or its factory.

On your own: carrying it gently

Grief can be lonely even with people around you. When you’re carrying it on your own, give the day a small shape, with a meal and a walk in it and one person you message. Expect harder days around birthdays and anniversaries, and plan something gentle for them. Writing to the person you lost, or about what you lost, can help, and nobody ever needs to read it. Some days the only goal is to get to tonight, and that is enough of a goal.

If someone close to you has died. Grief and later life (spreadloveandacceptance.com/grief) goes further, with family after a loss, coming back to people, and a new chapter on your own. On a heavy night, the page called For a hard evening (spreadloveandacceptance.com/grief#hard-evening) may help.

If you want to help someone else with this

Show up, and then keep showing up. Support floods in for about two weeks and then stops, so a text at three months, or on a birthday, can mean a great deal. Offer something specific, because “Can I drop dinner off on Thursday?” is far easier to say yes to than “Let me know if you need anything.” Say the name, too. Many grieving people find it a comfort to hear it, and a memory with it, and if you’re not sure, ask. Leave out the explanations, since “Everything happens for a reason” and “At least…” tend to hurt. “I’m so sorry. I’m here” rarely does. And if you’re upset too, lean on people further from the loss, not the ones closest to it. Comfort goes in toward the middle and venting goes out.

You could say “I don’t know what to say, but I’m here.” “I was thinking about your mom today. I remember her laugh.” “I’m going to the store. What can I bring you?”

Part Three · Chapter 9

Minds that work differently

How autistic, ADHD, sensory and learning differences work, why none of them is a character flaw, and how people with different minds can meet in the middle.

In this chapter

  1. Brains vary, like bodies do
  2. Autism is a different way of sensing and connecting
  3. ADHD is about steering attention, not lacking it
  4. Everyone has a sensory profile
  5. Learning differences aren’t about intelligence
  6. Masking costs energy
  7. Autistic burnout is more than being tired
  8. Meltdowns and shutdowns aren’t choices
  9. Stimming helps, so let it be
  10. Deep focus makes switching hard
  11. Deep interests are a source of joy and rest
  12. Meet in the middle, out loud
  13. Labels are tools, and they belong to the person
  14. Finding out later in life
  15. Getting things started and finished is a skill of its own
  16. When demands feel like a threat
  17. Not recognizing faces isn’t rudeness
  18. Not speaking isn’t the same as having nothing to say
  19. Telling friends and dates is your choice
  20. Finding your people
  21. In everyday life
  22. Common mix-ups
  23. If you want to help someone else with this
  24. Tools and reading on this site
  25. More for your situation

At a glance

  • Brains vary, like bodies do. A different mind is not a broken one, though differences can still be disabling in a world built for one kind of mind.
  • Nobody chooses overload. Meltdowns, shutdowns and burnout are what happens when a nervous system has had too much.
  • Less masking, room to stim, time for deep interests and real rest help a great deal.
  • Meet in the middle, out loud. Ask what helps, say what helps you, and use the words each person chooses.

Monday, 8:15am

“Shoes, please, just put them on,” you say, for the third time.

Your son is lying on the hall floor with his hands over his ears. The new socks are wrong. From where you’re standing, they are socks. From where he is, the seam across his toes is sandpaper, and the alarm clock upstairs that nobody has switched off is going straight through the middle of his head. You are already late. So is he, in a way you can’t see.

This chapter is for neurodivergent people, diagnosed or not, and for the people who live and work with them. It can’t diagnose anyone, and only you get to choose the words you use for yourself.

Two tools elsewhere rest on it. The “How to talk to me” card (Part One, Now, page 33) works because different minds need different input, and saying things plainly helps almost everyone. One owner per job and the written job list (Part Two, Chapter II, page 90) move memory out of anyone’s head and onto paper, which helps ADHD and autistic minds most and everybody a bit.

In quick strokes, a child on the hall floor with his hands over his ears is three things at once. On the surface, a fuss about socks. Underneath, a sensory system turned up high. Underneath that, a morning with no room left in it. The roots are state and setting, and quiet incentives, what the setup rewards. The chapter then takes the ways minds differ one at a time.

  1. Brains vary, like bodies do.

    Brains differ in how they take in the world, focus, move, read, remember and connect with people. “Neurodiversity” is the idea that this variety is natural. “Neurodivergent” describes people whose minds work differently from what gets treated as typical. A different mind isn’t a broken one. Differences can still be disabling, though, especially in a world built for one kind of mind, and that is just as true.

    Gary found out he was dyslexic at forty, and he sat in the car outside the assessment center for twenty minutes afterward with the report on the passenger seat, not reading it, obviously. What he mostly felt was relief. For thirty years he had half believed the teachers who wrote “lazy” in red pen.

    Dig deeper: neurodiversity and disability

  2. Autism is a different way of sensing and connecting.

    Autistic people often communicate more directly and literally. Many have deep, focused interests, feel senses more (or less) intensely than others do, and find predictability calming. Autism doesn’t run along one line from “mild” to “severe.” Each autistic person has their own mix of strengths and needs, which can change from day to day, and the misunderstandings between autistic and non-autistic people usually run both ways.

    The story that got lost in the middle In an experiment, a story was passed along chains of eight people. All-autistic chains kept as much detail as all-non-autistic ones, while mixed chains lost detail faster and reported less rapport, which supports the idea that the difficulty sits between two styles rather than inside one of them.

    Crompton and colleagues (2020) · Moderate: a careful experiment; modest sample, one task

    “Your slides have three typos,” Kate told her colleague, kindly. “One on slide four and two on the summary.” It was exactly what she would have wanted to be told. He went quiet for the rest of the afternoon and she had no idea why until a mutual friend explained it to her at a bar. They were using two different sets of rules for what kindness sounds like, and neither set is wrong, though it would help if they came with subtitles. If you’re the direct one, it can help to say so up front, something like “I like it when people say exactly what they mean, so you can be direct with me.”

    Dig deeper: autism and the double empathy problem

  3. ADHD is about steering attention, not lacking it.

    People with ADHD usually have plenty of attention, and the hard bit is pointing it. Boring tasks feel like pushing a car uphill, interesting ones swallow whole evenings, and time is slippery (there’s “now” and there’s “not now” and not much in between). Feelings arrive fast and big. It’s a real difference in how the brain manages itself. Effort and caring don’t come into it.

    Saffy forgot her best friend’s birthday. Completely. Not a text. Then she spent six hours making a card with pressed flowers from the yard, glued on one at a time with tweezers, and posted it four days late with a note that said “I KNOW.” The forgetting and the six hours came out of the same brain. If something keeps falling out of yours, move it into the world. A labeled alarm. A note on the door. A basket by the front door for the keys.

    Dig deeper: ADHD, time and motivation

  4. Everyone has a sensory profile.

    We all take in sound, light, touch, smell, taste, movement and signals from inside the body. Some people feel these strongly and get overloaded by noise, or a label in a sweater. Others need more input, like movement or strong flavors or firm pressure. Overload is a body at its limit, which is a very different thing from being fussy.

    Two roommates fell out over the kitchen radio, because one found silence creepy and the other found Radio 2 at breakfast physically painful. They settled on the radio until nine and headphones after, which has lasted two years.

    Notice one sound, light or texture that drains you and one that calms you, and change one small thing today.

    Dig deeper: senses, overload and needs

    Professor Puddles

    Knowing your own sensory profile is information, not a complaint. Write it down once and hand it over, and you don’t have to explain it every time.

    Tool: How you connect: how I like to be spoken to spreadloveandacceptance.com/wiring-card

  5. Learning differences aren’t about intelligence.

    Dyslexia (reading and spelling), dyscalculia (numbers), dyspraxia (coordination and planning movement) and language disorders are specific differences, and none of them measures how clever someone is. Plenty of people have a “spiky” profile, very strong in some areas and struggling in others. The right tools, audiobooks or extra time in exams or a reader for the long letters, can level things a good deal.

    Every Wednesday afternoon on the football field, fourteen-year-old Ewan is called clumsy, usually by a PE teacher who should know better. The same term he wrote and directed the school play, which had a revolving set made out of a bike wheel. Ask the people you live or work with how they find it easiest to take things in, and then actually use it.

    Dig deeper: spiky profiles and learning tools

  6. Masking costs energy.

    Many neurodivergent people learn to hide their differences. They copy other people, force eye contact, hold back movements, rehearse small talk in the car. This is called masking. It can get someone through a day. It also uses a great deal of energy, and over years it can wear a person down into exhaustion and burnout. For a long time the cost can be invisible even to the person paying it, which is rather the point of a mask.

    Style, not substance Across three studies, non-autistic people formed poorer first impressions of autistic people from a few seconds of video and were less keen to talk to them. Given only a transcript of what was said, the bias disappeared. That goes a long way to explaining why people mask.

    Sasson and colleagues (2017) · Moderate: three studies with consistent results

    Mia seems completely fine at college, chatty in the canteen and helpful in class and laughing in all the right places. She gets home at four fifteen, goes straight up to her room, and can’t say a word to anyone for an hour. Her dad used to knock and ask what was wrong, and now he leaves a cup of tea outside the door and goes away.

    Notice one place where you could drop the mask a little, and one person you can be fully yourself with. Spend a bit more time there.

    Dig deeper: masking, energy and burnout

  7. Autistic burnout is more than being tired.

    Autistic burnout is a deep, long-lasting exhaustion. Working with autistic adults, Raymaker and colleagues (2020) described it as long-term exhaustion, loss of skills (like speech, planning or self-care) and lower tolerance of noise, light and other input. It comes from long stress without enough support, and it often lasts months. Rest helps, and so do fewer demands and less masking. Pushing harder usually makes it worse. If you think you might be there, list three demands you could drop or hand to someone else for a month.

    Words you could use “I’m in burnout. What I need for a while is fewer demands.” “I can’t do phone calls at the moment. Can we message instead?”

    Dig deeper: burnout, rest and recovery

  8. Meltdowns and shutdowns aren’t choices.

    A meltdown is an involuntary loss of control when overwhelm gets too much, and it can look like crying, shouting, running off or lashing out. A shutdown is the quiet version: going still, losing speech, not being able to respond. Neither is a tantrum. In interviews by Phung and colleagues (2021), autistic young people described meltdowns and shutdowns as separate experiences, both linked to overload.

    For a lot of people words go first. What helps is less of everything. Less noise, fewer words, no questions, more space. Talking can wait, sometimes until the next day. On a calm day, agree a simple signal for “I’m overloaded” and a quiet place to go.

    Ways to say it (to someone else) “You’re safe. I’m right here. No need to talk.” (for yourself) “I’m overloaded. I need quiet for twenty minutes.”

    Dig deeper: meltdowns and shutdowns

  9. Stimming helps, so let it be.

    Stimming means repeated movements or sounds. Rocking, flapping, tapping, humming, pacing, fiddling with something. Most people stim a little. (Watch any meeting and count the jiggling feet.) For many autistic people it matters a lot. In interviews by Kapp and colleagues (2019), autistic adults described stimming as a way to cope with overwhelming emotions and sensations, and objected to efforts to stop harmless stimming. If it isn’t hurting anyone, it doesn’t need stopping. It’s worth noticing what your own hands do when you’re stressed or focused or happy, because that’s yours, and nobody needs to train it out of you.

    Dig deeper: stimming

  10. Deep focus makes switching hard.

    Some minds go deep into one thing at a time, often autistic and ADHD ones. That focus can be a real strength, because it builds expertise and brings a great deal of joy, and it also makes switching hard. Being interrupted can feel like being yanked out of water.

    “Dinner!” Nothing. “Tilly, dinner!” Still nothing. Third time, louder. The fish sticks are going cold and Dominic is getting really frustrated. His daughter is upstairs building a castle and has reached a delicate stage with the drawbridge. The next night he tries a ten-minute warning, then a five. She comes down on time, still talking about the drawbridge, and tells him at length what the problem with it is. He doesn’t entirely follow, but he eats his fish sticks while they’re still warm, which is the main thing. The warning, for the record, goes “Dinner in ten minutes, I’ll come and get you in five minutes,” shouted up the stairs, and it works about four nights out of five.

    Dig deeper: monotropism, flow and transitions

  11. Deep interests are a source of joy and rest.

    Many autistic people have deep, intense interests, often called special interests. The theory of monotropism (Murray, Lesser and Lawson, 2005) describes autistic attention as pulled strongly into a few things at a time. In a survey of autistic adults by Grove and colleagues (2018), people who were more motivated by and engaged with their special interests reported higher wellbeing, though very intense engagement went with lower wellbeing.

    Interests and wellbeing In a large Dutch survey of autistic adults, about two in three had a special interest, and being more motivated by it went with higher wellbeing. Very intense engagement went the other way. The joy is real, and so, some weeks, is the need for an off switch.

    Grove and colleagues (2018) · Moderate: a large survey, self-report, at one point in time

    Ask someone about their favorite subject and let them talk for five minutes without steering. It costs you five minutes. It’s one of the warmest things you can do for anyone.

    Dig deeper: special interests and wellbeing

    Tidbit

    The website can change to fit your mind too, with bigger text, calmer pages and fewer surprises. The settings are worth a look.

    Tool: Read your way spreadloveandacceptance.com/how-you-take-things-in

  12. Meet in the middle, out loud.

    When two kinds of mind live or work together, neither should have to do all the adjusting. Clear, plain words help everyone. Say what you mean, give times, write things down, ask what helps. And changes made for one person (a quiet space, an agenda, flexible hours) usually help plenty of other people too.

    A team started sending meeting agendas a day early, for one autistic colleague. Within a month most of them said meetings had got shorter. Two people who had never said a word in a meeting started saying things.

    Today, swap one “how I work best” fact with someone. Tell them one thing that helps you and ask for one that helps them. The website can bend a bit to your mind too, with Read your way (spreadloveandacceptance.com/how-you-take-things-in) (bigger text, calmer pages, fewer surprises).

    Dig deeper: adjustments that help everyone

  13. Labels are tools, and they belong to the person.

    A diagnosis can bring understanding, and sometimes support and a community too. Some people find their way to a label through self-discovery first. Many autistic adults prefer “autistic person” and others prefer “person with autism.” The kindest rule is to ask, use the words the person chooses, and never try to diagnose somebody else, least of all in an argument.

    The fight was about the dishes. It was going badly. “You’re so autistic,” Danny said, and the conversation ended right there, as it deserved to. In the morning, over toast that neither of them was eating, he said sorry, properly, and then asked what his partner actually needed from him when the kitchen was a mess. It was the conversation they should have had the night before.

    If you’ve wondered about yourself, write down what you’ve noticed and pick one small next step, like talking it over with someone you trust.

    Dig deeper: diagnosis, identity and words

  14. Finding out later in life.

    More and more adults are finding out they’re autistic, or have ADHD, in their thirties or fifties or seventies. Many were missed as children, especially women. In interviews by Leedham and colleagues (2020), women diagnosed at forty or older described how exhausting it had been to go so long without an explanation, and how much the diagnosis changed the way they understood their own lives. Relief and grief and something like joy can all turn up together, on the same afternoon. If that’s you, look for one autistic-led group or online space, and give yourself time.

    Dig deeper: diagnosis later in life

  15. Getting things started and finished is a skill of its own.

    Planning, starting, switching, remembering what you were doing and keeping track of time are called executive function. Many autistic and ADHD people find some of these harder, and harder on some days than others. A review of 235 studies by Demetriou and colleagues (2018) found differences in executive function in autism on average, with a lot of variation between people. The brain’s self-management system is working differently. Laziness doesn’t come into it.

    Siân wrote a forty-page report for her board in a week, and it was excellent. The same three weeks, she could not mail one package. It sat on the hall table while she walked past it forty times. Then she put it by the front door with a yellow sticky note on top (“MAIL ME”) and set an alarm for Tuesday at 8:10, and on Tuesday at 8:11 it went. See routines that help (spreadloveandacceptance.com/adhd-kids) and Wired differently (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wired-differently).

    Dig deeper: executive function in daily life

  16. When demands feel like a threat.

    Some people, often autistic, feel strong anxiety when asked or expected to do things, even things they want to do. Avoiding the demand can look like refusing, joking, changing the subject or a meltdown. The profile was first described as “pathological demand avoidance,” or PDA, by Newson and colleagues (2003).

    It isn’t in the main diagnostic manuals, and researchers disagree about it. A review by Kildahl and colleagues (2021) found the evidence limited and mostly based on parent reports. Many people who identify with it prefer the phrase “persistent drive for autonomy.” Honestly, I’d hold this one loosely until the research settles. What helps tends to be the same whatever it’s called. Less pressure. Requests that feel like invitations. “Put your coat on now” gets a flat no from Reuben every morning. “It’s cold out. Coat or sweater, your choice?” gets the coat, usually.

    Dig deeper: demand avoidance, carefully

  17. Not recognizing faces isn’t rudeness.

    Prosopagnosia, or face blindness, means finding it hard to recognize faces, sometimes even close friends seen out of context. It can be something you’re born with. Many autistic people also find remembering faces harder, as a review by Weigelt and colleagues (2012) found. People who don’t recognize you may be relying on your voice, your hair, your coat or where they usually see you.

    Clive walked straight past his neighbor in the supermarket without a flicker, and she went home feeling snubbed and told her sister about it on the phone. When he explained, a week later and very embarrassed, that he hadn’t known her without her spaniel, she laughed. Now she says “Hi Clive, it’s Jo from number twelve” every time, even when the spaniel is right there.

    Words to try “I’m bad with faces, so please say who you are when you say hi.” (to someone else) “Hi, it’s Jo from next door.”

    Dig deeper: face blindness

  18. Not speaking isn’t the same as having nothing to say.

    Some autistic people speak rarely, sometimes or not at all, and some lose speech when stressed. Many communicate through AAC (augmentative and alternative communication), which can mean typing, letter boards, picture cards, apps or sign. Using AAC doesn’t stop speech developing: a review by Millar, Light and Schlosser (2006) found it did not hold speech back, and may help it. The safest place to start is to presume competence, which means assuming the person understands and has something to say, and giving them the time and the tools to say it.

    At Sunday lunch at her grandma’s, fifteen-year-old Ruby types on her tablet. Her uncle used to talk about her across the table as if she wasn’t there (“Does she want gravy?”). Now he asks her, and waits, a bit longer than he’d like, while she types. Her answer was “Yes. Obviously.” Wait longer than feels natural, which will feel very long and isn’t.

    Dig deeper: non-speaking people and AAC

  19. Telling friends and dates is your choice.

    Whether to tell someone you’re autistic or ADHD, and when, is up to you. Telling can bring understanding. In a study by Sasson and Morrison (2019), people formed better first impressions of autistic adults when they knew they were autistic, especially if they knew more about autism.

    People don’t always respond well, though, and interviews by Au-Yeung and colleagues (2025) describe autistic adults weighing hope for support against fear of not being believed. Many share a little at a time, starting with what helps and leaving the label for later. Second date, outside a bar with a line. “I’m autistic,” Nina said, “so I’m quite direct, and I’d rather walk than sit in there.” Her date looked at the bar, then the line, then back at her. “Oh, thank God,” he said. They walked along the canal as far as the lock and back.

    Words you could use “I’m autistic. For me that means…” “I won’t always pick up hints, so please just tell me.” (if someone shares with you) “Thanks for telling me. What helps?”

    Dig deeper: disclosure in friendships and dating

  20. Finding your people.

    Lots of autistic people describe meeting other autistic people as a turning point, because at last they don’t have to translate or explain or mask. The research backs this up. Cooper, Smith and Russell (2017) found that autistic people who felt more connected to other autistic people had higher self-esteem, and through that, less anxiety and depression. Being autistic can be an identity and a community as well as a diagnosis.

    After his diagnosis at fifty-three, Bernard joined an online group of autistic adults who love old maps, specifically the Ordnance Survey kind with hand-drawn hachures. The first evening he talked to them for three hours about contour lines. When he logged off he had more energy than when he’d started, which hadn’t happened after a conversation in years.

    Dig deeper: autistic community and identity

Your part, and only your part. You can’t change how your brain, or anyone else’s, is wired. You can learn how yours works and say what helps, and ask others what helps them. Meeting in the middle means both people move a little. If you’re always the one adjusting, it’s fair to say so. More in Your wiring, weather and words (page 33)

Monday, 8:30am

You stop asking. You sit down on the hall floor next to him, which is cold, and say, “Socks feel wrong?” He nods without opening his eyes. You go upstairs, switch the alarm clock off, dig the old seamless pair out of the laundry basket. Two minutes later his shoes are on. You’re ten minutes late and nobody has shouted, which on a Monday is about as good as it gets. That night you order three more pairs and let him pick the colors.

Two ways to read this

Headphones at dinner, two ways

Some brains filter background sound without trying, so a busy kitchen is just company. Others take in every clatter, voice and hum at once, and filtering it by hand uses up the attention they wanted for the people. If you filter easily, headphones at the table can look like shutting everyone out, and for the other person they’re how they stay at the table at all. If you hear everything, it may help to say so: “The headphones mean I can stay. Talk to me and I’ll take one out.”

Where the fields meet. Holistic therapies start with the body before the argument, which fits overload well: less noise, fewer words, settle first and talk later. Some of these practices are well studied and some are debated, so only the plain everyday parts are used here. The root underneath is quiet incentives, because a setup that only rewards masking will get a lot of masking.

In everyday life

On your own

Knowing how your mind works helps you build a life that fits it, and spot burnout before it’s on top of you (see Get to know your wiring, spreadloveandacceptance.com/self-path). Partners can swap “how I work best” notes about plans, messages, touch and time alone. With children, behavior very often has a sensory or overload reason, so “What’s too much right now?” is worth asking before “Why are you doing this?” A friend who cancels at the last minute may just be out of energy, and offering something easier, like a walk, keeps the door open. At work, written agendas, clear deadlines and quiet spaces help far more people than the ones they were made for.

If you have ADHD and share a home, make the chore tools lighter. Log three days instead of seven, with a tally on the fridge. Own a few jobs completely, each with a labeled alarm, instead of helping a bit with everything. Forgetting is a setup problem to fix together. More in the expanded version (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-9-minds-in-depth).

Common mix-ups

“Everyone’s a bit autistic” is probably the commonest, and it makes real needs sound small. Everyone shares some traits, but autism is a whole pattern, present across life. ADHD doesn’t just mean not sitting still. Many people with it, girls and women especially, are mostly inattentive or restless on the inside. “They seem fine to me” overlooks how much masking can hide, and seeming fine can cost someone their whole evening. Adjustments aren’t special treatment; they remove a barrier, the way glasses do. And the idea that autistic people lack empathy is simply out of date. Many feel other people’s feelings very strongly, and the differences in how empathy is shown run both ways.

If you want to help someone else with this

Believe them about what’s hard and what helps, even when it’s different for you. Be clear, which means saying what you mean, giving times and writing down anything important. Ask what helps, because every neurodivergent person is different and their answer will beat any list, this one included. Protect their energy. Quiet time, warnings before changes and a way out of loud places matter more than they look. And enjoy their interests with them, if you can.

Ways to say it “Is there anything about this place, or this plan, that would make it hard for you?” “You don’t have to explain. Just tell me what you need.”

Part Three · Chapter 10

Values, meaning and a good life: what philosophy offers everyday life

What matters to you, how to find it, what to do when two good things pull against each other, and what a few very old ideas can offer an ordinary, busy week.

In this chapter

  1. Values are directions you keep walking in
  2. Your strong feelings point to what you value
  3. Two good things can pull in different directions
  4. Put your effort where it can land
  5. A good life is more than a good mood
  6. Meaning comes from ordinary places
  7. Different values aren’t wrong values
  8. Values live in small, everyday acts
  9. In everyday life
  10. If you want to help someone else with this
  11. Tools and reading on this site
  12. More for your situation

At a glance

  • Values are directions you keep turning toward. You never finish being kind, and that is why values still work on days when goals fall apart.
  • Strong feelings point to what you value. Anger often guards fairness, and hurt often guards closeness.
  • Meaning comes from ordinary places. People, care and everyday work give most of us most of our meaning.
  • Values live in small acts. One small thing this week, done because it matters, counts.

Sunday, 9pm

The week ahead has the car inspection on Tuesday, a dentist, two late meetings and your turn for the school drop-off, twice, and none of it feels like yours, somehow. You’re not sad, exactly. You just can’t remember the last time you did something because it mattered to you, and not because it was next on the list.

This chapter is about values, the things you care about and the direction you want your life to face, and about what makes a life feel worth living. It borrows from psychology, and from philosophy, which has been asking how we ought to live for more than two thousand years. You don’t need to have read any of it. I’ve tried to keep the old names to a minimum and the words plain.

In quick strokes, a full week looks like a diary problem. Underneath, it is a values problem, two good things wanting the same evening. Underneath that, what quietly gets rewarded at home. The roots are ownership and structure, and quiet incentives. The chapter then slows down on each.

  1. Values are directions you keep walking in.

    A goal is something you can check off, like painting the hall or passing the test. A value is a direction you keep walking in, like looking after your health, or making home feel cared for, or being a fair friend. Nobody ever finishes being kind. That’s exactly why a value still works on a day when a goal falls apart.

    Bethan was going to go to the gym three times this week. She went once, on the Monday. On Thursday evening she was on the couch in her gym clothes eating a family bag of fries and feeling like a failure. So she asked herself what the gym was for. Looking after her body, was the answer, and when she asked what that was for, it was so she’d have energy for the kids. On Friday she walked twenty minutes at lunchtime, around the little park behind the office, past the man who feeds the pigeons, and as far as she was concerned it counted.

    Dig deeper: goals and values

  2. Your strong feelings point to what you value.

    You don’t have to invent your values from scratch. They show up in your strongest reactions. Anger often means something you care about has been stepped on. Envy can point to something you want for yourself. Sadness tends to show what you love.

    A colleague stood up in the quarterly review and took credit for a whole team’s work, and Sacha was so angry he couldn’t eat his lunch. He spent the afternoon drafting emails he didn’t send. On the train home it dawned on him that it wasn’t really about the colleague. It was fairness. Seeing people’s effort. That was what had been stepped on. At the next team meeting he raised it as a fairness thing (“Can we agree how we credit joint work?”) instead of seething at one person for a month, and it went better than any of the emails would have.

    Dig deeper: finding your values

  3. Two good things can pull in different directions.

    Most hard choices aren’t between something good and something bad. They’re between two good things, honesty and kindness, say, or family and rest. Feeling torn just means you care about more than one thing. Even when you choose well, it’s normal to feel a bit sad about the side you didn’t pick.

    Pickles, the family Labrador, was very ill, and Megan’s eight-year-old kept asking. Megan cares about being honest, and she also cares about protecting her son. She sat on the kitchen floor next to the dog’s bed with him and tried to do both. “Pickles is very sick. The vet is helping. We’ll look after him together.” Her son thought about it for a long time, picking at the edge of the dog blanket. “Is he going to die?” “He might,” she said. “We don’t know yet.” He put his hand on Pickles’s side, very carefully, and left it there.

    If you’re stuck on a choice, write down the good thing on each side. You may be able to honor some of both, even if you can’t have all of either.

    Dig deeper: when values clash

  4. Put your effort where it can land.

    About two thousand years ago a teacher called Epictetus, who had been born into slavery, taught that some things are up to us and some aren’t. It’s one of the oldest ideas in this book and still one of the most useful. Your own choices and how you treat people are up to you. Other people’s choices, and the weather, and the past, are not. Worry tends to pile up in the second heap. Values do their work in the first.

    Ingrid wants her partner to enjoy Christmas at her mom’s, and she can’t make him. She has tried, for six years, mainly by telling him it’ll be fun. What she can do is plan a shorter visit, put a long muddy walk on the day after Christmas into it, which he’ll like, and be warm herself. That’s her part, and it turns out to be quite a lot.

    Dig deeper: what is up to us

  5. A good life is more than a good mood.

    Feeling good matters. But many thinkers, from the Greek philosopher Aristotle to psychologists now, also describe a second kind of wellbeing. It comes from growing, using your strengths, being a decent friend, and doing things that matter even when they’re hard. Aristotle called it flourishing, and he thought you build it the way you build any skill, by practice, a little at a time.

    Jade spent a whole month of evenings helping a friend move out of a damp, miserable apartment. She scrubbed black mold off a bathroom ceiling with a toothbrush. She carried boxes down three flights of stairs while the friend cried on the landing. It was tiring and not much fun, and at the end of the year, when she thinks back over it, she counts it as one of the best months she had.

    Dig deeper: happiness and flourishing

    Professor Puddles

    If you enjoy big questions, put philosophy next to psychology and see what they share. It’s one of my favorite rainy-day pastimes.

  6. Meaning comes from ordinary places.

    Researchers who study meaning often describe three parts to it: your life makes some sense to you, you’re heading somewhere, and your life matters to someone. Most meaning comes from people, from work done with care and from small roles other people count on, far more than from big moments.

    Three meanings of meaning The three parts above come from Martela and Steger, who split meaning into coherence (life makes sense), purpose (a direction) and significance (your life matters). It’s a way of thinking that has shaped later research rather than a finding in itself.

    Martela and Steger (2016) · Theory: a conceptual paper that has shaped later measurement

    Walter has lived alone since his wife died, and for a long time his days went very quiet. Now he reads to the under-fives at the library on Wednesday mornings. He irons a shirt for it on Tuesday nights. He does the voices, badly. When he had a cold in February and missed two weeks, a four-year-old called Albie asked the librarian every single day where the man was.

    Try listing the roles you play, big or small (neighbor, sister, the one who waters the office plants), and next to each one write who it matters to.

    Dig deeper: where meaning comes from

  7. Different values aren’t wrong values.

    Two people can share a home, a family or a team and still put the same good things in a different order, one putting safety first and another adventure. The philosopher Isaiah Berlin argued that there are many real goods in life and they can’t all be ranked on one scale, which leaves room to disagree without either person being bad.

    People who love you will sometimes try to change your mind, and that’s ordinary influence. They tell you why, they listen to your reasons, and the choice stays yours. It becomes pressure when it keeps coming after you’ve said no, when saying no costs you something, such as days of coldness, money or being left out, or when it’s aimed at the people and things that matter most to you. A good test is whether you can say “I see it differently” and still be treated warmly the next day.

    Jasper likes a calm, tidy house. His roommate Darnell likes an open door and people dropping in. For months each of them privately thought the other was a bit much, uptight in one direction, messy in the other. It came out one night over takeout. “I just like knowing who’s going to be in the kitchen,” Jasper said. Darnell said, “I just like it when anyone is.” Fridays are open house now, and Sundays are quiet, or as quiet as Darnell can manage.

    In your next disagreement, you might ask, “What matters to you about this?” and listen for the value under the position.

    Dig deeper: living with different values

  8. Values live in small, everyday acts.

    A good life is built mostly from small things done again and again. How you say hello. Whether you keep small promises. How you talk about someone who isn’t in the room. The Chinese teacher Confucius taught that small, everyday courtesies shape who we become, and later thinkers who wrote about care said that being good starts with paying attention to the person in front of you.

    Kindness does something for the giver A meta-analysis of 27 experiments found that acts of kindness gave the person doing them a small-to-medium lift in wellbeing. The authors flagged worries about study quality, so take the size with a pinch of salt and the direction with rather less.

    Curry and colleagues (2018) · Moderate: the authors noted concerns about study quality and possible publication bias

    An older man at the self-checkout can’t get the card machine to take his card. The line behind him is growing and somebody near the back tuts, loudly. You’re next, and you don’t sigh. You say, “No rush.” He says, “It’s always this one, isn’t it,” and you agree that it is. The whole thing costs you about forty seconds.

    Pick one value, choose one tiny act that shows it, and do it every day this week. You’ll drift, as everyone does, and turning back is the practice.

    Dig deeper: everyday ethics

    Sugarfoot

    A value can be as small as a cup of tea made just the way someone likes it. A “What feels like care” card helps you learn what that is for each of you.

    Tool: How you connect: what feels like care spreadloveandacceptance.com/love-languages

Your part, and only your part. You can choose your direction. When you notice you’ve drifted, you can turn back without shame. You can’t choose other people’s values for them, and you don’t have to adopt theirs to love them. You can share what matters to you, listen to what matters to them, and look for the places where your directions overlap.

Sunday, 9:20pm

On the back of an envelope you write people, health and making things, and under each one, a small thing for this week. See Grandma, walk on Wednesday, finish the shelf in the spare room, the one that has been “nearly done” since Easter. The week is just as full as it was. You prop the envelope against the kettle, where it’ll be the first thing you see.

Two ways to read this

Values, two ways

Some people hold a value as a rule: honesty means saying the true thing, every time. Others hold it as a direction, adjusted to the moment. If you hold rules, the direction person isn’t being slippery. They’re weighing two good things at once. If you hold directions, the rule person isn’t being harsh. A clear rule is how they stay steady.

Where the fields meet. Politics has a lot to say about two people with different values under one roof: a fair way to decide, and a say for everyone, and a way to change the rule later. The root is ownership and structure, plus quiet incentives, because a home drifts toward whatever it rewards.

In everyday life

Partners may rank the same values differently, security and adventure, say, and it helps to say what each of you is protecting before you argue about the plan. Two generations of a family can both value family and mean very different things by it, from living around the corner to being free to go, so it’s worth asking what the word means to each of you. When a job keeps asking you to act against a value, the strain often shows up as tiredness or cynicism, and naming the clash is a first step. A club, a faith group or some volunteering can give you a place to act on a value alongside other people.

If you want to help someone else with this

“What matters most to you about this?” helps more than telling someone what they ought to care about. People often see their values for the first time in someone else’s words, so it can help to notice them out loud. “You stayed late to help your friend. Loyalty really matters to you, doesn’t it?” With children, naming the value when you see it teaches more than any lecture. Try not to use values as a weapon, because “I thought you valued family” lands as a guilt trip. You can disagree with someone’s choice and still see the good thing they were reaching for.

You could say “What would a good outcome look like to you?” “What do you want to be able to say about how you handled this, a year from now?”

A limit to keep in mind: This chapter shares ideas to think with, not answers to follow. Your values are yours to find, and it’s fine if they change as your life does.

Part Three · Chapter 11

Healing after hurt: repair, forgiveness and old hurts

How hurt heals, why it lingers, how small breaks get mended, what a real apology sounds like, and what forgiveness is and isn’t.

In this chapter

  1. Hurt is real, and healing takes time
  2. Every close relationship has breaks. Repair is what counts
  3. Telling someone they hurt you
  4. A real apology names it, owns it, and mends it
  5. Forgiveness isn’t forgetting, excusing or going back
  6. You can heal even if they never say sorry
  7. Trust comes back in small, kept promises
  8. Going back is a choice
  9. Look after the hurt part of you
  10. How old hurts shape new reactions
  11. In everyday life
  12. If you want to help someone else with this
  13. Tools and reading on this site
  14. More for your situation

At a glance

  • Hurt is real, and healing takes time. Replaying a hurt says more about how much it mattered than about any weakness in you.
  • Repair is what counts. Every close relationship has breaks, and a real apology names what happened, owns it and offers to mend it.
  • Forgiving and going back are separate choices. You can forgive without forgetting, excusing or letting someone back in.
  • Going back is a choice. You can heal even if they never say sorry.

Thursday, 2am

It was one sentence, three weeks ago, said over your shoulder in somebody’s kitchen at a party on the way to the fridge, and they have almost certainly forgotten it.

You haven’t. It plays again, word for word, tone and all, followed by every clever thing you could have said back and didn’t. You’re very tired of carrying it about, and you honestly don’t know where you’d put it down if you could.

Everyone gets hurt, and everyone hurts other people, mostly without meaning to. This chapter looks at how hurt works and how relationships mend, and at how you can heal with or without the other person, for small hurts and bigger ones.

Seen fast, a sentence from three weeks ago is three things. On top, the words, which you can still quote. Under them, what they seemed to say about you. Under that, the question of whether it will happen again. The roots are balance and signal and noise. The chapter slows down on repair.

  1. Hurt is real, and healing takes time.

    Being hurt by someone shows that something mattered, whether it was the person, or your trust in them, or your sense of being respected. The mind replays hurts because it’s trying to understand them and keep you safe from the next one. Healing rarely goes in a straight line. The hurt can come back on an anniversary, or out of nowhere, which doesn’t mean you’ve failed.

    What a hurt is about When Leary and colleagues asked people about times their feelings were hurt, the common thread was feeling less valued by someone, usually someone they knew well. A stranger’s remark stings for an afternoon. A friend’s can stay for months.

    Leary and colleagues (1998) · Moderate: based on people’s recollections; the idea is widely supported

    Months after a friend said something cruel to him at a party, Kwesi still feels a jolt whenever the song that was playing comes on the radio. It happened again on Sunday, chopping onions. He said, out loud, to nobody, “Oh, that,” turned the radio down, and carried on with the onions.

    Thoughts you could try “This hurts because it mattered.” “A feeling coming back doesn’t mean I’m back at the start.”

    Dig deeper: why hurt lingers

  2. Every close relationship has breaks. Repair is what counts.

    No relationship is smooth all the time, because people snap, forget, misread each other and let each other down. Research on parents and babies, on couples and on therapy all points the same way. Breaks are normal, and what matters most is whether they get mended. A small repair, made soon, often leaves a relationship feeling safer than before the break.

    Even therapy has ruptures Across 11 studies, repairing breaks in the relationship between therapist and client went with better results. Training therapists in repair didn’t show a clear effect on outcomes in the six studies that tested it, which is a useful bit of honesty.

    Eubanks, Muran and Safran (2018) · Strong: a meta-analysis, though the main finding is correlational

    Orange juice, a full glass, right across the breakfast table and into the toast rack. Toby’s dad shouted, not a huge shout, but enough. Twenty minutes later he sat down next to him on the couch. “I was grumpy and I shouted. That wasn’t fair, spills happen. Want to help me make a new one?” They went and did it together. Toby poured, very slowly, with his tongue out, and slopped some, and they both pretended he hadn’t.

    Dig deeper: breaks and repair

  3. Telling someone they hurt you.

    People can’t mend what they don’t know about. Saying “that hurt” is a risk, but it gives the relationship a chance. It works best when you describe what happened and how it felt, and leave out what kind of person they are. Pick a calm moment, well away from the middle of a fight.

    Amara had a stronger word ready, one she’d been working on for days. On a walk with her friend, not over the phone, she said this instead. “When you told the group about my breakup before I was ready, I felt exposed. I’d like to be the one who shares my news.” Her friend, who had honestly thought she was helping, went bright red. There was a long, awful pause next to a bench with a brass plaque on it for somebody called Maud. Then the friend said, “God. Yes. Sorry,” and they walked on. It was a bit stiff for the rest of the walk and fine by the following week.

    Before you say it, try writing it down in three short lines, one for what happened, one for how you felt and one for what you’d like.

    Dig deeper: saying “that hurt”

  4. A real apology names it, owns it, and mends it.

    “Sorry if you were upset” doesn’t heal much. A real apology says what you did, takes responsibility without excuses, shows you understand what it did to the other person, and offers to put it right or do things differently. Research, such as a study led by Roy Lewicki (2016), suggests owning it and offering repair are the parts that matter most.

    At the Tuesday meeting, Leila presented an idea she’d worked out with a colleague as if it were all hers. She saw his face. She spent the evening telling herself it didn’t matter, then the next morning went and found him at the coffee machine. “I presented our idea as mine. That wasn’t fair to you. I’ll email the team today and say it was joint work.” He said, “Okay,” and then, after a moment, “Thanks.” She sent the email at 9.40 and copied him in.

    Next time you say sorry, check it has each of the four parts. If it went wrong in a conversation, Rewind the talk (spreadloveandacceptance.com/carrier-wave-decoder) helps you find the words, and Apology languages (spreadloveandacceptance.com/apology-languages) has more.

    Dig deeper: what makes an apology work

    Professor Puddles

    An apology lands best when it’s plain: what happened, that it was yours, and what you’ll do now. Rewind the talk can help you find those words.

    Tool: Rewind the talk spreadloveandacceptance.com/carrier-wave-decoder

  5. Forgiveness isn’t forgetting, excusing or going back.

    Forgiveness is usually described as letting go of resentment and the wish to get even, and it happens inside you. Forgiving someone doesn’t mean saying what happened was okay. It doesn’t mean forgetting, or trusting them again, or keeping them in your life. It’s a choice, often a slow one, and you never owe it on anyone else’s schedule.

    Danielle forgave her father for missing most of her childhood, though it took her well into her thirties. She keeps his visits to an hour and won’t leave the children with him if he’s been drinking. He knows why. They don’t discuss it. For her the forgiving and the protecting sit side by side without much strain.

    Things to tell yourself “I can let go of wanting to get even, and still keep my limits.” “I don’t have to forgive today. I can just stop feeding the anger today.”

    Dig deeper: what forgiveness is

  6. You can heal even if they never say sorry.

    Waiting for an apology that never comes can keep you stuck for years, because the person may be gone, or unwilling, or unable to understand. Your healing doesn’t have to depend on them. You can make sense of what happened, tell your story to someone safe, and decide what it means for you now.

    Writing helps, a bit Pooling 146 randomized studies, Frattaroli found that writing about something painful had a small but real benefit on average. Small is the honest word, and it varies a good deal from person to person.

    Frattaroli (2006) · Moderate: a real but small effect that varies by person

    After the breakup, Martha wrote a letter she never sent. Four pages in pen, both sides, about what hurt and what she’d hoped for and what she was taking with her, which was mostly the good saucepans. She folded it into the back of a notebook and for a while she read it most nights, then less, and then one day in April she realized she hadn’t looked at it for a month.

    Writing works for a lot of people. Write about the hurt for fifteen minutes on three or four days in a row, the facts and the feelings both. If it ever makes you feel much worse, stop and talk to someone instead.

    Dig deeper: healing on your own

  7. Trust comes back in small, kept promises.

    After trust is broken, one big apology rarely rebuilds it. Trust grows back slowly, in lots of small moments where someone does what they said they’d do. If you broke trust, being patient and consistent matters more than a grand gesture. If you were let down, it’s fair to watch what someone does as well as what they say.

    Declan hid a credit card debt from his partner for most of a year. When it came out it was very bad for a while. After that, on the first of every month, he left his bank statement on the kitchen table without being asked, with no speech, just the statement left by the fruit bowl. About a year in, one ordinary evening, his partner said she could breathe again. He went into the yard so she wouldn’t see his face.

    Dig deeper: how trust is rebuilt

  8. Going back is a choice.

    After a hurt, you can mend the relationship or change its shape. You can also step away. All three can be healthy.

    Ellie’s roommate borrowed money twice and didn’t pay it back. Ellie let the first time go, because it was only ten dollars and she’d been broke herself. The second time it was fifty dollars for a train ticket to Chicago, and she said, “I won’t lend money again. I still want us to get along in the house.” The roommate went quiet for two days and left a slightly pointed note about the recycling. They still do Sunday dinner together most weeks, and nobody mentions Chicago.

    Three questions can guide what comes next. Has the hurt stopped? Has it been owned? Do you want this relationship in your life?

    It also helps to tell one hurt from a pattern of hurt. A single hurt, owned and repaired, is something most relationships survive, and many come out closer. A pattern looks different. The same hurt keeps happening after you’ve named it, apologies arrive without any change, and you notice yourself saying less to avoid the next one. One bad month isn’t a pattern, and neither is a partner who is slow to apologize but changes what they do.

    Dig deeper: limits, distance and safety

  9. Look after the hurt part of you.

    Hurt lives in the body as well as the mind, as poor sleep or a jumpy feeling that won’t settle. Healing goes better with basic care, which means rest and food and moving about, people who are kind to you, and talking to yourself the way you’d talk to a hurting friend. Some people find they grow after something painful and some don’t, and neither is a test you can fail.

    A man at the back of the 38 bus shouted at Idris and called him names, the whole way from downtown to the end of the line, and nobody else said a word. For days afterward Idris felt shaky. He told a friend. He went for long walks after work. He kept reminding himself it was about the man, and that he was safe now. Over a couple of weeks the shakiness faded, though he sat downstairs on the 38 until well into the spring.

    Pick one small act of care for today, an early night or time with someone kind. Calm tools are in Upset right now? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/upset-right-now)

    Dig deeper: healing in body and mind

Your part, and only your part. You can say what hurt, apologize for what you did, and look after your own healing. You can’t make someone apologize or change, and you don’t have to wait for them to start feeling better. Forgiveness, trust and going back are all yours to choose, in your own time.

Saturday, 11am

You wrote it all down last night, every word of it, two pages. This morning you wrote a much shorter version. When you said that, I felt small. I just wanted you to know.

You haven’t sent it. It’s sitting in your drafts between a half-finished email to the city about trash pickup and a shopping list that just says “eggs??” But the two o’clock replays have gone a bit quieter since it went onto paper.

zqaxunderstandingx11xhealingxxoldxhurtsqzHow old hurts shape new reactions

What happened earlier in life can make some reactions more likely now. In surveys of tens of thousands of adults in 24 countries, most had lived through at least one traumatic event (Kessler and colleagues, 2017 · Strong evidence), and many studies have linked hard childhood experiences with health and relationship problems decades later (Felitti and colleagues, 1998 · Strong evidence). That is an association across large groups, not a forecast for any one person. A mark can be left at any age.

  • In early childhood, a child who learned to watch a parent’s mood may grow into an adult who scans every face in a meeting.
  • In the school years, being shamed in front of a class can make any public correction sting.
  • In the teens, months of being left out can make a group chat that goes quiet feel like a verdict.
  • In early adulthood, a first job or first home that went badly can make the next change feel dangerous.
  • In a partnership, a betrayal can make an innocent late text feel like the start of another one.
  • As a parent, a frightening birth or a child’s illness can leave you braced for the next emergency.
  • In midlife, a layoff, a divorce or caring for a parent can wear down the reserves that used to absorb a bad day.
  • In later life, losses and illness can arrive close together, with less time to recover between them.

Most people who go through something terrible recover without lasting problems (Bonanno, 2004 · Strong evidence). For some, especially after repeated or very severe events, the body’s alarm stays switched on. Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is the clinical name for one form of this. It follows exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury or sexual violence, and most people who go through such events don’t develop it (Koenen and colleagues, 2017 · Strong evidence). Trauma responses can look like being on edge, startling easily, avoiding reminders, going numb, or meeting a small thing with the force of the old one. Those responses once helped someone get through. In a conversation they usually make things harder, because the person is answering the past as well as the present.

You might recognize it in yourself when a reaction feels older than the moment, arrives in your body before you can think, follows the same kind of trigger each time, or is hard to explain afterward. You might notice it in someone else when their reaction is far bigger than what just happened. These signs are for understanding. They are not a diagnosis, and you can’t diagnose yourself or anyone else from them.

Having lived through something hard is never the person’s fault. The aim is to take back control, so the old event stops running today’s reaction. That usually starts small: noticing “this feels older than today,” naming it, steadying your body, and then choosing what to do next. Trauma-focused therapies have the strongest evidence for PTSD (NICE, 2018 · Strong evidence).

Two ways to read this

Fine all day, two ways

Some people show how they feel as they go, so a hard day shows during the day. Others hold it together for hours, at work or school, and let go only once they’re somewhere safe, which is often home. If you show it as you go, the person who falls apart at home isn’t saving their worst for you. Home is where it’s safe to stop holding on. If you’re the one who holds it in, saying “I’ve used it all up today” helps the people at home read the crash for what it is.

Where the fields meet. Finance gives repair a plain picture: a real apology tops up a reserve of goodwill that small hurts draw down. Psychology adds the reason repairs are needed even between kind people, that intent isn’t impact.

In everyday life

Between partners, small breaks happen most days, and a quick “That came out wrong, can I try again?” mends most of them (see How to apologize so it counts). Old family hurts often need a different kind of talk from new ones, and sometimes more time apart. A friend may not know they hurt you, and “Can I tell you something that stung? I’d rather say it than drift” keeps the door open. You can even heal a hurt with someone who has died, by writing to them or talking it through with someone you trust.

  • After an affair. The shock is real for both people. Couples can recover, and some decide to part; both can be done with care. Trust returns through kept promises over months. More in the expanded version (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-11-healing-in-depth).
  • If you decide to separate. Part as kindly as you can. Tell children together, without blame, and never ask them to choose. Write decisions down, and consider family mediation. More in the expanded version (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-11-healing-in-depth#separating).

If you want to help someone else with this

Listen before you advise. “That sounds really painful” helps far more than “You should just let it go.” Don’t rush them toward forgiveness, which can feel like being told their hurt doesn’t matter. Don’t push them to cut someone off, either; it’s their relationship and their choice. If you were the one who caused the hurt, give a real apology and then give them time, and don’t ask them to make you feel better about it.

Words you could use “Do you want to talk it through, or would it help more to take your mind off it?” “Whatever you decide about them, I’m on your side.”
