Part Three · Chapter 12

Helping others well: support without fixing, boundaries, and not burning out

How to help someone without taking over, by asking what they need, listening first, caring without drowning and keeping kind limits, and how to keep going without burning out.

In this chapter

  1. Ask what kind of help they want
  2. Listening is a kind of help
  3. Fixing it for them can take away their power
  4. Care without drowning in their feelings
  5. Your limits make your help last
  6. Notice when you’re running on empty
  7. Don’t wait for someone else to step in
  8. Let other people help you too
  9. In everyday life
  10. Caring a lot, or losing yourself?
  11. Common mix-ups
  12. If you want to help someone else with this
  13. Tools and reading on this site
  14. More for your situation

At a glance

  • Ask what kind of help they want. “Ideas, or just someone to listen?” saves a lot of misfires.
  • Listening is help. Fixing a problem for someone can take away their power.
  • Your limits make your help last, and caring from a steady place helps more than drowning in their feelings.

Wednesday, 7:15pm

Your friend is telling you about her awful week. Before she’s finished her first sentence you have five good ideas. You give her all five, in order, with reasons.

“Yeah,” she says. “Maybe.”

You both hang up feeling slightly worse, and neither of you could say why.

Most of us want to help the people around us, and helping well is a skill, because good intentions don’t always land. This chapter looks at how support works, why fixing can backfire, and how to care for people in a way you can keep up. Two tools elsewhere grew out of it. One owner per job (Part Two, Chapter II, page 90), because caregivers burn out when everything counts as “just helping” and nobody else owns a job. And How much are you carrying? (Part Two, Chapter III, page 109), which helps you notice you’re running on empty before you snap or stop.

A friend’s awful week, in quick strokes. The surface is a phone call. Underneath, two kinds of help on offer and only one wanted. Underneath that, how much each of you has left. The roots are ownership and structure, and limited capacity. The chapter slows down on both.

  1. Ask what kind of help they want.

    Help comes in kinds. Some people want ideas. Some want someone to listen. Some want a practical hand, a meal or a ride, and some just want company on the couch, and giving the wrong kind, however kindly, can leave someone feeling unheard.

    That phone call could have gone differently. “That sounds like a rotten week. Do you want ideas, or do you just want to have a rant?” It feels a bit formal the first few times you say it, like reading off a card, but people tend to love being asked.

    Dig deeper: kinds of support

  2. Listening is a kind of help.

    Being properly heard helps people calm down and think, and quite often they find their own answer. Good listening means paying attention, letting them finish, checking you understood, and showing that their feelings make sense even if you’d feel differently.

    Matching the help to the problem Cutrona and Russell proposed that support works best when it fits the problem: practical help for things that can be changed, comfort for things that can’t. Later studies back this in part.

    Cutrona and Russell (1990) · Moderate: widely cited; later studies support it in part

    Ravi came home furious about his boss. His partner had “Just quit” ready on her tongue and kept it there. “So he went off at you in front of everyone,” she said, “after you’d stayed late all week. No wonder you’re livid.” Ravi’s shoulders came down about two inches. Ten minutes later he was sketching out a plan on the back of a takeout menu. It was a better plan than “just quit,” which he’d have hated being told anyway.

    In one conversation today, listen for two whole minutes without giving advice, then sum up what you heard. Two minutes is longer than you think.

    Dig deeper: how listening helps

    Sugarfoot

    Sometimes the best help is sitting close and listening, with no fixing. Listening takes energy too, so check your own tank now and then.

    Workpaper WP-02: How much are you carrying? spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-02

  3. Fixing it for them can take away their power.

    When we love someone we want the problem gone. But doing things for people that they could do themselves can leave them feeling less capable, so helping well often means helping someone do it themselves. It’s their life, and their choice.

    Rosalind’s son is twenty-four and struggling with a job application for the city, and she is itching to rewrite it. She can see three things wrong with the first paragraph alone. She sits on her hands. “Would you like me to read it and say what stands out?” He makes the changes himself, some of them, not the ones she’d have made. When he gets the interview he’s quietly, enormously proud, and so is she, and she doesn’t mention the paragraph.

    Dig deeper: support without taking over

  4. Care without drowning in their feelings.

    Feeling someone’s pain as if it were yours can wear you out fast. Researchers separate this “empathic distress” from compassion, which is warm concern from a steadier place, still caring deeply without sinking alongside the other person. A steady helper is more use than a second person drowning.

    When Abi’s roommate went through a breakup, Abi cried with her every night, stopped sleeping, and was a wreck by the end of the first week. So she changed tack. Still kind, still there. But a run in the mornings, and Friday evening with her own friends, and a quiet reminder to herself, roughly hourly, that this was her roommate’s pain to feel and hers to keep company with.

    Dig deeper: empathy and compassion

  5. Your limits make your help last.

    Saying yes to everything leads, eventually, to resentment, exhaustion and not being able to help at all. Limits tell people what you can actually give, so your yes means something. And a kind no that comes with an offer of what you can do is still help.

    Kojo’s sister keeps asking to borrow money, fifty here and eighty there, and none of it comes back. He loves her and he’s running out, of money and of something else. On the phone one evening, with the TV on mute, he says it. “I can’t lend money anymore. I can help you go through your bills on Sunday, if you want.” There’s a silence long enough for him to hear her kettle click off. “Fine,” she says, not fine. On Sunday she turns up with a grocery bag full of envelopes.

    Ways to say it “I can’t do that, but I can do this.” “I want to help, and I need to stop at nine tonight.”

    If you need words for a “not this time,” Say no kindly (spreadloveandacceptance.com/refusals) helps you make your own, with something to offer instead.

    Dig deeper: boundaries in helping

    Professor Puddles

    Your limits keep your help going for longer. When you need to say “not this time,” Say no kindly helps you find the words, with something to offer instead.

    Tool: Say no kindly: make your scripts spreadloveandacceptance.com/refusals

  6. Notice when you’re running on empty.

    People who help a lot can burn out: caregivers, parents, nurses, teachers, the friend everyone calls. The signs include feeling exhausted most of the time, or numb and cynical about the people you help, or dreading the next call, and any of them means you need a hand too.

    Gwen has looked after her husband since his stroke two years ago. Last month she snapped at him over the remote control, really snapped, and felt terrible for the rest of the day. That night she told her sister, on the phone, “I think I’m running on empty.” Her sister took Tuesday mornings from then on, and Gwen walked to the end of the road and back, alone, on purpose. She has, she says, about a third of herself back.

    Rate your energy from 1 to 10 each evening for a week. If it’s often 3 or lower, ask someone for one specific kind of help. See Caring for someone you love (spreadloveandacceptance.com/caregivers).

    Dig deeper: burnout and refilling

  7. Don’t wait for someone else to step in.

    When lots of people see something going wrong, each one can assume someone else will deal with it. Psychologists call this the bystander effect, and knowing about it helps you break it. Small, safe actions count. “Are you okay?” Getting a staff member.

    On a train out of Philadelphia, a man was making a young woman uncomfortable, leaning in and asking where she was getting off. Yvonne didn’t confront him. She sat down in the seat next to the woman and said brightly, “Hi! Is this the train to Chicago?” The woman grabbed the conversation with both hands. They talked about Chicago, which neither of them knew much about, until the next stop, when the man got up and moved down the car.

    It helps to decide in advance what your safe move would be, distracting or getting help or checking in afterward. People with a plan act. People without one tend to freeze.

    Sometimes the person in trouble is someone you know well. If someone tells you they’re thinking of ending their life, or you’re worried they might be, it’s okay to ask them plainly. A review led by Dazzi and colleagues (2014) found that asking doesn’t put the idea in someone’s head, and it can bring relief. You don’t need perfect words, and you don’t have to fix anything. Listen, stay with them, and help them tell someone else they trust.

    Dig deeper: helping strangers and community

  8. Let other people help you too.

    Helping goes both ways, and people who are good at giving help are often hopeless at receiving it. Letting someone help is a gift to them as well, because most people like being useful to someone they care about. And relationships where only one person ever helps start to feel lopsided.

    People say yes more than we think In a set of experiments and field studies, people asking for help underestimated, by as much as half, how many others would agree, mainly because they forgot how awkward it is to say no. It has been repeated many times since.

    Flynn and Lake (2008) · Strong: several experiments and field studies, widely replicated

    After the baby came, Nkechi said “We’re fine, thanks” to every single offer, including several when she very much wasn’t. When she finally said yes to the woman next door, who had offered a lasagna four times, the neighbor was so pleased she nearly dropped it. They walk their strollers around the park together on Thursday mornings now. Say yes to the next small offer of help you get, even if you could manage.

    Words you could use “Yes, thank you. That would really help.” “Could you do one thing for me this week?”

    Dig deeper: receiving help

Your part, and only your part. You can offer help and listen well, and be honest about your limits. You can’t make someone accept help or get better on your schedule. Their life and their choices are theirs.

The next Wednesday, 7:15pm

She rings again. This time, before she gets going, you ask. “Ideas, or do you just need to vent?”

She laughs. “Vent.”

So you listen, through her manager, and her landlord, and the cat’s vet bill ($260, for a sock). At the end she says she thinks she knows what she’s going to do. You realize you haven’t offered a single idea, and you had at least four.

Two ways to read this

Help, two ways

Some people want ideas the moment they share a problem. Others want to be heard and nothing more, and an idea offered too soon feels like being corrected. If you fix, the listener isn’t ungrateful. They wanted company first. If you need to be heard, the fixer isn’t dismissing you. Ideas are how they show they care. Asking “Ideas, or just listening?” saves both of you an evening.

Where the fields meet. Business explains the bystander moment exactly: work that belongs to everyone belongs to no one, so one person has to own it. Holistic therapies add the other half, which is to start with the body, because a helper who never rests stops being able to help. Some of these practices are well studied and some are debated.

In everyday life

Helping yourself counts too, and you can ask yourself the same question, ideas or rest. Caring for a parent, or a child with extra needs, is long-haul help, so share the load early (see Caring for someone you love). The friend everyone calls needs someone to call too. Covering for a struggling coworker is kind for a week, and after that it needs a real conversation with the team. In an emergency, point to one person (“You in the blue coat, please get help”), because a crowd tends to wait. If you have ADHD, helping can feel interesting and urgent, so a fast yes comes easily, and “I’d like to help. Let me check my week and come back to you tonight” buys you time. More in the expanded version (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-12-helping-in-depth).

Caring a lot, or losing yourself?

People sometimes call a devoted helper “codependent.” Codependency is not a diagnosis, and researchers debate how to define it, so it’s worth being careful with it.

For something to be caring that has tipped into losing yourself, these are usually all present:

  • your mood rises and falls with the other person’s, most days,
  • you can’t say no to them, even when you want to,
  • you keep covering for choices that hurt them or you,
  • your own needs, friends and rest have quietly disappeared for months.

Not enough on its own:

  • caring a lot about someone,
  • helping a partner or parent through a hard year,
  • being the person who organizes the family,
  • a culture or family where people come first and look after each other.

If you recognize yourself in the first list, the aim is to take some of yourself back, not to care less. One protected evening a week is a start.

Common mix-ups

People think helping means solving the problem. Often it means listening, or being there, or helping someone find their own answer. People think good helpers never say no, when it’s knowing their limits that lets good helpers last. And “I’ll make it worse if I step in” stops a lot of people. There are small, safe ways to help, and doing nothing often feels worse to the person in trouble.

If you want to help someone else with this

The helpers around you need looking after too. Notice them, the caregiver, the friend everyone calls, the coworker who always covers, and ask how they are as if you mean it. Offer something specific, because “Can I take the kids on Saturday morning?” is far easier to accept than “Let me know if you need anything.” Give them permission to rest (“You’re allowed a night off. I’ve got this”). And if a helper seems burned out, share Caring for someone you love. Sometimes it’s as simple as asking them, “You look after everyone. Who looks after you?”

Part Three · Chapter 13

Anger: what it’s for and what to do with it

What anger is for, what to do in the hot minutes, how to repair afterward, and how to tell when anger has turned into harm. For anyone, in any kind of relationship, or on your own.

In this chapter

  1. Anger is a signal about something that matters
  2. Anger often guards a softer feeling
  3. Anger rises in the body fast
  4. In the hot minutes: slow the body first
  5. Letting rip doesn’t empty it
  6. Step back and look from the outside
  7. Say it, don’t throw it
  8. After anger, repair
  9. When anger becomes harm
  10. If you’re a teenager
  11. In everyday life
  12. Common mix-ups
  13. If you want to help someone else with this
  14. Workpapers, tools and reading on this site
  15. More for your situation

At a glance

  • Anger is a signal that something seems unfair, blocked or threatening. The feeling is allowed, and what you do with it is the part you choose.
  • The first minutes are about the body. Slow down, breathe out long, and step away with a time to come back.
  • Letting rip doesn’t empty anger. Shouting tends to feed it, while calming the body, putting it into words and repairing any sharp moments help more.
  • Anger that hurts someone has become harm. The feeling is yours to own, and so is what you do with it.

Tuesday, 6:10pm

Your brother. Cant do thurs after all sorry!! work thing

Thursday is Mom’s hospital appointment. The one with the specialist, the one you’ve been going on about for three weeks, and it’s the third time this month he’s done this. Your jaw goes and your face goes hot. Your thumbs are already moving, TYPICAL. You never, and the message is one tap from sent.

Plenty of us were taught that anger was rude, or dangerous, or grew up around anger that was frightening. Anger itself is an ordinary human feeling, though, and it very often points at something real. It also sits under two tools elsewhere. The Calm-Down Kit (Part One, Now, page 33) works because anger rises in the body first and slowing the body is what makes words possible. And letting a comment land before you react (Part Two, Chapter IV, page 126) is the stepping back described further on.

The canceled appointment, seen quickly. The surface is a sibling who let you down again. Underneath, anger, fast and hot. Underneath that, fear about Mom and tiredness. The roots are signal and noise, and state and setting. The chapter goes back through those layers slowly.

  1. Anger is a signal about something that matters.

    Anger usually says something is unfair, or something’s in your way, or a line has been crossed. It pushes you toward a problem so you’ll change it. It can also land on the wrong person, or come out far bigger than the thing in front of it.

    Anger moves you toward things Most unpleasant feelings make us back away. A review by Carver and Harmon-Jones argued that anger usually does the opposite: like eagerness, it pushes you toward the goal or the obstacle. That’s what makes it good at showing what matters, and risky to act on at full heat.

    Carver and Harmon-Jones (2009) · Moderate: an influential review; the approach view is still debated

    Somebody keeps eating Shabnam’s lunch from the office fridge. Week one, she assumes a mistake. Week two, she writes her name on the box in marker. Week three, the box is empty again and has been put back in the fridge, neatly, with the lid on, which is the bit that does it. Her anger has now told her very clearly that a line has been crossed, and it’s the anger, frankly, that gets her to raise it at the Monday meeting. (It was the new hire. He thought the fridge was communal. He bought her a meal deal and looked like he wanted to die.)

    Next time you’re angry, finish this privately. “I’m angry because something I care about, which is ___, seems ___.”

    Dig deeper: what anger is for

  2. Anger often guards a softer feeling.

    Anger can arrive first because it feels stronger and safer than whatever is under it, which is often hurt, or fear, or shame, or plain exhaustion. Chapter 1 (page 160) calls this layers, and the layer underneath usually tells you what you actually need.

    Frankie was an hour late home. She is sixteen. Her dad was waiting in the hall when the key went in the door and what came out of him was mostly about curfews and rules and respect, at volume. She gave as good as she got. It was only later, sitting on the stairs, that he told her about the hour itself. Standing at the front window. Phone in his hand. Checking the bus app over and over. Working out which ER. She went quiet then. “Sorry,” she said, and this time she meant it.

    You could say “I’m angry, and I think underneath I was really scared.” “I came across as angry, but I think I’m actually hurt.”

    Dig deeper: what anger can cover

  3. Anger rises in the body fast.

    A hot face, a tight jaw, a pounding heart and a voice going up are the body getting ready for a fight, and it takes seconds. When anger is high, careful thinking gets a lot harder, and listening harder still. Chapter 2 (page 174) calls this being flooded.

    Halfway through an argument about the trash (whose turn, and also, it emerged, whose turn for the last four years) Meera noticed that her hands were shaking. She also realized she hadn’t heard a single thing her roommate had said for at least a minute. She’d been composing, and that was her sign. Learn your own early signs, if you can, whether it’s a tight jaw or talking faster or being very, very reasonable in a slightly high voice.

    Dig deeper: anger in the body

    Professor Puddles

    Anger moves faster than words. The Calm-Down Kit is a plan you make on a calm day, for the hot minutes.

    Workpaper WP-11: The Calm-Down Kit spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-11

  4. In the hot minutes: slow the body first.

    When anger is high, settle your body before you try to sort anything out. Stop talking. Stop typing. Breathe out slowly, so the out-breath is longer than the in-breath. Unclench your hands. If you can, get out of the room for a bit. A large review of 154 studies by Kjærvik and Bushman (2024) found that activities which calm the body, like slow breathing, relaxation and mindfulness, reduced anger, while ones that rev you up showed little or no benefit.

    Fractions, at the kitchen table, 7:30, question four. Ben could feel his voice getting tighter with every “But why is it a half?” “I’m getting frustrated,” he said in the end, “and that’s not your fault. I’m getting a glass of water. Five minutes.” He stood at the sink, looking out at the dark backyard, and drank the whole glass. When he came back they did the rest of the sheet together, and both of them got number six wrong, confidently.

    Make the plan on a calm day. Your early sign, the words you’ll say, where you’ll go for ten minutes. Upset right now? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/upset-right-now) has steps for the very worst moments.

    Dig deeper: what to do in the moment

  5. Letting rip doesn’t empty it.

    A lot of people believe anger works like steam. Shout, slam a door, hit a pillow, and it’s out, and you’re calmer. It’s a lovely tidy idea. The research doesn’t support it. In a well-known study by Bushman (2002), angry people who hit a punching bag while thinking about the person who annoyed them ended up angrier than before.

    Going over what happened again and again in your head has a similar effect. In studies by Bushman and colleagues (2005), people who dwelled on a provocation were later more aggressive, even toward someone who only mildly annoyed them. Anger fades faster when the body is calmed and the mind has something else to do for a while.

    After a fight with a colleague, Neville spent his lunch break telling three separate people how awful she was. Each telling got a bit better. By two o’clock he was angrier than he’d been at noon, and had a headache. The next time it happened he walked to the river and back instead and didn’t tell anyone anything, which nearly killed him. By two he could think about the actual problem. He still thinks she was out of order, and says so, but at a normal volume and to fewer people.

    Dig deeper: venting and going over it

  6. Step back and look from the outside.

    Once your body has come down a bit, try looking at the moment as if you were watching from the other side of the room. What actually happened? What might the other person have been dealing with? In experiments by Mischkowski, Kross and Bushman (2012), people who looked back on an annoying moment “like a fly on the wall,” instead of reliving it, felt less angry and acted less aggressively. Rethinking what happened, which psychologists call reappraisal (Gross, 1998), helps too.

    One way in is to write two lines about it in the third person, with your own name. “Wes got angry because…” It feels a bit mad. It works annoyingly well. Wes himself, canceled on by a friend for the third time, got as far as “Wes got angry because Matt canceled again, and Matt is…” and stopped, because Matt is looking after his dad, who has been in and out of the hospital since June. The anger didn’t go. It turned, slowly, into worry, which was at least pointing the right way.

    Dig deeper: stepping back

  7. Say it, don’t throw it.

    Anger is often a fair message sent in a hurtful way. Once you’re calmer you can still say you were angry, and why, without going for anyone, by keeping to what happened and how you felt and what you’re asking for.

    Two versions of the same fight When people wrote about a time they angered someone and a time someone angered them, the two kinds of story differed in how serious the harm seemed, how understandable it was and whether it was over. Same sort of event, told from two different places.

    Baumeister, Stillwell and Wotman (1990) · Moderate: a classic study of people’s own written memories

    “You always let me down” was what Carol wanted to say to her sister. What she actually sent, after two drafts and a cup of tea, was this. “When you canceled Mom’s appointment again I felt really angry, and on my own with it. Can we sort out who takes her for the next three months?” It’s longer, and it is also the only version that gets anyone to the hospital. Chapter 4 (page 203) has more on saying hard things.

    You could say “I was angry about what happened on Monday. Can I tell you why?” “When ___ happened, I felt ___, and what I’m asking for is ___.”

    Dig deeper: saying anger in words

    Sugarfoot

    Say it slowly, in one plain sentence. A soft start makes it far easier for the other person to hear you.

    Tool: Cool-down corner: soften a tense moment spreadloveandacceptance.com/tools/soften-a-tense-moment

  8. After anger, repair.

    Everyone gets angry, and most of us say something sharp now and then. What happens next matters a lot, because a short, real repair rebuilds trust. Name what you did, with no “but” on the end, and say what you’ll do differently.

    The blue vase from the hall table is on the floor in about nine pieces and Grandma Jean has just shouted, really shouted, and Jayden is crying. An hour later she finds him on the stairs. She sits down next to him, which takes her a while with her knees. “I shouted, and that was scary,” she says. “You matter to me far more than any vase. I’m sorry.” He leans on her shoulder for a bit, and then he asks if they can glue it, so they try. It now has a very visible crack and lives on the landing, where she says it reminds her of something. Chapter 11 (page 307) has more on apologies that land.

    You could say “I was sharp with you earlier. That wasn’t fair, and I’m sorry.” “I’m still upset about what happened, and I also shouldn’t have spoken to you that way.”

    Dig deeper: repair after anger

  9. When anger becomes harm.

    Feeling angry is human. But some things done in anger are harm, whatever the feeling behind them: hitting, pushing, throwing things at or near someone, breaking their things, threatening, or shouting so someone is scared. Anger is never a reason someone deserves to be hurt.

    Being angry, even loudly, is different from intimidation. Anger becomes intimidation when these are present together: it happens again and again, it arrives when the other person disagrees or says no, it decides what happens next, and people start changing what they say and do to avoid it. A raised voice in one hard conversation that gets repaired isn’t that. Neither is being loud by nature, saying a strong feeling plainly, or crying and shouting during a meltdown. Ask yourself whether your anger passes and gets repaired, and whether the other person can still say no to you.

    For example, a man realizes his partner and children go quiet when he comes home in a bad mood. He doesn’t hit anyone, but they have started keeping out of his way, and he decides to do something about it.

    You could say “I think my anger is scaring people I love. I want help with it.”

    Dig deeper: when anger becomes harm

Your part, and only your part. You can learn your early signs, settle your body, say what made you angry in words, and repair when you get it wrong. You can’t make someone else calm down.

Tuesday, 6:40pm

You put the phone face down on the arm of the sofa and walk around the block, breathing out long and feeling slightly silly about it, and somewhere near the mailbox on the corner you notice what’s underneath, which is that you’re tired and you’re frightened about Mom. Back home you delete the capitals and write, “I’m really frustrated. This is the third time and I feel on my own with Mom’s care. Can we talk tonight and make a plan?”

He reads it at 6:52. By ten there’s still no reply, and you go to bed not knowing who’s driving her on Thursday.

zqaxunderstandingx13xangerxxteensqzIf you’re a teenager

Ten o’clock, and Maisie’s dad has taken her phone. Right in the middle of a group chat about Saturday. She shouts and slams her bedroom door hard enough to rattle the picture on the landing, and then lies on her bed composing speeches. The next morning, calmer and also starving, she tells him it felt like he didn’t trust her, says sorry about the door, and asks for ten minutes’ warning next time. He says fine. He also says he’d much rather hear this over breakfast than through a door, which she thinks is a bit much, but lets go.

Being angry with a parent is normal, and the fights often feel most intense in the middle teens. A rule given out of care is not control, even when it feels unfair, and a calm request the next day works more often than a slammed door.

You could say “I’m too angry to talk properly. Can we talk tomorrow?” “I don’t mind the rule so much as how it happened.” “Could we try it for two weeks and then check?”

Dig deeper: more worked examples

Two ways to read this

Anger, sent and heard

Some people say anger fast and plainly and are over it within minutes. Others go very quiet and very polite, and it can last for days. If you’re quick, the quiet person may still be furious long after you’ve moved on, so check. If you’re slow and quiet, the quick one’s outburst may be bigger in sound than in meaning. Both versions carry the same message: something mattered.

Where the fields meet. The art of debating offers a useful rule for the hot minutes: separate the claim from the person, and say the strongest version of their point first. Music explains why it so often goes wrong anyway, because tone and tempo carry more than the words, and a rising voice is heard before any sentence is.

In everyday life

Anger at yourself counts. “I’m so stupid” is anger turned inward, and it helps to talk to yourself the way you would to a friend who’d done the same thing (Chapter 7, page 248, goes further). With a partner, agree a pause word on a calm day, and a time you’ll always come back. Children copy what we do with anger far more than anything we say about it. At work anger is common and rarely spoken, and “I’m frustrated about the deadline change, can we talk about what’s realistic?” keeps it useful.

If you have ADHD, anger can come fast and big and go just as fast, so plan for the speed. A three-word pause line (“Back in ten”) and a rule to wait before you send anything. If you’re managing a clash between two other people, hear each of them on their own first and then together, always about what happened and never about each other. Quite often the fight is about the setup, two people who both believe they own the same job. The expanded version has a worked example (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-13-anger-in-depth).

Common mix-ups

Anger itself isn’t a bad feeling. It’s normal and it carries information, and it’s some of the things done in anger that cause harm. Letting it out isn’t the healthy option it sounds like, because shouting and hitting things tend to keep anger going. “They made me angry, so it’s their fault I shouted” mixes up two separate things. Someone can do something unfair, and what you do next is still yours. And holding it in isn’t as safe as it looks. Anger swallowed for years comes out sideways, as coldness or sarcasm or a sudden explosion over a teaspoon, so saying it calmly and early is the safer road.

If you want to help someone else with this

You don’t have to stay and calm someone down. If you do stay, speak lower and slower and leave the argument until they’ve come down. Then listen for the message underneath. There’s often something fair in it, and you can take that part seriously while still saying the way it came out wasn’t okay. Something like “I want to hear this, and I can’t while we’re both shouting. Can we try again at seven?” keeps hold of both halves.

14

Part Three · Chapter 14

Personality, temperament and change across life

What personality is, where temperament comes in, how people change across their lives, and how to live and work with people who are made differently from you, without putting anyone in a box.

In this chapter

  1. Traits work like dials
  2. Temperament is the starting point
  3. Situations matter too
  4. Introvert and extravert is about energy, not liking people
  5. People change across life
  6. You can change on purpose, a little at a time
  7. Every trait has gifts and costs
  8. Differences are usually about fit
  9. In everyday life
  10. Narcissistic, toxic and other labels people reach for
  11. Common mix-ups
  12. If you want to help someone else with this
  13. Tools and reading on this site
  14. More for your situation

At a glance

  • Traits work like dials. Everyone sits somewhere along each one, and most people are near the middle.
  • Temperament is a starting point. Babies already differ in how active, cautious or easily upset they are, and what happens next matters too.
  • People keep changing. On average people grow steadier and more organized as they get older, and you can change on purpose, slowly.
  • Most clashes between personalities are about fit, and nobody has to be at fault.

Saturday, 3:00pm

Your aunt’s seventieth, in the function room above the golf club. You’re standing by the cake, minding your own business, when she tells the whole room, “Oh, she was always the shy one!”

Everybody laughs, and you laugh along with them, and something stings.

You’re forty-two. Every weekday at 8:40 you stand in front of thirty eight-year-olds and get them to sit down, which takes some doing. So are you still the shy one? Were you ever?

We describe each other by personality all the time, as laid-back, or a worrier, or the organized one, and descriptions like those have a way of setting hard. This chapter is about how personality actually works, what stays put and what moves. Two tools elsewhere build on it. The “How to talk to me” card and the style quiz (Part One, Now, page 33) describe how you lean on a few dials, which is more use than knowing which box somebody once put you in. And One owner per job (Part Two, Chapter II, page 90) arranges the jobs around people’s differences, so nobody has to turn into someone else to share a house.

Quickly, one “difficult” colleague has three layers. On the surface, behavior you don’t like. Underneath, a trait, a dial set differently from yours. Underneath that, a situation that suits one setting and not the other. The roots are limited capacity and ownership and structure. Slowly now, dial by dial.

  1. Traits work like dials.

    Personality is the usual pattern in how you think and feel and act. Many psychologists describe it with five broad traits, often called the “Big Five”: openness (curious about new ideas and experiences), conscientiousness (organized and careful), extraversion (drawn to people and busy places), agreeableness (warm and cooperative) and emotional stability (how steady your moods are).

    The same five turned up in work such as McCrae and Costa (1987), whether people rated themselves or were rated by people who knew them well. Each runs from low to high, and most people sit near the middle of most of them. That’s the bit online quizzes leave out. Two friends did one on the train to Santa Cruz and were told, very confidently, that one was an introvert and the other an extravert. Then they looked at the actual numbers. Four points apart, both bang in the middle. They spent the rest of the journey arguing about which of them was more middle.

    If you’re curious, mark where you think you sit on each dial from one to ten, and ask a close friend where they’d put you. The gap is often the interesting bit.

    Dig deeper: the five dials

  2. Temperament is the starting point.

    Temperament is the part of personality you can see very early on. Some babies are on the go from the moment they wake. Some are calm. Some take to a new routine right away and some need a week. Some flinch at every loud noise. In their long-running study, Thomas and Chess (1977) described these early differences and the idea of “goodness of fit,” meaning how well a child’s temperament suits what the people and places around them expect.

    Sensitive isn’t the same as shy Elaine and Arthur Aron described a trait they called sensory-processing sensitivity, taking things in deeply, and found it was partly separate from introversion. Researchers still argue about its exact shape. Still, the child hanging back may be taking everything in rather than shrinking from it.

    Aron and Aron (1997) · Moderate: a widely used measure; the trait’s structure is still debated

    Isla is two and cried at every new playgroup. Her mom tried coaxing her into the circle, then bribing her, then (once, quietly) begging. In the end she just sat at the edge of the church hall with Isla on her lap, feeling a bit silly, while everyone else did “The Wheels on the Bus.” It smelled of orange drink and floor polish. Week three, Isla climbed down on her own, walked to the sand table, and didn’t look back. Her mom, slightly put out, had a cookie.

    You could say “You like to watch first. That’s fine. Join in when you’re ready.” (to yourself) “I need time to warm up. That’s how I’m made.”

    Dig deeper: temperament and fit

  3. Situations matter too.

    Personality describes a pattern, and patterns have exceptions. The same person can be loud with family and quiet at work, endlessly patient with toddlers and very short with call centers. A trait tells you what someone tends to do across lots of situations and a good deal less about the one in front of you.

    Anita had decided her new colleague was cold. Polite, competent, cold. Then came the fundraiser soccer game, and there he was in a borrowed bib two sizes too small, shouting encouragement at a goalkeeper who was letting in everything. On Monday Anita sat looking around the open-plan office with its gray partitions and humming lights and wondered how much of what she’d seen was the room.

    Dig deeper: person and situation

  4. Introvert and extravert is about energy, not liking people.

    People who are more introverted often like people a lot. What they find is that busy, noisy company uses energy up, and they need quiet afterward to get it back. People who are more extraverted tend to be topped up by company. Most of us are a mix (sometimes called an ambivert), and every point on the dial just needs different things to be at its best.

    Happy now, tired later Forty-eight people tracked for twelve days felt better while acting outgoing and more tired about three hours later, introverts and extraverts alike. It’s a small study, and the authors say so.

    Leikas and Ilmarinen (2017) · Early: a small study (48 people); the authors asked for it to be repeated

    Eleven o’clock at a wedding in a barn outside Asheville. Fraser wants the after-party in the local bar. Luke wants bed and silence and possibly never to hear “Mr. Brightside” again. They’ve had this exact standoff at four previous weddings. This time Fraser goes for an hour and Luke walks back to the hotel along the lane with his shoes in his hand, and they meet at breakfast, one of them hoarse and the other one smug, both of them happy. What Luke said, for once, was “I loved tonight, and I’m out of social energy,” which he’d practiced on the walk from the car.

    Dig deeper: introversion and extraversion

    Tidbit

    Some people recharge in a busy park and some under a quiet blanket. Both are fine. A short quiz can show you your own style.

    Tool: How you connect: the 2-minute style quiz spreadloveandacceptance.com/wavelength

  5. People change across life.

    Personality is fairly stable. It also moves. A large review by Roberts, Walton and Viechtbauer (2006) found that, on average, people become more organized, more emotionally steady and more confident with others as they move through adult life, with much of the change between 20 and 40. A later review by Bleidorn and colleagues (2022) found that emotional steadiness went on growing right across the lifespan. Big life events play a part, and so do the roles people take on and who they love.

    At school Tunde lost his keys about once every two weeks and once turned up to a math exam on the wrong day. He’s a charge nurse now, forty-six, the calm one people look for when it goes wrong at three in the morning. At the reunion his old friends kept staring at him across the room in the banquet room, and eventually one of them came over with two beers and said, “What happened to you?” He thought about it. “Life kept asking me to cope,” he said, “and eventually I learned how.”

    Dig deeper: how personality changes with age

  6. You can change on purpose, a little at a time.

    If you want to change a trait you can, slowly, mostly by acting differently in small ways over and over. In a study by Hudson and Fraley (2015), people who set goals to change one of their traits tended to move in the direction they wanted over sixteen weeks. A review by Roberts and colleagues (2017) found that therapy was often linked to lasting change too, especially toward more emotional steadiness.

    Noor wanted to be less quiet at work. She made a rule. One thing in every team meeting, even if it was only “I agree with Neil.” The first two weeks her heart thudded so hard she was sure people could see it through her sweater. By the end of the second month it had become ordinary, and somewhere in the third month she forgot it had ever been a rule. Pick one small thing that fits who you’d like to be more of, and do it three times this week. Chapter 6 (page 234) has more on habits.

    Dig deeper: changing on purpose

  7. Every trait has gifts and costs.

    There’s no good personality. Every trait helps in some places and gets in the way in others. Very agreeable people are lovely to be around and may find “no” almost impossible to say. Very conscientious people are the ones you’d leave your keys with, and they can’t always stop. People high in openness love anything new and can be bored to tears by routine.

    For most of a year Alys was irritated by her roommate. His sneakers in the hall. His “it’ll be fine.” Then the water heater died on the coldest night in January, and while Alys stood in the kitchen in her coat reading the manual, he called around until he found a plumber who’d come out at ten o’clock, and then he filled everybody’s hot water bottles from the kettle. “It’ll be fine,” he said, and it was, apart from the hot water bottle that leaked.

    A one-page card, “How to talk to me,” (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wiring-card) turns a trait people complain about into plain information about what helps.

    Dig deeper: gifts and costs

    Professor Puddles

    Every trait has gifts and costs. Writing down what helps you on a one-page card turns a “flaw” into useful information.

    Tool: How you connect: how I like to be spoken to spreadloveandacceptance.com/wiring-card

  8. Differences are usually about fit.

    When two people with different personalities share a home or a family or a job, friction is normal. A tidy person and a relaxed one can both be right in their own way, and so can a planner and someone spontaneous, or a talker and someone who needs quiet. What helps is naming the difference and agreeing how to live with it, without either of you being the problem. Personality is also different from neurodivergence and from mental health conditions. If something feels bigger than personality, Chapter 9 (page 275) may help.

    A couple argue about every single vacation, because one wants every hour planned and the other wants to wander about and see what happens. This year they plan the mornings and leave the afternoons free, and they still argue about the mornings. I’d count that as progress.

    Dig deeper: fit, not fault

Your part, and only your part. You can get to know your own mix, look after what you need, and practice one small change if you want to. You can’t change someone else’s personality, and you don’t have to change yours to be loved. If you’re always the one bending to fit, it’s fair to say so. More in Know your own wiring (spreadloveandacceptance.com/know-yourself), free online.

Saturday, 5:30pm

People are drifting off with slices of cake in paper towels. You think about sitting down next to your aunt and telling her about the thirty eight-year-olds. You don’t. You help stack the plates. On the drive home you’re still turning it over, half annoyed with her and half with yourself, and somewhere around the beltway you start drafting what you’ll say at Christmas if she does it again. It’s quite a good line.

Two ways to read this

The same lunch, two ways

For some people a new lunch is a small pleasure, and the same sandwich every day sounds dull. For others every new food is a small gamble on taste, texture and how it sits, and a known lunch is one decision they never have to make. If you like variety, the same-lunch person isn’t stuck. They’re saving their energy for the rest of the day. If you like sameness, the variety person isn’t restless. Trying something new is part of what makes lunch a break for them.

Where the fields meet. Economics treats attention as a budget, and personality is partly about where the budget goes and how fast it runs out. Business has a related habit: match each job to the person whose strengths suit it, and give it one owner, so nobody has to pretend to be someone else to get it done.

In everyday life

On your own

Knowing your own mix helps you build a life that suits you, with about the right amount of company and quiet. “I’m just not a people person” might be true. It might also be an old label that deserves testing at least once. With a partner, a shared plan (one does the bills, the other does vacations) usually goes better than trying to change each other. A quiet friend who hardly texts may still care a great deal, so ask what kind of contact suits them. A child’s temperament says nothing about good or bad parenting, and adjusting to fit them is a skill you pick up. And family roles like “the clever one” or “the difficult one” can hang on long after they stop fitting. You’re allowed to grow out of them, whether or not your aunt has noticed.

Narcissistic, toxic and other labels people reach for.

Words from clinics have drifted into everyday arguments. Narcissistic personality disorder is a clinical diagnosis, and a diagnosis is a complicated judgment that a short chapter, a test or a stranger on the internet can’t make. It describes a long-lasting pattern across most of a person’s life, not a bad week or a bad breakup. “Toxic” isn’t a clinical word at all.

For something to be a personality pattern of this kind, these are usually all present:

  • it shows up across many years and most settings, at home, at work and with friends,
  • it includes a constant need for admiration and very little room for other people’s feelings,
  • it doesn’t change when the person is calm, rested and happy,
  • it causes real, lasting harm to the person or to the people around them.

Not enough on its own:

  • confidence, ambition or self-promotion at work,
  • one selfish choice, or a defensive reaction to criticism,
  • talking about yourself a lot when you’re nervous,
  • someone you’ve fallen out with.

Describing what happened helps more than a label. “You talked over me three times tonight” can be answered. A diagnosis thrown at someone in an argument usually ends the conversation, and it’s often wrong. “Toxic” works the same way. It names no specific behavior and no effect over time, and a hard week, a single conflict or a bad day isn’t enough to earn it.

Common mix-ups

You aren’t simply an introvert or an extravert. Most people are somewhere in the middle, and where you sit shifts with the setting and your mood. Personality isn’t set in stone by thirty, either. It keeps moving slowly all through life. Online type quizzes are good for fun and for starting a conversation, and that includes the website’s own Wave Code, which shows four leanings on four dials, but they sort people into a handful of types when real people are spread along each dial. “They’re just difficult” often means “they’re different from me,” and it can hide stress or illness or a need nobody has asked about. And practicing something new isn’t being fake. It feels odd at first, like new shoes, and then it’s yours.

If you want to help someone else with this

Drop the old labels, and notice if you still describe someone the way they were twenty years ago. Ask instead of guessing. “What helps you recharge?” or “How do you like to plan things?” will tell you more than any theory. Say it when you see someone grow, because “You handled that so calmly” can show a person a change they hadn’t spotted. And describe what happened, not who someone is. “You’re so uptight” shuts doors that a plain description would leave open.

Words to try “I used to think of you as the shy one. I don’t think that fits anymore.” “What do you need to be at your best this week?”

Part Three · Chapter 15

Closeness and love: being known, at every age

How closeness grows, what it means to feel truly known, how love changes over the years, and how it looks in every kind of relationship, at every age, including for people on their own.

In this chapter

  1. Love comes in many forms
  2. Closeness grows from being known
  3. Closeness is built a step at a time
  4. Feeling understood matters most
  5. Old maps show up in love
  6. Love changes over time
  7. Love at every age
  8. Love is something you do
  9. If you’re a teenager
  10. In everyday life
  11. Common mix-ups
  12. If you want to help someone else with this
  13. Reading on this site
  14. More for your situation

Friday, 10:30pm

Eleven years in this house with Charlie. Tonight you’re both on the couch, both on your phones, with a cooking show on in the background that neither of you is watching. Someone on it is crying about a soufflé.

You try to remember the last time the two of you talked about something that wasn’t bills, or the water heater, or whose turn it is to cook. You can’t. You love Charlie, which isn’t in question. You feel oddly on your own, a foot away from them.

This chapter is about closeness in all its forms, far beyond romance. It looks at what helps people feel near to each other, and why closeness fades and how it grows back, and it builds on Chapter 5 (page 220), on attachment and trust.

Two people on a sofa, scrolling, in quick strokes. The surface is a quiet evening. Underneath, a closeness that has thinned without anyone deciding it should. Underneath that, months of small bids missed on both sides. The roots are balance and feedback loops. The chapter goes back over them slowly.

  1. Love comes in many forms.

    The ancient Greeks had several words for love, for friends, family, romantic partners and strangers. People love in many ways now too, through lifelong friendships, partners of any gender, more than one partner, chosen family, and among people who are asexual or aromantic and build deep closeness without romance or sex. Some people on their own pour love into friends, family, pets, work and community. A life can be full of love without a partner in it.

    Frances is fifty-six and has never wanted a partner. Ask her about her great love story and she’ll tell you about Denise, her best friend of thirty years. Between them there have been two house moves, one cancer scare, a camping trip in Cape Cod that they still can’t discuss without one of them leaving the room, and more Sunday phone calls than either of them could count. “People feel sorry for me,” she says. “I feel quite sorry for them.”

    Dig deeper: the many forms of love

  2. Closeness grows from being known.

    Intimacy is about much more than touch or romance. At its heart is being known. The psychologists Reis and Shaver described it as a back-and-forth, in which one person shares something real about themselves and the other responds in a way that leaves them feeling understood and cared for. In a diary study by Laurenceau, Barrett and Pietromonaco (1998), feeling that the other person really responded was a big part of what made everyday conversations feel intimate.

    Two brothers who mostly talk about football were driving to their dad’s nursing home. Somewhere on the highway, staring straight ahead, one of them said, “I find these visits really hard.” There was a long pause before the other said, “Yeah. Me too. I always feel guilty on the way home.” It was the longest conversation they’d had in years. It lasted all the way to the parking lot, where they sat with the engine off for another ten minutes. Then they went in and talked about football.

    Dig deeper: intimacy as being known

  3. Closeness is built a step at a time.

    People usually get close by sharing a little more, then a little more, when it feels safe. In a well-known study by Aron and colleagues (1997), pairs of strangers who took turns asking gradually more personal questions, now known as the “36 questions,” felt closer after forty-five minutes than pairs who made small talk. The same idea works in friendships and long relationships, where closeness grows when both people take small, matched steps.

    Two new neighbors start with the weather, and the parking, which on their street is a serious subject. A few months later one asks how the other’s mom is getting on. Some time after that, over the fence, with a hosepipe running, one of them says, “Can I tell you what’s actually been going on?”

    Dig deeper: building closeness step by step

    Professor Puddles

    Closeness grows when you know what feels like care to the other person, not just to you. A “What feels like care” card is a gentle way to find out.

    Tool: How you connect: what feels like care spreadloveandacceptance.com/love-languages

  4. Feeling understood matters most.

    What makes someone feel loved is often less about grand gestures and more about feeling understood. Researchers call this responsiveness, meaning noticing, understanding and caring about what matters to the other person, and it shows in small moments such as how you react to good news. Gable and colleagues (2004) found that people whose partners usually met their good news with real interest and warmth felt closer and more satisfied together.

    “I got into the band.” She’s fourteen, coat still on, trying to sound casual about it. Her grandpa put the paper down, properly down, folded, and said, “Which instrument? When’s the first concert?” She talked for twenty minutes, mostly about the trombone section and a boy called Luca who can’t count. Next time someone shares good news with you, put your phone face down and ask two follow-up questions.

    Dig deeper: responsiveness

  5. Old maps show up in love.

    The patterns from Chapter 5 (page 220) often come out strongest with the people we love most. Hazan and Shaver (1987) suggested that adult love uses the same attachment system as childhood bonds. When closeness feels shaky, some people reach harder for reassurance and others pull back to feel safe. Both are ways of protecting something precious.

    When his partner goes quiet, Leo texts, and once it was five times in an hour. His partner goes quiet to calm down, and five texts feels like being chased around the house. What they agreed, eventually, was that his partner would say, “I need an hour, and I’ll message you at eight.” Leo found, somewhat to his surprise, that he could wait quite happily for a known time, and that the waiting had never really been the problem.

    Dig deeper: attachment in adult love

  6. Love changes over time.

    Early love is often intense, with racing thoughts and a lot of longing, and over the years it usually settles into something calmer and deeper. A review by Acevedo and Aron (2009) found that some people in long relationships still report strong romantic love, without the anxious, all-consuming edge of early love, and that this was linked to being happier together.

    Thank-yous as a booster In a daily diary study of couples living together, feeling grateful for a partner’s thoughtful act predicted feeling more connected and more satisfied the next day, for both of them. Correlational, but cheap to test at home.

    Algoe, Gable and Maisel (2010) · Moderate: a daily diary study; correlational

    In experiments by Aron and colleagues (2000), couples who tried a new, mildly challenging activity together felt better about their relationship afterward than couples given a dull task. After twenty-five years together, Howard and Lynne signed up for a pottery class at the community center. They were both dreadful. Lynne’s bowl collapsed twice and Howard got clay in his ear. They laughed most of the evening and brought home a bowl that won’t stand up, and on the walk back Howard said, “That felt like a date.” Something new matters more than something big. A new walk. A new recipe. A café in the next town.

    Dig deeper: how love changes

    Sugarfoot

    Little rituals, a Sunday walk, a goodnight text, keep love warm through the years. Most couples have more of them than they think.

    Workpaper WP-15: Keep your little rituals alive spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-15

  7. Love at every age.

    Love looks different across a life. Teenagers’ first loves can be huge and real. Adults juggle love with work and children and, often, aging parents. Many older people choose to spend their time with fewer, closer people, which Carstensen and colleagues (1999) linked to feeling that time is more limited, so that the most meaningful relationships matter more. People find new love at seventy and eighty, and people lose great loves and carry them always.

    Arthur is seventy-eight, and he met Irene at his walking group, in the drizzle, arguing about a stile. When his children looked surprised, and then worried, and then started asking careful questions about wills, he said, “I loved your mother for fifty years. I still do. And I’m allowed to be happy now.” His daughter cried. His son changed the subject to the car. Irene is coming for Christmas, with a trifle.

    Dig deeper: love across the lifespan

  8. Love is something you do.

    Feelings of love come and go. The actions of love can be steady. Turning toward someone when they speak. Keeping small promises. Saying thank you, and sorry. Making room for who they are. Physical closeness, like a hug or holding hands, matters a lot to some people and less to others, and sex is part of closeness in some relationships and not in others. What matters is that both people feel comfortable and free to say yes or no.

    Bids, and turning toward them Watching 49 newlywed couples over dinner, Driver and Gottman found that partners who turned toward each other’s small bids, a comment or a question or a look, showed more humor and affection later, even in a disagreement. It’s a small, correlational study, so it can’t say which causes which.

    Driver and Gottman (2004) · Moderate: observational, small sample; direction of cause not established

    Her friend had gone quiet after his divorce. Paula has never once told him she loves him and would be mortified to. Every Thursday she texts one word, Walk?, and turns up at his door at six in her old wax jacket, whatever the weather. Some weeks they talk and some weeks they just walk. A “What feels like care” card (spreadloveandacceptance.com/love-languages) is a gentle way to find out what the small thing is for someone you love.

    Dig deeper: love as action

Your part, and only your part. You can share a little of yourself, listen well, turn toward the people you love and keep small promises. You can’t make someone love you, or love you in the way you want.

The next Friday, 10:30pm

The phones go on the kitchen counter and you make two cups of tea. You ask Charlie, feeling a bit silly, what they’ve been thinking about lately that they haven’t told you. Charlie looks at you for a moment as if you might be ill. Then they talk about their dad getting older, and how they dread the phone ringing late at night. You didn’t know that, and you listen. Then you tell them about the restructure at work, which you hadn’t mentioned either. The tea goes cold, and it’s midnight before either of you looks at the clock.

If you’re a teenager

First love can be huge and real, and so can a first breakup. Ines is sixteen when she’s dumped by message on a Tuesday night, and she cries until two in the morning. Being told by adults that she’ll get over it does not help, at all. Telling her cousin, who just listens, does. So does muting the chat instead of rereading it, and a rule of no checking his profile after ten, which she breaks twice. A few weeks later she notices a whole day has gone by without her thinking about him, and is slightly offended.

You could say “I don’t need advice, I just need to tell someone.” “Can we reply when we can, rather than all day?” And if you are the one ending it, “I don’t want to go out anymore. I’m sorry. It isn’t about something you did wrong.”

Dig deeper: more worked examples

Two ways to read this

Love, two ways

Some people show love by saying it. Others show it by doing: the lunch from home, the bike fixed, the car filled up. If love reaches you through words, the doer may be saying it all day in a language you don’t hear yet. If it reaches you through deeds, the talker isn’t being cheap with words. For them, the words are the deed.

Where the fields meet. Finance has a neat picture for the small moments: turning toward someone’s little bid is a deposit, turning away is a small withdrawal. Aromatherapy, read modestly, adds touchstones, a familiar place or scent that brings a shared memory back. The claims for particular oils are debated, so it’s the familiarity that counts.

In everyday life

On your own

Being single, widowed, divorced or happily alone doesn’t mean a life without love. Friendships, family, community and the way you treat yourself are all places where love lives. If you want a partner and don’t have one, that longing is real and worth being gentle with (see On my own, spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own). Most partners drift into talking only about jobs and bills, and one real question a week can bring them back. Friendship needs tending like any other love. And families often love each other enormously and say so about once a decade, so a short “I’m glad you’re my sister” can land like a brick, in a good way.

  • Different levels of desire. This is very common in long relationships and is nobody’s fault. Talk at a calm time, keep some affection that doesn’t have to lead anywhere, and remember that a kind “no” is a no to the moment and never a rejection of the person. More in the expanded version (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-15-love-in-depth).

Common mix-ups

The spark fading doesn’t mean love is over. Early intensity usually settles, and many long relationships stay warm and close and lively for decades. Nobody reads minds, either, however much they love you, so saying what helps is a gift rather than a failure of romance.

  • “A boundary is just an ultimatum with a nicer name.” A boundary says what you will do. “If the shouting starts, I’ll leave the room and we can try again later.” An ultimatum tries to decide what the other person does, with a threat attached. “Stop seeing your friends or I’m leaving.” Both can be said calmly and both can be said in anger. Ask whether it’s about your own actions or theirs, and whether you’d accept the same rule turned around.
  • “Jealousy proves love.” Feeling jealous is human, and saying so (“I felt left out when you went without me”) is honest. Jealousy turns into something else when it becomes checking up, rules about who someone can see, or coldness as a penalty for time spent apart.

If you want to help someone else with this

Respect their kind of love, without assuming that everyone wants a partner or children. Be a safe person to tell things to, which means listening without judging and keeping what they share to yourself. After a loss or a breakup, keep showing up, because most people get plenty of support for two weeks and very little after that.

  • If you’re worried about someone’s relationship, stay close and kind rather than criticizing their partner.

Words you could use “I’m always glad to hear from you.” “You don’t have to explain your relationship to me. I just want you to be happy and safe.”
