Part Three · Chapter 16

Worry, low mood and trauma

How worry and anxiety work, the difference between a low patch and depression, what trauma is and isn’t, what helps day to day, and how to support someone. For anyone, in any kind of relationship, or on your own.

In this chapter

  1. Worry and anxiety are the body’s alarm
  2. Avoiding keeps fear going
  3. Give worry a time and a place
  4. Low mood is common. Depression is more than a bad week
  5. Doing often comes before feeling better
  6. Sleep, moving and people do a lot of the work
  7. Trauma is about what happened, and what it left behind
  8. After something frightening: safety, choice and no pressure
  9. Telling one person helps
  10. If you’re a teenager
  11. In everyday life
  12. Common mix-ups
  13. If you want to help someone else with this
  14. Workpapers, tools and reading on this site
  15. More for your situation

At a glance

  • Worry, low mood and the after-effects of trauma are common, human and treatable. They are not weakness, and they are not your fault.
  • They all run through the stress system from Chapter 2 (page 174). Small, steady things that settle the body and reconnect you with life help more than big pushes.
  • Avoiding and withdrawing feel safer but keep things going. Small steps back in, a little at a time, help most.
  • Telling one person helps, and you don’t need the right words.

Sunday, 10:50pm

The house is quiet. You’ve checked the front door twice and the back door once, and you’re thinking about the front door again. Tomorrow is the hospital, ten o’clock, and it goes around and around. What if it’s bad. What if I can’t cope. Who would I even tell.

And if you’re honest, it isn’t only tonight. You haven’t really wanted to see anyone for a few weeks. Even replying to a text has started to feel like lifting something.

Almost everyone worries, feels low or goes through something frightening at some point. For some people it settles by itself, and for others it sticks, and grows, until it shapes every day. This chapter is about how these things work, what tends to help, and when it’s time to ask for more. It can’t diagnose anyone. If any of this is about you right now, you aren’t alone in it, and it can get better.

Some tools elsewhere lean on this chapter. The daily check-in’s “low, medium or high” (Part Two, Chapter I, page 76) lets people adjust when worry or low mood has shrunk the room you have. “A full tank means later, not never” (Part Two, Chapter III, page 109) names a time to come back, because avoiding a thing keeps fear going. And picking one small goal (Part One, Next, page 48) suits low mood, since doing very often comes before feeling better.

Quickly, then slowly. On the surface, checking the door twice. Underneath, an alarm that keeps going off with nothing to point at. Underneath that, sleep, people and days that have narrowed. The roots are state and setting, and feedback loops, since avoiding keeps the alarm going. The rest of the chapter takes each part in turn.

  1. Worry and anxiety are the body’s alarm.

    Fear is the body’s alarm for danger that’s here now. Anxiety is the same alarm ringing about something that might happen. Worry is the thinking part, the “What if…?” going around. All three run through the stress system from Chapter 2 (page 174), which is why they come with a racing heart and a tight chest and a churning stomach and nights of bad sleep. The alarm is trying to protect you. The trouble is it can be set far too sensitive, and it can’t tell a tiger from an email.

    Fear of not knowing One review argues that fear of the unknown, the not-knowing itself, may sit underneath a lot of anxiety. It’s a proposal rather than a settled finding, but it fits the night before a hospital appointment better than most explanations do.

    Carleton (2016) · Theory: an influential review; the central claim is a proposal

    Before every presentation in class, Leah’s heart hammers so hard her hands shake her notes. She is fifteen, and nothing bad has ever happened to her in a presentation. Her alarm still treats a room full of people she’s known since first grade, one of whom once ate a worm for 50 cents, as somewhere dangerous.

    When it rises, try breathing out slowly five times, each breath out longer than the breath in. Then name three things you can see. It tells the body the danger isn’t here right now, and while it won’t switch the alarm off, it can usually turn it down a notch.

    Dig deeper: how anxiety works

  2. Avoiding keeps fear going.

    When something makes us anxious, stepping away brings quick relief, and the relief teaches the brain that escaping was clever. So next time the fear is a little bigger and the world a little smaller. What helps is going back toward the feared thing in small, chosen steps, and staying long enough to find out you can cope. Psychologists call this exposure. Craske and colleagues (2014) describe how it works best when each step tests what you expect to happen.

    After a panic attack on the 42, Graham started walking everywhere, in the rain, three miles to work and three miles back. His sister didn’t argue. One Saturday she just stood at the bus stop with him and they got on, and off again, after one stop. A week later, two stops. It took most of the spring before he did the whole run into town, sitting by the doors, feeling sick, reading the same ad for a lawyer over and over. But he did it, and his brain had slowly learned that buses are survivable.

    Dig deeper: avoidance and small steps
  3. zqaxunderstandingx16xworryxxworryxtimeqz

    Give worry a time and a place.

    Trying hard not to worry rarely works. What helps a lot of people is postponing it. You notice a worry, write it down, and save it for a set “worry time” later in the day. In an early study by Borkovec and colleagues (1983), people who practiced this for four weeks reported worrying less each day. In worry time, go through the list and ask of each one whether there’s anything you can do about it. If there is, plan one step. If there isn’t, practice letting it go, which is easier said than done, I know.

    Desmond looks after his dad and keeps a small red notebook by the kettle. Worries go in it all day. At six, with a cup of tea, he gives the notebook fifteen minutes. By then half the morning’s worries look smaller, and a couple have quietly worked themselves out. The one about the water heater has been in there since August, and he has decided to let it stay. When one turns up at the wrong time of day, the trick is to tell it, more or less, “Noted. I’ll think about that at six.”

    Dig deeper: worry time and problem-solving

  4. Low mood is common. Depression is more than a bad week.

    Everyone has low days, and sadness after a loss or a let-down is normal. Depression is different. It means low mood, or losing interest in things you used to enjoy, for most of the day, nearly every day, for two weeks or more, often with poor sleep, tiredness, appetite changes, feeling worthless or guilty, and finding it hard to think. It can look like sadness. It can also look like irritability, or just running on empty. It is a health problem, and nobody gets it by being weak.

    Lionel taught geography for thirty-one years. Lately he has stopped going to the Thursday walking group. He isn’t reading. He wakes at four every morning and lies there listening to the water heater come on. Getting old, he tells himself. It was his daughter, up for the weekend, who said it, carefully, while they were doing the dishes. “Dad, I think this might be depression. And that can be treated.” He was pretty annoyed with her for about a day.

    You could say “I’ve not been myself for a few weeks, and I don’t think it’s just tiredness.” “I don’t enjoy things I used to. Can I talk to you about it?”

    Dig deeper: low mood and depression

  5. Doing often comes before feeling better.

    Low mood tells you to wait until you feel like it. But withdrawing makes life emptier, and that deepens the low. A well-tested approach called behavioral activation turns this around. You plan small, doable things that bring a bit of pleasure or a sense of having done something, and you do them whether you feel like it or not. A review of 26 trials by Ekers and colleagues (2014) found it helped with depression, though many of the studies were small.

    After her divorce, living on her own, Lorraine planned three small things a day, a ten-minute walk to the mailbox and back, one call or message, and one job she could finish, like wiping the stove. Most days, honestly, they felt pointless. She did them anyway, and over a few weeks the days started to feel less dull, though she couldn’t tell you which day it changed.

    Dig deeper: behavioral activation

  6. Sleep, moving and people do a lot of the work.

    These sound too simple to matter. The evidence is solid all the same. Improving sleep can lift mood: in a large trial with university students, Freeman and colleagues (2017) found that an online sleep course reduced insomnia, and with it some other mental health difficulties.

    Exercise helps depression too. A review of 218 trials by Noetel and colleagues (2024) found walking or jogging, yoga and strength training all helped. Belonging to groups protects as well. Cruwys and colleagues (2013) found that people with depression who joined groups were less likely to relapse.

    People are not an optional extra A meta-analysis of 148 studies, with over 300,000 people, found that people with stronger social ties had about 50% better odds of survival over the years they were followed. The studies observe rather than prove cause, but it’s hard to read that and call time with friends a luxury.

    Holt-Lunstad, Smith and Layton (2010) · Strong: a large meta-analysis of observational studies; cause not established

    A new dad, exhausted and low, sat down with his partner and a calendar and between them they blocked out one protected long sleep each on the weekend, a stroller walk every morning around the park whatever the weather, and his old Wednesday five-a-side, which he’d dropped when the baby came and missed more than he’d admitted. He was terrible at five-a-side the first week, and went back anyway. Calm sounds help some people wind down at night, too, and Cool-down corner (spreadloveandacceptance.com/soundscapes) has some.

    Words you could use “I need help protecting my sleep for a while.” “Would you come for a short walk with me? I find it hard to go on my own.”

    Dig deeper: sleep, exercise and connection

    Professor Puddles

    Small, steady things help: a walk, a regular bedtime, time with someone kind. Calm sounds can be a soft way to wind down at night.

    Tool: Cool-down corner: calm sounds and music spreadloveandacceptance.com/soundscapes

  7. Trauma is about what happened, and what it left behind.

    Trauma usually means going through, or seeing, something that threatened life or safety, such as violence, abuse, a serious accident, war, or the sudden death of someone close. It is very common. In surveys across 24 countries, Kessler and colleagues (2017) found about 7 in 10 adults had been through at least one.

    Most people recover over time. A smaller number develop post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), with memories that come back vividly, avoiding reminders, feeling on high alert, and sleep problems. Ordinary hard times and stress hurt too, even when they aren’t trauma in this sense.

    Months after a crash at a wet intersection, Shirin still jumps at the sound of brakes and won’t drive after dark. Her partner has started saying “It’s fine, it’s fine” before she’s even flinched, which she finds both sweet and maddening. Her alarm learned that cars can mean danger and hasn’t unlearned it yet. That is a long way from overreacting. Trauma-focused therapies help many people.

    Dig deeper: what trauma is and isn’t

  8. After something frightening: safety, choice and no pressure.

    After a frightening event, people need safety, practical help, warmth and choice. They don’t need to be made to talk. A review of single-session “debriefing” after trauma by Rose and colleagues (2002) found it did not prevent PTSD, and might make things worse for some. Services that are “trauma-informed” (SAMHSA, 2014) put safety, trust, choice and working together first, and the same ideas help in families, friendships and workplaces.

    Someone had been in Grandma’s house while she was at the store. They took her purse from the drawer and her late husband’s watch. She didn’t want to talk about it, and said so, twice. Her grandson didn’t push. He fixed the lock on the back door, which took him most of the afternoon and two trips to the hardware store, and slept on her sofa. “If you ever want to talk about it, I’m here,” he said in the morning, and went to work. A week later she called him at nine at night and talked for an hour, mostly about the watch.

    Dig deeper: trauma-informed care

  9. Telling one person helps.

    Starting is the hardest part. You don’t need the right words or a name for it. “Something has been off for a while” is enough to begin, and the person listening only has to stay and hear it.

    Zack was too embarrassed to tell anyone about the panic attacks. Then one kept him from getting on the 7:40 for the second week in a row, and he stood on the platform watching it go. That evening he told his sister. She didn’t try to fix it. She asked what it felt like, and from then on she rode the first few stops with him on Mondays. He takes the train to work again now, with a book and a bottle of water for the bad days, and there are still some bad days. When you tell someone, it helps to have three lines ready: what you’ve noticed, how long it has gone on, and what it’s stopping you doing.

    Words to try “I’ve been struggling with my mood, and it’s been going on for a while.” “I don’t need you to fix it. I’d like you to hear it.”

    Dig deeper: what the research says about getting support

Your part, and only your part. You can learn how your alarm works, keep the basics going, take small steps back toward life, and let the people close to you know when it’s more than you can carry. You can’t think your way out of depression by trying harder, and you can’t fix someone else’s. Being kind to yourself, and letting people in, are part of the work.

Monday, 7:30am

Last night you wrote the three worries on the back of an envelope from the gas board and told them, out loud, feeling ridiculous, that they could wait till morning. You slept a bit. Now you breathe out long at the kitchen window and text your neighbor. Hospital at ten and I’m a bit scared, cup of coffee after?

Three hearts and “course.” The appointment is still the appointment. You look at the envelope again, and the weeks of not wanting to see anyone, and add a fourth line at the bottom, smaller than the others. Tell my neighbor about my mood.

If you’re a teenager

Exams, friends, group chats and the future can all land at once, usually at about one in the morning. Tolu is seventeen and can’t sleep the night before her biology exam. She writes the worry down for tomorrow’s ten-minute worry time, plans one small step (ask Mr. Okafor what kind of questions come up) and puts her phone out on the landing, which she hates. The next day she tells her mom, who says, “Why didn’t you wake me?” and it helps more than Tolu expected.

If worry or low mood is stopping you sleeping or going to school most days for a few weeks, tell someone you trust.

You could say “I keep worrying at night. Can I talk it through?” “I don’t need you to fix it. I just need to say it.”

Dig deeper: give worry a time and a place

Two ways to read this

Worry, from both sides

Some people worry out loud, talking it through until it shrinks. Others keep it in, and talking about it too soon makes it grow. If you talk it out, the quiet worrier may need a walk side by side more than a conversation. If you keep it in, the talker isn’t making a fuss. Saying it is how they get it out of their head.

Where the fields meet. Holistic therapies start with the body, which is where worry lives first: slow breathing out, a walk, a regular bedtime. Some of these practices are well studied and some are debated. Aromatherapy adds that the setting matters, a quieter room or softer light. The evidence for particular oils is weak, so the help here is the room, not the bottle.

In everyday life

Living on your own can make worry louder at night and low mood quieter and easier to miss, so one small contact a day is worth protecting, even a two-minute call (see On your own: when it’s lonely, spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own). With a partner, low mood can look like not caring, and anxiety can look like nagging when it’s really a worried mind asking again for reassurance. Describe what’s going on instead of leaving the other person to guess: “I’m low today, and I’m not mad at you.” Children and teenagers get anxious and low too, and calm, routine and listening help them more than reassurance on a loop. A friend who keeps canceling may be struggling. Keep inviting them, with no pressure to say yes.

Grief and depression overlap without being the same thing, and Chapter 8 (page 262) looks at grief on its own terms. At work, a short honest line to a manager often opens up more support than people expect. If you have ADHD, avoidance often looks like putting things off, so make the first step almost silly (“open the envelope”), set a ten-minute timer, or do it with someone else in the room. More in the expanded version (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-16-worry-in-depth).

Common mix-ups

Anxiety doesn’t mean something is wrong with you. It’s a normal alarm. It only becomes a problem when it rings too loud or too often, or starts shrinking your life. Depression isn’t just sadness, and nobody snaps out of it. It affects sleep, energy, thinking and the body as well as mood, and many people recover, with time and support. Not everything bad that happens is trauma in the clinical sense, which usually means a threat to life or safety. Other hard things still hurt and still deserve care, and the word doesn’t need to fit for help to be fair. Talking about trauma right away doesn’t help everyone either. Some people want to and some don’t, forcing it can make things worse, and safety and choice come first.

If you want to help someone else with this

Notice, and ask. “You’ve seemed a bit low lately. How are you doing, really?” opens the door, and after that it helps to listen more than you talk. Don’t argue with the feeling. “Cheer up” and “It could be worse” push people away. “That sounds really hard” keeps them close. Offer something specific, a walk or a meal or a ride somewhere, because a small practical offer is much easier to accept than a big vague one.

If you’re worried someone may be thinking of ending their life, it’s okay to ask them plainly, in your own words. Asking doesn’t put the idea in their head (a review by Dazzi and colleagues, 2014, found no sign that it does). If they say yes, stay with them, listen, and help them tell someone else they trust. And look after yourself too, because supporting someone who is struggling is tiring (see Chapter 12, page 321).

Words you could use “I’m not trying to fix it. I just want you to know I’m here.” “Would it help if I came with you?”

17

Part Three · Chapter 17

Fitting in: groups, influence and culture

Why fitting in pulls so hard, how groups shape what we say and do, how culture and family set the unwritten rules, and how to stay yourself, and disagree kindly, without losing your place, whether the group is a family, a friendship, a team, a faith, a neighborhood or a group chat.

In this chapter

  1. The pull to fit in is old and strong
  2. We go along more than we think
  3. Authority can lead people a long way
  4. “Us and them” forms fast
  5. Norms are the rules nobody wrote down
  6. Cultures differ, and so do people inside them
  7. Every family is a small culture
  8. Online groups pull harder and faster
  9. You can belong and still be yourself
  10. Disagree kindly, and early
  11. If you’re a teenager
  12. Influence, pressure and manipulation
  13. In everyday life
  14. If you want to help someone else with this
  15. Reading on this site
  16. More for your situation

Thursday, 9:20pm

The family group chat is going. Uncle Trevor has posted a joke about your cousin’s new partner, and the laughing faces are stacking up underneath it. Six, then seven, and your mom has done one.

You don’t find it funny. You also don’t want to be the one who can’t take a joke. Your thumb is already over the little laughing face.

We all belong to groups, and we need them. Chapter 5 (page 220) looks at belonging, at why we need each other and how trust grows. This chapter looks at the other side, at how groups pull on us, why we go along, and how to stay true to yourself while staying connected.

A joke in the family chat, quickly. On the surface, a picture and a laughing face. Underneath, the pull not to be the one who spoils it. Underneath that, a norm nobody wrote down. The roots are quiet incentives and ownership and structure. Then slowly, one pull at a time.

  1. The pull to fit in is old and strong.

    For most of human history, being in a group meant surviving, and being left out still feels alarming. In studies by Williams and colleagues (2000), people who were simply left out of an online ball-throwing game, by strangers they would never meet, felt worse and less as if they belonged. So we bend to stay in. We laugh at the jokes, keep quiet, go along.

    At the warehouse, the new guy gets called “Prof” in his first week, because he wears glasses and once, fatally, used the word “ostensibly.” He hates it. He laughs anyway, every time, because more than anything that first month he wants to be one of them. By Christmas he’s down as Prof on the schedule, and has mostly stopped minding.

    Dig deeper: why being left out hurts

  2. We go along more than we think.

    In Solomon Asch’s famous experiments (Asch, 1956), people judged which of three lines matched another line. When the actors around them all gave the same wrong answer, people went along with the group on about a third of the answers, even though the right answer was obvious.

    Many people never went along at all. Later research, such as a review by Bond and Smith (1996), found the effect is real but varies, smaller in more recent studies and larger in cultures that put the group first.

    Groupthink Irving Janis named the moment a close group’s wish to agree crowds out a realistic look at the options. His evidence was case studies of big policy decisions, so it’s an idea more than a measurement, but two of his remedies travel well: the person in charge holds back their view at first, and someone is asked to argue the other side.

    Janis (1972) · Mixed: an influential idea built on case studies

    Everyone in the meeting loved the new schedule. Bukola could see a hole the size of a bus in the Friday cover, and said nothing, because everyone loved the new schedule. Afterward, waiting for the elevator, two colleagues said quietly that they’d had doubts too. All three of them went back to their desks. The schedule started on the Monday and the Friday cover fell over on the first Friday. Writing your own view down before a group decides, and only then listening, makes it a good deal easier to say it.

    Dig deeper: Asch and what came after

  3. Authority can lead people a long way.

    In Stanley Milgram’s experiments (Milgram, 1963), many ordinary people kept giving what they believed were painful electric shocks to a stranger because a man in a lab coat told them to, although no shocks were real. Burger (2009) repeated part of the study safely and found similar results. The studies are also debated. Later researchers, such as Haslam and Reicher (2012), argue that people went along when they believed in the cause, and many people refused.

    Safe to speak up In 51 teams at one manufacturing company, Amy Edmondson found that a shared sense that it was safe to take interpersonal risks went with more learning, and learning went with better performance. Most later studies are correlational, but the idea has held up widely.

    Edmondson (1999) · Strong: a highly replicated idea, though mostly correlational

    On a night shift, a senior doctor tells a staff nurse to give a dose that looks wrong to her. It’s three in the morning, and he is very senior and very tired. She checks anyway, and then says so, and she’s right. Checking was the loyal thing to do. He said thank you, eventually, and sounded as if he meant it.

    Dig deeper: Milgram and its critics

  4. “Us and them” forms fast.

    Part of how we see ourselves comes from our groups, whether that’s a family, a town, a team, a faith or a job. Tajfel and Turner (1979) called this social identity. It brings pride and loyalty. It also makes us quick to favor “us” and to see “them” as all the same, even when the groups are formed on almost nothing.

    Two branches of one family have always sat apart at weddings, and nobody can quite remember why. Something about a christening in 1994. At the most recent one a cousin quietly rearranged the seating plan, and the two sides discovered, over the cheese course, a shared and passionate weakness for terrible music. They were the last ones on the dance floor. They still sit apart at funerals, but it’s a start.

    Dig deeper: social identity

  5. Norms are the rules nobody wrote down.

    Every group has norms about what you wear, how you speak, what you laugh at and what you never mention, and we often guess them wrong. In studies at one university, Prentice and Miller (1993) found that most students were privately less comfortable with heavy drinking than they thought everyone else was. Each person thought they were the odd one out, so everyone kept going along.

    In one office everybody answered emails at midnight, because everybody thought it was expected. Then a manager said, quite casually, in a meeting about something else, that she didn’t expect replies after six. You could almost hear the room breathe out. “We have always done it this way” usually means a rule nobody has checked in years, so it’s worth asking when anyone last did.

    Dig deeper: norms and wrong guesses

  6. Cultures differ, and so do people inside them.

    Cultures differ in how much they put the individual or the group first, which researchers call individualism and collectivism (Hofstede, 1980). In some, standing out is admired, and in others fitting in and keeping harmony are signs of maturity. Labels need care, though. A large review by Oyserman and colleagues (2002) found the differences were smaller and less tidy than often claimed, and individuals vary hugely within every culture.

    Anjali calls her mom every day, sometimes twice. Her partner Sean, who was raised to “do his own thing” and calls his parents on birthdays, thought this was clingy. She thought he was cold, and said so, once, in the car. Each of them was following rules they’d learned before they could tie their shoes. It came out properly over a Sunday dinner at her mom’s, when her mom asked Sean when he’d last called his own mother, and he genuinely couldn’t remember.

    Dig deeper: culture, with care

  7. Every family is a small culture.

    Families have their own norms about how loud people are and how feelings are shown. Some things get talked about and some never do, and there are rules about how you say sorry, if you do. Usually we only notice our family’s rules when we live with someone from a different family. Where your lens came from (page 18) looks at the rules you grew up with.

    Two roommates clashed over the kitchen for most of a semester. In one family you wash up straight after eating. In the other you leave it to soak and do it in the morning. Each thought the other was lazy, or fussy, depending. Neither was. Each was obeying a rule from a kitchen two hundred miles away, and once they’d worked that out they made a third rule, which neither of them likes and both of them keep.

    Dig deeper: family cultures
  8. zqaxunderstandingx17xgroupsxxonlineqz

    Online groups pull harder and faster.

    Group chats, forums and social media make group pressure quicker and more public, because likes and replies show the norm instantly. In a study of over half a million posts, Brady and colleagues (2017) found that messages with more moral and emotional words spread further, mostly among people who already agreed. Outrage travels fast. Quiet doubts stay put.

    A parents’ group chat turned against a teacher after one angry post about a detention, forty messages in an hour. One dad, who knew her a little from the PTA, sent something calm. He said he’d want to hear her side before anyone decided anything. Two other parents agreed with him, and the thread went quiet and stayed quiet. Before you react to a heated post, wait ten minutes. The Chat analyzer (spreadloveandacceptance.com/signal-translator) can help you read a message calmly first.

    Dig deeper: groups online

    Tidbit

    Group chats move fast. Before you send a reply, a helper on the website can read the room with you.

    Tool: Chat analyzer spreadloveandacceptance.com/signal-translator

  9. You can belong and still be yourself.

    Belonging means being accepted as you are, whereas fitting in means changing in order to be accepted (Chapter 5, page 220, says more). Good groups have room for difference. It helps to know your own values, to have more than one group, and to have at least one ally. In Asch’s experiments, when just one other person gave the right answer, going along with the group dropped sharply.

    Rory loves chess and his friends tease him about it, relentlessly. He didn’t drop chess and he didn’t drop his friends. He joined the club that meets in the library on Wednesdays as well, so now he has two groups and neither of them gets to decide who he is. He gets teased, and he’s also county under-16 runner-up, which he mentions more often than strictly necessary.

    Dig deeper: staying yourself
  10. zqaxunderstandingx17xgroupsxxdissentqz

    Disagree kindly, and early.

    You don’t have to choose between going along and starting a war. A kind disagreement is short and calm, it’s about the issue, and it leaves room for other people. Speaking early is easier than speaking late, and a private word often works better than speaking up in front of everyone.

    Some people keep a sentence ready, for exactly this. “I see it a bit differently. Can I say why?” “I’m not comfortable with that joke.” “Can we hear from people who haven’t spoken yet?” Pick the one that sounds most like you and say it out loud a few times in the car, so it’s there when you need it. Say it so it lands (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-09-say-it-so-it-lands) helps with the words.

    Dig deeper: kind dissent

    Professor Puddles

    Disagreeing early and kindly is easier with the words ready. This workpaper helps you say it so it lands.

    Workpaper WP-09: Say it so it lands spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-09

Your part, and only your part. You can notice the pull to fit in, check what you actually think, choose your groups, and say “I see it differently” kindly.

You can’t control what a group does, and you don’t have to stay in a group that keeps asking you to hide who you are or go against what’s right.

Thursday, 9:40pm

You don’t press it, and you message your aunt instead, privately. I know it was meant to be funny but it might hurt if they see it. Could we leave it?

Four minutes later the joke vanishes, and then a message comes through to you. It was only a bit of fun. People are so sensitive these days. At ten thirty your cousin messages to say thank you, because she saw it before it went. At Sunday lunch your aunt passes you the gravy without looking at you, and you don’t yet know whether that’ll pass.

If you’re a teenager

Group chats are where a lot of friendship happens, and a lot of hurt. Mason is fifteen when he finds a photo of himself from gym class being passed around his class chat with comments under it. He doesn’t answer back.

He screenshots it and mutes the chat. Then he tells his sister, and together they tell his homeroom teacher. Then a girl in his class messages him privately to say it wasn’t funny and that she’s sorry she didn’t say anything. Most people in a group chat don’t like what’s happening, and each of them thinks everyone else does.

You could say “I’m not okay with this. Please delete it.” To a friend, “That wasn’t okay. Are you alright?” To an adult, “Something’s happening online and I need help with it.”

Dig deeper: groups online

Influence, pressure and manipulation.

Groups and people shape each other all the time, and most of it is ordinary. You pick up a team’s jokes, a family’s habits and a friend group’s taste in music, and people who care about you will sometimes try to change your mind. That’s influence, and it happens in the open. “Manipulative” is a much stronger word.

For something to be manipulation, these are usually all present:

  • the person wants something they aren’t saying, or gives you information they know is false,
  • they use your feelings, such as guilt, fear or love, to get it,
  • it’s deliberate and it repeats,
  • saying no costs you something, such as your place in the group or warmth from them.

Not enough on its own:

  • persuading you openly, even hard,
  • asking more than once,
  • being disappointed or sad when you say no,
  • hinting instead of asking, which is a normal style in many families and cultures.

A good test is whether you could say “I see it differently” and still be welcome next week. If something feels off, describe the moment rather than the motive: “When you said the others would be let down if I didn’t come, I felt pushed. Can you just ask me straight?”

Two ways to read this

A group, two ways

Some people pick up a group’s unwritten rules in a week without anyone saying them. Others only find a rule out by breaking it. If the rules reach you easily, say them out loud for the people they don’t reach. If they don’t reach you, asking “What’s the rule here?” is a fair question, not a weakness.

Where the fields meet. Politics says every group needs a fair way to decide and a say for everyone. Behavioral science adds that norms are habits the whole group keeps without noticing. The root is quiet incentives, because a group drifts toward whatever it rewards.

In everyday life

Having no group can be as hard as having a pushy one, and groups built around something you enjoy bring belonging along with the activity. Partners bring two families and two sets of rules, which are worth talking about openly before you make your own. Children and teenagers feel peer pressure strongly, and practicing a “no” that saves face helps them. Old family roles, the peacekeeper or the black sheep, can be hard to step out of. At work, when everyone agrees too fast, it helps if whoever leads shares their view last and asks each person to name one risk before deciding (more in the expanded version, spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-17-groups-in-depth). And online, you’re allowed to mute, leave, or take a break from groups that leave you feeling worse.

If you want to help someone else with this

If someone speaks up, back them up, even quietly (“I think that’s a fair point”), because one ally makes a huge difference. In any group you lead, invite the quieter people and the different views by asking what nobody has thought of yet. If someone seems to be going along against their wishes, ask gently, away from the group. And keep an eye on who gets left out of the chats and the plans, so you can bring them in.

Words you could use “I noticed you went quiet when they said that. Are you okay?” “I’d like to hear what you think, even if it’s different.”

  • Authority can lead people a long way.

  • Online groups pull harder and faster.
  • Disagree kindly, and early.

Afterword

Afterword

What the book adds up to

A short look back at the whole book: what each part was for, the few ideas that run through all of it, and where to go next. For anyone who has read some or all of it, in any kind of relationship, or on your own.

In this chapter

  1. Three parts, one idea
  2. Six threads that run through the book
  3. Notice before you judge
  4. Settle before you speak
  5. Say it plainly and kindly
  6. Small steps beat big pushes
  7. Repair is normal
  8. Your part, and only your part
  9. Where to go from here

At a glance

  • Part One was about you: where your lens came from, how you work now, and where you want to go.
  • Part Two was about sharing a life: seeing the work, sharing it fairly, and talking about it kindly.
  • Part Three was about people: how feelings, stress, trust, change, loss, minds and groups work.
  • The thread through all of it: notice before you judge, settle before you speak, say it plainly and kindly, take small steps, repair, and keep everyone safe.

You don’t need to have read every page to get something from this one. If you skipped around, that’s how most people read. The book was written so you could start anywhere, stop anywhere and pick it up again.

Three parts, one idea

Part One: Yourself (page 18) looked at the lens you see through: what life taught you, how your mind and body work now, and what matters to you next. It came first because everything else depends on it. You can’t share a life well if you don’t know how you work.

Part Two: Between us (page 62) looked at the quiet work of running a shared life, a home, a family, a team, and how to see it, share it fairly and talk about it without blame. Each chapter came with a worksheet, because ideas only help when they turn into something you do.

Part Three: Understanding people (page 160) looked at how people work: feelings, stress, how we see each other, how we talk, why we need each other, how we change, our worth, loss, different minds, values, healing, helping, anger, personality, love, worry and low mood, and the pull of groups.

Underneath all three is one idea: most of what goes wrong between people is understandable, and much of it can be put right. Mostly by seeing a little more clearly and acting a little more kindly, which is easier than trying to be perfect.

Six threads that run through the book

The book rests on five big ideas, set out at the front: see the whole load; fix the setup, not the person; read your state first; tune how you send and receive; and notice the quiet incentives. The six threads below are the same ideas said as everyday habits. The table after the list shows how they match.

  1. Notice before you judge.

    A sharp word, a forgotten job or a quiet evening usually has a reason: tiredness, a full stress tank, a different family rule, a different kind of mind. Asking “What might be going on?” before “What’s wrong with them?” changes most conversations. See Chapter 3 (page 189).

  2. Settle before you speak.

    When the body is flooded, nobody listens well. Slow the breath, step away with a time to come back, then talk. See Chapter 2 (page 174) and Chapter 13 (page 334).

  3. Say it plainly and kindly.

    What happened, how it felt, what you’re asking for. Clear is kind, for everyone. See Chapter 4 (page 203).

  4. Small steps beat big pushes.

    One job with one owner. One walk. One message. One step on the ladder. Change that lasts is usually small and repeated. See Chapter 6 (page 234).

    Tidbit

    That’s the end. Pick one small thing from the book and try it this week, and leave the rest for later.

    Tool: Ten-minute start spreadloveandacceptance.com/start-in-10-minutes

  5. Repair is normal.

    Everyone gets it wrong. What keeps relationships going is coming back: a short, real apology and a plan for next time. See Chapter 11 (page 307).

  6. Your part, and only your part.

    You can change what you do. You can’t make anyone else change. You can change what you bring to the next conversation, and that is usually where things start to move.

How the six threads match the five big ideas

ThreadBig idea
Notice before you judgeSee the whole load; fix the setup, not the person
Settle before you speakRead your state first
Say it plainly and kindlyTune how you send and receive
Small steps beat big pushesFix the setup, not the person; notice the quiet incentives

Your part, and only your part.Not one of the five: the frame around all of them

Where to go from here

  • On your own: The self path (spreadloveandacceptance.com/self-path) turns Part One into a few steps you can take at your own pace.
  • With someone: The six-week program (spreadloveandacceptance.com/prog-01) turns Part Two into one small step a week, for a home, a family or a team. Miss a week? Pick up anywhere.
  • With a question: Ask Professor Puddles (spreadloveandacceptance.com/ask), the site’s private helper, about anything in the book.
  • Want the evidence? The research behind this book lists every study the book draws on, in plain words, with how strong the evidence is.
  • Read it again, differently: every chapter has an expanded version, and the contents (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/) lists them all.

Any day, any time

You close the book. Nothing at home has changed yet. But maybe next time a sharp word lands, you’ll wonder what’s under it. Maybe you’ll breathe out before you answer. Maybe you’ll say the thing plainly, or say sorry sooner. That’s all this book was ever asking for: a little more understanding, a little more often. Thank you for reading.

This book is general education, not therapy.

Professor Puddles

zqnumbersqz

How the numbers work

Every number in this book is arithmetic you can do with a pencil. None of them is a test, a diagnosis or a verdict on anyone: they describe a week, a load or a way of sharing work. The weights and cut-offs are this book’s own rules of thumb, not research findings, and you are free to disagree with them. The worked examples are the book’s own, so you can check them against the chapters.

Two habits run through all of them. Scores are rounded to two decimal places before their band is read, so the number you see and the words you see always agree. And nobody’s score is ever worked out for them: if someone’s own answer is missing, the total waits.

The stress tank: How much are you carrying?

You score five things from 0 (not at all) to 4 (very true), about the last day or two: sleep debt, workload elsewhere, unresolved conflict, your physical state, and time pressure today.

tank = (sleep + workload + conflict + body + time) ÷ 20

The answer runs from 0 to 1, and higher means fuller. Under 0.30 is light, 0.30 up to 0.60 medium, and 0.60 or more high. (The worksheet splits each band in two for its words: very light under 0.15, light, medium on the lighter side under 0.45, medium on the heavier side, high under 0.80, and very high from 0.80.) Your battery is the other side of the same thing, the energy you have left, so a full tank means a low battery. The battery is a picture in words, not a second score.

Worked example Rosa, from Part Two, Chapter III, page 109, scores sleep 3, workload 4, conflict 1, body 2 and time 3.

3 + 4 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 13; 13 ÷ 20 = 0.65, which is in the high band.

Two or more of you: each person scores only themselves, and the shared figure is the plain average of everyone’s own scores. If any one person is at 0.60 or more, treat that as the headline, whatever the average says.

Coming back after a pause (the Calm-Down Kit): if you like numbers, take the score again after a calming round. Under 0.50, go back at the time you named. From 0.50 to 0.59, take another round. At 0.60 or more after two rounds, put it off to a named time. The kit’s line sits at 0.50 on purpose: you don’t need an empty tank to come back, just one less than half full.

My weather today: the room in your day

My weather today shows words, not numbers: a sky (clear, gusty or fogged in) and how much room you have today. Behind the words sits a rough tally from 0 to 100, where higher means a heavier day. You only see it if you check “Show the numbers behind this.”

What you pickedAdds
The sky: clear, gusty, fogged in0, 26, 34
The pressure: light, building, heavy (skipped: 6)0, 10, 20
Last night’s sleep: properly rested, about enough, short night, barely slept (skipped: 6)0, 2, 10, 18
People load: barely any, a normal amount, a lot, nonstop (skipped: 4)0, 3, 9, 14
Ground conditions (hungry, thirsty, in pain and so on)4 each, up to 14
What’s blowing in (work, money, health and so on)3 each, up to 10

Under 45 reads as lots of room today, 45 to 64 as some room, and 65 or more as very little room.

Worked example Joel, from Part One, Now, page 33, picks gusty, building pressure, a short night, a lot of people time, one ground condition (hungry) and one thing blowing in (work).

26 + 10 + 10 + 9 + 4 + 3 = 62: some room today, with less than usual, so the forecast says to go gently and settle first.

Workload balance: how evenly the hours are shared

Two people. Work out each person’s share of the logged hours as a percentage.

balance = 1 − (the difference between the two percentages ÷ 100)

50/50 scores 1.00; one person doing everything scores 0.00. It doesn’t matter which of you does more. Balance ignores the total, which is one reason the stress tank sits beside it.

Worked example Rosemary logs 14 hours and Ken 10 (Part Two, Chapter II, page 90). Out of 24 hours, that is 58.3% and 41.7%.

1 − (58.3 − 41.7) ÷ 100 = 1 − 0.167 = 0.83

Three or more people, or an agreed split. The same idea, said more generally: how much of the week would have to change hands to reach the target, compared with the most that ever could.

each share = that person’s hours ÷ everyone’s hours target = an even share (1 ÷ number of people), or the split you agreed moved = ½ × the sum of every |share − target| most = 1 − the smallest target share balance = 1 − moved ÷ most

Worked example Three partners log 15, 9 and 6 hours (Chapter II, page 90): shares 0.50, 0.30 and 0.20, against a third each.

moved = ½ × (0.167 + 0.033 + 0.133) = 0.167, most = 1 − 0.333 = 0.667, and balance = 1 − 0.167 ÷ 0.667 = 0.75. In hours, 0.167 × 30 = 5 hours a week would change hands for an even split.

With an agreed split, use it as the target: co-parents who agreed 60/40 and log 12 and 8 hours score 1.00.

Ownership: does every job have a name?

ownership = jobs with a named owner ÷ all the jobs on the list

The calculator counts a job as owned when it has one named owner. A backstop, the person who notices if it slipped, is a good habit and has its own column, but the score only needs the owner. The starter jobs on the worksheet don’t count until you give them an owner or change them. Never raise the score by deleting the jobs nobody owns: they are exactly what the score is there to show.

Worked example Rosemary and Ken list 12 regular jobs, and 9 have an owner: 9 ÷ 12 = 0.75.

Who carries more of the list. A score of 1.00 can still mean one person owns everything, so One owner per job also shows each person’s share of the list, with each job weighted by how often it comes around and how big it is:

weight of a job = how often × size how often: daily 5, weekly 1, ongoing 1, monthly 0.25, as needed 0.1 size: small 0.5, medium 1 (the default), big 2 (or, where you gave the hours each time: hours ÷ 0.5) share = the weights of that person’s jobs ÷ the weights of all the jobs

A job you decide together counts the same for each of you; on a list for two homes it shows as “Together” instead.

Worked example One person owns the cooking (daily, medium: 5) and the bills (monthly, medium: 0.25). The other owns the laundry (weekly, big: 2) and the car (as needed, medium: 0.1). Each owns two jobs, but 5.25 ÷ 7.35 = 71% of the list’s weight sits with the first person, and 29% with the second.

Who’s carrying more right now. Who did what flags the busiest person when their share of the logged minutes (or of the work done without being asked) is at least half, and at least 20 points over an even share: 70% or more for two people, 53% or more for three. In the example in the Preface, page 62, one partner did 105 of the 115 minutes that were noticed and handled without anyone asking: 91%, so the sheet says so.

The setup score: can the way you share the work last?

setup score = balance × 0.40 + ownership × 0.35 + (1 − the average tank score) × 0.25

The weights add up to 1, so the score runs from 0 to 1, and here higher means the setup is working better, the opposite of the tank score. The tank is the only part that counts against the score, which is why it enters as 1 − tank. 0.70 or more reads as working well (the “Who does what?” page says “holding”). From 0.40 up to 0.70 it reads as needs a look (“drifting”), and below 0.40 as needs a rethink, together. It is a snapshot of the setup, never a probability and never a verdict on anyone.

Worked example Rosemary and Ken (Chapter II, page 90): balance 0.83, ownership 0.75, and their own tank scores are 0.45 and 0.30, an average of 0.375.

0.83 × 0.40 + 0.75 × 0.35 + (1 − 0.375) × 0.25 = 0.333 + 0.263 + 0.156 = 0.75: working well.

The shortfall is what each part could have earned minus what it did earn: balance 0.40 − 0.333 = 0.067, ownership 0.35 − 0.263 = 0.088, and tank 0.25 − 0.156 = 0.094. The biggest shortfall is the tank, which usually eases outside the chore list (more sleep, a lighter week elsewhere). The calculator’s “what would help most” is the single change with the biggest gain: handing about 2 hours a week from Rosemary to Ken would take balance from 0.83 to 1.00, worth 0.067. Naming one more job’s owner would be worth 0.029, and a tank score lower by 0.10 on average 0.025.

The overall score adds a fourth part, retuning: of the moments that landed badly this week, how many you retuned before answering.

overall = balance × 0.35 + ownership × 0.30 + (1 − tank) × 0.20 + retuning × 0.15 (no rough moments this week: leave retuning out, and divide the first three parts by 0.85)

In Chapter II’s first worked example (balance 0.60, ownership 0.80, an average tank score of 0.40, and 3 of 5 rough moments retuned): 0.21 + 0.24 + 0.12 + 0.09 = 0.66.

The 30-day look-back: what shifted this month?

The look-back splits the last 30 days into four weeks (the first takes the first ten days). For each part you filled in (balance, ownership, the stress tank, and last-minute rescues), it compares the start of the month with the end:

start = the average of weeks 1 and 2 end = the average of weeks 3 and 4 it shifted if end − start is 0.10 or more (balance, ownership, tank), or 1 a week or more (rescues); anything smaller didn’t shift

One next step: a part that moved the wrong way comes first (the biggest move for its size). Otherwise, the first of these that is still true at the end: ownership under 0.70, balance under 0.70, 2 or more rescues a week, or anyone’s tank at 0.60 or more. If none is, keep the same rhythm and look again in 30 days.

Hours to change hands over the month: for each person, the hours they did minus their share of everyone’s hours, added up week by week. Half the sum of those gaps (ignoring the minus signs) is how many hours would change hands to make the month even.

Worked example Suppose Rosemary and Ken keep going for a month (made up, like them). Their four weeks look like this. Hours: 14 and 10, 15 and 9, 13 and 11, 12 and 12. Jobs with an owner: 9, 9, 11 and 11 of 12. Rosemary’s tank: 0.45, 0.50, 0.40 and 0.35, and Ken’s 0.30 every week. Rescues: 3, 2, 1 and 1.

PartStart (weeks 1–2)End (weeks 3–4)ChangeReads as
Balance(0.83 + 0.75) ÷ 2 = 0.79(0.92 + 1.00) ÷ 2 = 0.96+0.17Better
Ownership0.750.92+0.17Better
Average tank score0.390.34−0.05About the same
Rosemary’s own tank0.480.38−0.10Lighter
Rescues a week2.51−1.5Fewer

Three of the four parts shifted, all for the better, and nothing is left on the watch list, so the next step is to keep the rhythm. The setup score went from 0.73 to 0.87. Over the month Rosemary did 54 hours and Ken 42, so 6 hours would have changed hands for an even month.

On your own: is your week sustainable?

The “Who does what?” page’s “just me” view adds up the hours your week is spoken for (jobs, the thinking work, care and so on) and compares them with a waking week of about 112 hours (16 waking hours, 7 days).

share = the hours spoken for ÷ 112

Under 50% reads as sustainable, 50% up to 70% as full but workable, and 70% or more as stretched. For example, 50 hours spoken for is 45%, which leaves real room; 80 hours is 71%, a lot to keep up week after week.

All of these are this book’s own ways of putting things into numbers. They have not been tested in research studies, and they shouldn’t be quoted as findings. The free calculators on the website do the arithmetic for you, and each one has a “How is this worked out?” note.

zqglossaryqz

Words used in this book

The book’s own words, each in one plain sentence. More at spreadloveandacceptance.com/glossary.

Alexithymia
Finding it hard to notice, name or describe your own feelings. It is a trait on a scale, not an illness, and it is more common in some autistic people. Naming body signals first can help.
Backstop
The second name on a job: someone who notices if it slipped and checks in kindly. Not a supervisor. A job counts as owned once it has an owner; the backstop is a good habit on top.
Battery
Your battery is how much energy you have left today. Full means you have room to spare; low means you’re running on empty. “How much are you carrying?” measures the other side of it, how full your stress tank is: a fuller tank means a lower battery. For example: After a poor night and a long workday, your stress tank is nearly full and your battery is low, so a small request feels big.
A bid
A bid is any small reach for attention or connection, like “look at this,” a sigh or a joke. For example: They show you a photo of a dog. Looking and smiling back is turning toward it.
Calm-Down Kit
Your Calm-Down Kit is your own short list of what settles your body, chosen ahead of time so you don’t have to think when you’re wound up. For example: A glass of cold water, a walk to the corner, and three long breaths out.
Check-in
A check-in is a short, planned talk that keeps small things small. The daily one takes about ninety seconds, with no debating. For example: “Load today: heavy. Thank you for the dishes. One small thing: the car. My ask: could you fill it up?”
Complacency
Complacency is what happens when something has worked for a long time and you stop checking on it. It comes from a setup nobody has looked at lately, and it says nothing about laziness or love. For example: “How was your day?” “Fine.” Months go by and nobody has asked a real question.
Double empathy
The idea, from the autistic researcher Damian Milton, that misunderstandings between autistic and non-autistic people run both ways: each finds the other hard to read, so neither side is simply “missing” something.
Drift
Drift is how two people slowly fall out of step when nobody checks in, even when nothing is wrong. For example: Three busy weeks, no real talk, and small things start to feel big.
Flooded
Flooded means being so wound up that listening stops working for a while. The kind thing is a short pause with a time to come back. For example: “I need twenty minutes. Can we talk again at eight?”
Frequency
Your frequency is your natural pace: how fast you decide, talk, reply and recover. For example: One person answers a text in a minute. The other answers at the end of the day. Neither is wrong.
Gatekeeping
Holding on to how a home or child-care job must be done, so the other person steps back. Researchers first described it in mothers (“maternal gatekeeping”), but anyone can do it.
Groupthink
When a close group wants agreement so much that doubts go unsaid and a poor decision goes ahead. Irving Janis named it in 1972.
If-then plan
A small plan written as “If this happens, then I will do that,” which makes a new habit easier to start (Peter Gollwitzer).
A kind no
A kind no says what you can and can’t do right now, without blaming anyone. For example: “I can’t take that on this week. I could help on Saturday.”
Kinship care
When a grandparent, aunt, older sibling or family friend raises a child whose parents can’t.
The ladder
Three everyday states: calm and connected, revved up, running on empty. My weather today calls them clear, gusty and fogged in. A best guess about your state, not a measurement.
Ledger
A notebook where you write down what happened, so you can look at it calmly later. The book works the same way: see what is really going on, without blame, then change one small thing.
The load
The load is all the work of a shared life, including the thinking, planning and remembering that nobody sees. For example: Buying the gift is one job. Remembering the birthday, picking the gift and wrapping it are three more.
Masking
Masking is hiding the way you’re wired to fit in, which can be very tiring over time. For example: Forcing eye contact and rehearsing small talk all day, then needing the evening to recover.
Mental load
The noticing, planning and remembering behind running a shared life: knowing the shoes are too small, booking the appointment, keeping the list. It is real work, even though nobody sees it.
Monotropism
A theory of autistic attention: attention gathers deeply on a few things at a time, rather than spreading thinly across many. Switching away can take real effort.
My weather today
My weather today is a one-minute check on your own conditions today, like sleep, stress and energy: Clear means calm and connected, Gusty means revved up, and Fogged in means running on empty. For example: Short night, busy day: the forecast says to keep big talks for tomorrow.
Owner (one owner per job)
The owner of a job is the one person who makes sure it gets done from start to finish, so nobody has to keep asking. For example: Sam owns the recycling: noticing it’s full, taking it out and buying the bags.
Parallel parenting
Co-parenting with as little direct contact as possible: each home runs its own way, and messages stay short, polite and about the children.
Pressure
Pressure, in My weather today, is how much you were already carrying today: light, building or heavy. Behind the forecast sits a rough tally from 0 to 100; under 45 leaves room in the day, 65 or more means go gently. It is a reading of what you told it, not a score or a grade. For example: A pressure of 40 leaves room in the day; 75 means go gently and leave big things for later.
Prolonged grief
Grief that stays intense and gets in the way of daily life for a long time after a death (6 to 12 months or more, depending on the guideline).
Psychological safety
A shared sense in a group or team that you can speak up, ask a question or admit a mistake without being punished or embarrassed (Amy Edmondson).
Repair
A repair is anything that stops a tense moment from getting worse, like a joke, a softer tone or “Can we start over?” For example: “I said that badly. What I meant was…”
Retune
To retune is to notice you’ve fallen out of step with someone and adjust together: slower, softer, or at a better time. For example: “Can we start that again? I came in too fast.”
The rulebook from home
The rulebook from home is the unwritten set of rules you grew up with, about love, upset, chores and rest, that you may still expect others to follow. For example: “Whoever notices the mess cleans it” was the rule at home, so a messy kitchen feels like “It’s always me.”
Rumination
Going over the same worry or regret again and again without getting closer to an answer.
Second arrow
The extra pain we add on top of a hard moment, such as being angry at ourselves for being sad. The first arrow is the event; the second is what we tell ourselves about it (a Buddhist image).
Setup score
The one number from Is the setup working for everyone?: balance, ownership and stress added up with weights (0.40, 0.35 and 0.25), from 0 to 1. 0.70 and up is working well, 0.40 to 0.69 needs a look, under 0.40 needs a rethink, together. It judges the setup, never a person.
Static
Static is the crackle between two people when the words are fine but the tone, pace or timing doesn’t match. For example: You ask “When will you do it?” calmly. They hear pressure. Nobody meant harm, but it crackles.
Stress tank
How much stress you are already carrying, from How much are you carrying?, scored from 0 (empty) to 1 (full). Under 0.30 is light, 0.30 to 0.59 medium, 0.60 and up high. A fuller tank means less room to take more on. (Your battery is the other side of it: energy left.)
Turning toward
Turning toward means answering someone’s small bids for attention, even briefly, instead of missing or brushing them off. For example: “Oh, that’s a funny one!” instead of scrolling on.
Unbilled debt
Unbilled debt is the work of a shared life that got done but was never noticed or thanked. For example: You remembered the dentist appointment, and nobody knew there was anything to remember.
Wave Code
Four letters from the style quiz in How you connect, one for each of four preferences about how you take in and send words. Each letter shows where you lean on a dial today: a shorthand for preferences, not a personality type.
Window of tolerance
The range in which you can feel strong feelings and still think and talk. Above it you are flooded or revved up; below it you shut down. A phrase from the psychiatrist Dan Siegel.
Wired differently
Being wired differently means your brain works in a less common way, such as being autistic, ADHD, dyslexic or highly sensitive, which changes how words land. For example: A hint like “the trash is full” may be heard as a plain fact, not a request.
Wiring
Your wiring is the way your brain and senses take in words, sound, change and people. It stays the same from day to day. For example: Some people need a plan in writing. Others think best out loud.
Workpaper
A page you fill in, on your own or with someone, about your own week or your own side. Every workpaper is free to print or to fill out on the website. For example: “Who did what” is a week’s log of who did what.
Your lens
Your lens is the set of understandings about yourself, other people and what they owe you that you picked up growing up and still use without noticing. For example: “Rest is earned” can feel like plain fact, until you notice it was your family’s rule.
